title: Extreme Harness Engineering for Token Billionaires: 1M LOC, 1B toks/day, 0% human code, 0% human review
author: Ryan Lopopolo (OpenAI), interviewed by swyx & Vibhu

metadata.author: Ryan Lopopolo (OpenAI), interviewed by swyx & Vibhu
metadata.title: Extreme Harness Engineering for Token Billionaires: 1M LOC, 1B toks/day, 0% human code, 0% human review

sections.tldr: OpenAI's Frontier team built a 1M+ LOC internal product over 5 months with **zero human-written code** — all via Codex agents. The key insight is that the bottleneck has shifted from code generation to human attention: the harness (tooling, context, skills, observability) is now the engineering surface, not the code itself. They open-sourced the orchestration layer as **Symphony**, an Elixir-based system that removes humans from the agent loop entirely for PR lifecycle, code review, and deployment.
sections.whats_new:
The article reveals OpenAI's internal "Dark Factory" paradigm in detail for the first time. Several non-obvious claims:

1. **Post-merge review only.** Human code review happens *after* merge, not before. The agent autonomously pushes PRs, waits for CI, resolves merge conflicts, handles flakes, and merges. Humans do spot-checks on a representative sample, like a tech lead over a 500-person org — not like a reviewer approving individual PRs.

2. **Build times are agent-critical invariants.** When GPT-5.3 introduced background shells, it became less patient with blocking builds. The team had to retool from Make → Bazel → Turbo → NX within a single project to keep builds under 1 minute. The agent doesn't tolerate latency the way a human does.

3. **Ghost libraries over shared source code.** Software can be distributed as a spec rather than as code. A coding agent reproduces the full system from a high-fidelity spec, then a review loop between agents tightens the spec until it faithfully reproduces the upstream. This is a new distribution primitive.

4. **Self-improving via trajectory distillation.** The team collects all agent session logs across the team, runs daily agent loops over them to discover cross-team improvements, and reflects those back into the repository's skill files. The agent system has a built-in flywheel for institutional knowledge accumulation.
sections.counterintuitive_claims:
- "It would be borderline negligent if you aren't spending >1B tokens/day" (~$2-3k/day) on coding agents.
- Building an internal observability tool for debugging was *wrong* — it kept humans in the loop unnecessarily when Codex could just analyze the trace directly.
- The agent *chose* Elixir for Symphony because Beam/OTP's process supervision maps naturally to agent orchestration. The human's Elixir proficiency is irrelevant when the human writes no code.
sections.steelman: This is the most concrete, production-grounded description of a fully autonomous software development pipeline to date. The key steelman: **if the harness is good enough — skills, docs, tests, observability, guardrails — the model's code quality converges with "good engineering" because every non-functional requirement is prompt-injected into context.** The human's role shifts permanently from author to systems architect. The evidence is real: 1M LOC, 1500+ PRs, shipped to internal users, across multiple model generations (GPT-5 through 5.4). This isn't a weekend demo.
sections.steelman_rebuttal:
1. **Greenfield privilege.** Ryan explicitly acknowledges this was a "completely greenfield repository" — no legacy code, no pre-existing architectural opinions, no external API contracts. Most enterprise codebases don't have this luxury.
2. **Electron app, not infrastructure.** They're building a native application with manual release cycles, not a 99.99% SLA backend. The tolerance for agent errors is higher when you're not doing continuous deploy to production.
3. **Internal product with internal users.** The tolerance for broken builds and reworked PRs is much higher when the users are your colleagues, not paying customers.
4. **Model cost at scale is unclear.** $2-3k/day for a 3-person team is one thing. For a 500-person org, that's $500K-$1.5M/day in token spend, plus the cost of building and maintaining the harness itself.
sections.forward_looking_hypotheses:
- **Agent-legible code will diverge from human-legible code.** Software architecture will be optimized for model context windows, not human reading patterns. 500-package monorepos make no sense for 3 humans, but perfect sense for 150 concurrent agents.
- **Dependencies will be inlined.** Brett Taylor's prediction: software dependencies are going away. If code is free, it's cheaper to vendor and customize than to manage transitive dependency trees.
- **Symphony-like orchestration becomes infrastructure.** Every enterprise will need a "Frontier-style" dashboard to manage thousands of concurrent agents. Multiple unicorns will emerge in this space.
- **The harness/training tension is load-bearing.** Ryan notes the tension between investing in better harnesses vs. better model training. His view: build the harness "on policy" — using only patterns the model already generates — so harness improvements don't fight model improvements.
sections.technical_insights:
- **Skills architecture:** 6 total skill files for the entire codebase. Core beliefs.md includes team composition, product vision, customer segments. Quality score and tech tracker are markdown tables that Codex uses as self-review scaffolds.
- **Agent code review protocol:** Review agents are instructed to "bias toward merging" and not surface anything below P2 priority. Code authors can push back on review feedback. This prevents the thrash loop where two agents endlessly debate.
- **Rasterization for UI perception:** When agents need to verify UI layouts, they rasterize screenshots to ASCII and feed both the image and the ASCII to the agent — dual-channel perception.
- **CLI-first for token efficiency:** They wrap verbose CLI output in scripts that suppress passing tests and only surface failures. Agents don't need to see 500 passing test suites.
sections.second_order_implications:
1. **Engineering hiring shifts from coding to systems design.** If the Frontier pattern scales, the most valuable engineers are the ones who can design the harness, define the invariants, and architect for agent-legibility — not the ones who write the fastest PRs.
2. **SaaS DevTools face existential risk from ghost libraries.** If teams can reproduce Datadog-level observability from a spec in an afternoon, the value proposition of managed DevTools shrinks to "scale testing and security" — which many teams don't need.
3. **Compounding correctness is the real RSI.** This is not recursive self-improvement in the "AI builds smarter AI" sense — it's institutional knowledge compounding via trajectory distillation. The system gets better at *being a team*, not at *being a model*. This is the practical, deployable version of RSI that Tim should track. (Connects to `kb/seed/8d617b70e44d-recursive-self-improvement-discourse-clarified.md` — the distinction between "several overlapping debates" in RSI.)
sections.my_take:
This is the single most important piece on agent deployment I've seen in 2026. Not because of the zero-human-code headline (which is provocative but greenfield-dependent), but because it describes **the organizational operating system for agent-native development** in granular, reproducible detail. The Symphony spec, the skill architecture, the trajectory distillation loop, the post-merge review model — these are concrete, stealable patterns.

The OpenAI → Anthropic competitive dynamic is fascinating here. OpenAI's Frontier is the enterprise deployment platform; Anthropic's Managed Agents is the rival. But the harness engineering patterns Ryan describes are model-agnostic. The real moat is the organizational knowledge encoded in skills, specs, and the feedback loop — not the model.

Tim should watch: (1) whether Anthropic's Managed Agents platform ships Symphony-equivalent orchestration, (2) whether the ghost library primitive gains traction as a new open-source distribution model, and (3) whether enterprise token spend per engineer becomes a standard productivity metric.
sections.talking_points:
- **"The bottleneck isn't code generation — it's human attention."** OpenAI's own team runs 0% human code review and post-merge only spot checks. If that's where the frontier lab is, enterprise teams clinging to PR approval workflows are leaving 10x productivity on the table. (Good for founder chats.)

- **"Ghost libraries are the new open source."** Software distributed as a spec, not as code. A coding agent reproduces the full system locally, then a review loop tightens spec-to-implementation fidelity. This could make dependency management obsolete. (Good for VC roundtables on DevTools.)

- **"Agent-legible code is architecturally different from human-legible code."** 500 NPM packages for a 3-person team is absurd for humans but optimal for 150 concurrent agents. The software architecture of the future is designed for model context windows, not human comprehension. (Good for X.)

- **"The real RSI is institutional knowledge compounding."** Not AI building smarter AI — agents collecting session logs, distilling cross-team patterns, and encoding them back as skills. The system gets better at being a team, not at being a model. That's the deployable version of recursive self-improvement. (Good for investor calls.)

- **"$2-3k/day in tokens per engineer is the new baseline."** If you're spending less, you're under-leveraging agents. That reframes AI infrastructure as an operating expense per head, not a project cost. (Good for LP updates on portfolio company AI adoption.)

title: AI Cybersecurity After Mythos: The Jagged Frontier
author: Stanislav Fort

metadata.author: Stanislav Fort
metadata.title: AI Cybersecurity After Mythos: The Jagged Frontier

sections.tldr: **The moat in AI cybersecurity is the system, not the model.** AISLE tested Anthropic's Mythos showcase vulnerabilities on small, cheap, open-weights models and found they recovered much of the same analysis. Eight out of eight models detected the flagship FreeBSD exploit — including a 3.6B-parameter model at $0.11/M tokens. The cybersecurity capability frontier is "jagged": rankings reshuffle completely across tasks, with no stable best model.
sections.whats_new:
**This is the first rigorous empirical challenge to Anthropic's Mythos cybersecurity narrative with reproducible data.** While Anthropic presented Mythos as a singular capability breakthrough justifying restricted access, Fort's team decomposed the cybersecurity pipeline into modular stages (scanning → detection → triage → patching → exploitation) and showed that most stages are broadly accessible with current cheap models. The key insight: once a well-designed scaffold narrows the search to the relevant code, detection-grade capability is commoditized. A 3.6B-parameter model correctly identified a 17-year-old FreeBSD remote code execution vulnerability, computed the buffer overflow math, and assessed it as critical — in a single zero-shot API call.

The "jagged frontier" finding is the structural contribution: Qwen3 32B scores a perfect 9.8 CVSS on FreeBSD but confidently declares OpenBSD SACK code "robust to such scenarios." GPT-OSS-120b recovers a full exploit chain for OpenBSD but fails a trivial OWASP false-positive test. There is no smooth capability gradient — rankings reshuffle completely across tasks.
sections.counterintuitive_claims:
**Small open models outperformed most frontier models on a basic security reasoning task (OWASP false-positive discrimination).** GPT-OSS-20b (3.6B active params, $0.11/M tokens) correctly traced data flow that Claude Sonnet 4.5 and every GPT-4.1/5.4 model got wrong. The pattern showed near-inverse scaling: smaller, cheaper models outperformed larger, more expensive ones. This directly contradicts the assumption that cybersecurity capability scales smoothly with model size.

**A thousand adequate detectives outperform one brilliant detective.** Because cheap models handle most detection work, you can deploy them broadly across an entire codebase rather than judiciously deploying one expensive model. The economics flip: coverage × cheapness > per-token intelligence for defensive use cases.
sections.steelman:
**Fort's strongest argument is the decomposition.** By separating the cybersecurity pipeline into detection, triage, exploitation reasoning, and creative exploit engineering, he shows that Mythos's genuine advantage lives in only one stage: the creative engineering step (e.g., splitting an exploit across 15 sequential RPC requests to work within a 304-byte constraint). Detection, triage, and even exploitation reasoning are broadly accessible. Since Project Glasswing is ostensibly about *defense* (finding and patching bugs), the most relevant capabilities are already democratized.

The sensitivity vs. specificity analysis (added April 9) strengthens this further: most models have 100% detection sensitivity but terrible specificity on patched code — only GPT-OSS-120b reliably recognizes when a bug is fixed. This proves the *system* around the model (triage, validation, maintainer trust) is where production value lives, not raw model capability.
sections.steelman_rebuttal:
**Fort's methodology has a significant scoping limitation he acknowledges but undersells.** All tests provided models with the isolated vulnerable function plus contextual hints. The hardest part of Mythos's achievement is finding which of hundreds of thousands of files to examine in the first place — the broad-spectrum scanning that turns a full codebase into a tractable search. This is precisely where scale and long-context reasoning might matter most, and it's untested here.

The "jagged frontier" finding may also be an artifact of the test suite's small size. With only three tasks, sample noise dominates. A systematic study across dozens of vulnerability types might reveal smoother scaling in some categories while confirming jaggedness in others.

Additionally, the AISLE team has a commercial interest in this argument: they sell an AI cybersecurity system that works with *any* model, so demonstrating model-agnosticism is directly on-thesis for their business. The analysis is rigorous, but the incentive structure is worth noting — just as Anthropic has incentives to hype Mythos's exclusivity.
sections.technical_insights:
**The three-test methodology is well-designed for revealing jaggedness:**

1. **OWASP false-positive** — trivial Java snippet where user input is discarded via list manipulation. Tests data-flow tracing. Small models excel; most frontier models fail. Near-inverse scaling.
2. **FreeBSD NFS detection (CVE-2026-4747)** — 17-year-old buffer overflow. Tests pattern recognition. Fully commoditized: 8/8 models detect it, including 3.6B-parameter model.
3. **OpenBSD SACK analysis** — 27-year-old signed integer overflow requiring mathematical reasoning about `SEQ_LT`/`SEQ_GT` macro wraparound. Tests deep reasoning. Only GPT-OSS-120b (5.1B active) recovers the full chain.

The sensitivity/specificity analysis on patched vs. unpatched FreeBSD is particularly revealing: 100% sensitivity across all models, but only 1 of 6 models reliably avoids false-positives on patched code. This is exactly the verification problem that pervades the broader AI agent landscape — see [verification-and-evaluation topic](../../topics/verification-and-evaluation.md).

The exploitation reasoning results are surprisingly strong for cheap models: DeepSeek R1 proposed a more pragmatic exploit strategy than Mythos's actual approach (escalate to root via minimal ROP chain, then do file operations in userland, vs. Mythos's 15-round kernel-mode SSH key writer).
sections.key_assumptions:
- That scaffolding quality (targeting, iterative deepening, validation pipelines) matters as much as or more than per-token model intelligence for production cybersecurity.
- That defensive use cases (Project Glasswing's stated purpose) don't require the creative exploit engineering where Mythos genuinely separates.
- That the three tested vulnerabilities are representative of the broader cybersecurity landscape.
sections.second_order_implications:
**If the moat is the system and not the model, then Anthropic's restricted-access model for Mythos is suboptimal for its stated defensive mission.** More organizations running cheaper models with good scaffolds would patch more bugs than fewer organizations waiting for Mythos access. This reframes Project Glasswing from a capability demonstration to a coalition-building exercise — the value is the 40 organizations committing to AI-assisted security, not the specific model they use.

**The jagged frontier finding has implications well beyond cybersecurity.** If capability rankings reshuffle completely across tasks even within a single domain, then the "best model" question is meaningless without specifying the task distribution. This supports the emerging consensus that harness/scaffold design matters more than model selection — directly extending the thesis in [blog-latentspace-extreme-harness-engineering](../2026/04/11/blog-latentspace-extreme-harness-engineering.md) and the [verification-and-evaluation topic](../../topics/verification-and-evaluation.md).

**For Tim's investment thesis:** AISLE represents a category of AI-native security companies that are building the *system* layer. If Fort is right, this layer captures more durable value than model-provider lock-in. Watch for: model-agnostic security platforms, maintainer-trust networks, and verification-as-a-service in cybersecurity.
sections.my_take:
**This is the strongest empirical challenge to Mythos's framing published so far, and it's rigorous enough to take seriously despite AISLE's commercial interest.** The three-test methodology is reproducible (transcripts published on GitHub), the results are surprising and internally consistent, and the structural argument (pipeline decomposition + jaggedness) is sound.

The piece also connects to Tim's deepest KB themes: the generation-verification gap applies to cybersecurity directly (detecting bugs is generation; avoiding false positives is verification), and the jagged frontier is a specific instance of the verification asymmetry that Wei, Catalini, and Ball have been mapping across domains.

Where I push back on Fort: the broad-spectrum scanning problem is non-trivial, and Mythos's "thousands of zero-days across every major OS" claim implies a capability in the *search* stage that cheap models probably can't replicate yet. The jagged frontier may be real for detection-given-context while still favoring frontier models for search-across-codebase.

**Rating: essential reading.** This should be in Tim's first three links when discussing Mythos with founders or investors.
sections.talking_points:
> **The cybersecurity moat is the scaffold, not the model.** AISLE tested Mythos's showcase vulnerabilities on 3.6B-parameter models costing $0.11/M tokens — and they found the same bugs. The capability frontier in cybersecurity is "jagged": no single model dominates across tasks. *(Best for: founder chats, especially AI security startups)*

> **Anthropic's Mythos framing may actually slow down the defensive mission.** If cheap open models handle most detection work, restricting access to Mythos delays the very patching Project Glasswing is meant to accelerate. A thousand adequate detectives scanning everything beats one brilliant detective guessing where to look. *(Best for: investor calls on AI security)*

> **The jagged frontier finding generalizes beyond cybersecurity.** Model rankings reshuffle completely across tasks — even within a single domain. This is why harness engineering is eating model selection as the key technical decision. *(Best for: VC roundtables on AI infrastructure)*

> **Inverse scaling on a trivial security task.** A $0.11/M-token model correctly traced data flow that Claude Sonnet 4.5 and every GPT-5.4 model got wrong. Bigger isn't always better — sometimes it's confidently worse. *(Best for: X)*

title: AI Will Be Met With Violence, and Nothing Good Will Come of It
author: Alberto Romero

metadata.author: Alberto Romero
metadata.title: AI Will Be Met With Violence, and Nothing Good Will Come of It

sections.tldr: Alberto Romero documents an emerging pattern of real-world violence directed at AI industry targets — Molotov cocktails at Altman's home, gunshots at a datacenter-supporting councilman's house, threats at OpenAI offices — and argues this escalation is the predictable consequence of an industry that loudly announces it will displace workers while offering no transition plan. The piece connects the current moment to the Luddite movement but notes a key difference: modern targets are far harder to reach, so violence redirects toward people.
sections.whats_new:
The pattern aggregation is the contribution. These incidents individually made news; Romero's synthesis shows them as a trend, not outliers. Three distinct attacks in 6 months — a Molotov cocktail (Altman's home, April 2026), gunshots (Indianapolis datacenter councilman, April 2026), and armed threats (OpenAI offices, November 2025) — all targeting AI infrastructure or leadership.

Romero's structural insight: as AI infrastructure becomes impenetrable (datacenters behind fences, algorithms distributed across continents), violence redirects from machines to people. The Luddites broke looms. Modern protestors can't break datacenters, so they target the humans associated with them.
sections.counterintuitive_claims:
- **The AI industry's self-awareness is its worst PR strategy.** By constantly broadcasting "we're building technology that will displace white-collar workers," AI leaders make themselves look like psychopaths to the people they're displacing. Romero argues they should be "less self-conscious and more self-aware."
- **AI has become the perfect scapegoat.** Most layoffs aren't actually caused by AI, but it's socially acceptable for employers to blame AI. This amplifies public anger beyond what the actual displacement warrants.
sections.key_assumptions: The escalation thesis depends on people feeling they have "no place in the future" — that skills become obsolete, earning capacity disappears, and the transition plan is nonexistent. If visible economic benefits flow to displaced workers (UBI, retraining programs, new job categories), the escalation pressure dissipates.
sections.second_order_implications:
- **Physical security of AI leadership and infrastructure becomes an investable category.** This isn't hypothetical — it's happening now.
- **The "AI labor displacement" narrative has political valence.** Romero notes this could become bipartisan: not just white-collar Democrats losing knowledge-work jobs, but blue-collar Republicans losing warehouse/trucking jobs to automation (connecting to the O-ring dimensionality argument from Imas/Gans).
- **Public perception risk for frontier labs.** The gap between "we're building something amazing" and "we might take your job" is where the violence lives. Labs that manage this gap well (Anthropic's economic index framing, perhaps) fare better than those that don't (Altman's repeated proclamations).
sections.my_take:
This is an important early-warning piece that Tim should have in his model. The investment implications are non-obvious: the political backlash risk to AI companies is underpriced. A single high-profile attack could shift the Overton window on AI regulation faster than any policy paper. For Anthropic specifically, its positioning as the "responsible" lab — and its economic index work measuring displacement patterns — is a form of political risk insurance that other labs lack.

The Luddite parallel is instructive but incomplete. The original Luddites failed because textile automation delivered massive consumer surplus that overwhelmed the political coalition against it. The question for AI is whether the consumer surplus will be similarly overwhelming, or whether displacement will be concentrated enough to sustain a political movement.
sections.talking_points:
- **"Physical attacks on AI infrastructure and leadership are now a trend, not a one-off."** Three incidents in six months — Altman's home, an Indianapolis councilman, OpenAI offices. This is the Luddite pattern starting, but modern targets are people, not machines. (Good for VC roundtables on risk)
- **"AI's biggest PR problem is that its leaders keep loudly saying they'll take your job."** The industry's self-awareness is its worst self-own. Constant public discourse about displacement without transition plans makes CEOs look like antagonists. (Good for founder conversations on communications strategy)
- **"Political backlash risk to AI companies is underpriced."** A single high-profile attack could shift the Overton window on regulation faster than any policy paper. Anthropic's economic index work is a form of political risk insurance. (Good for Anthropic equity discussions)

title: The AI Data Center Backlash is Now Impossible to Ignore
author: Alex Kantrowitz

metadata.author: Alex Kantrowitz
metadata.title: The AI Data Center Backlash is Now Impossible to Ignore

sections.tldr: **The physical infrastructure buildout for AI is hitting a political wall.** An Indianapolis legislator's house was shot up with a "No Data Centers" note left at the door. $156 billion across 48 projects have been blocked or stalled by community opposition. Maine is en route to become the first state to pass a data center construction moratorium. Only 6% of Americans polled believe data centers have a positive impact on nearby communities. The AI industry needs massive infrastructure expansion just as public support is collapsing.
sections.whats_new:
**The datacenter backlash has become bipartisan, violent, and politically organized — a category shift from NIMBYism to something structurally harder to overcome.** The Indianapolis shooting is an inflection point: data center opposition has moved from city council hearings to political violence. Combined with Bernie Sanders (left) and Ron DeSantis (right) both calling for moratoriums, this is no longer a fringe concern. It's a mainstream political issue with bipartisan energy.

The scale of disruption is staggering: $156 billion in projects across 48 sites with publicly disclosed values have been blocked or delayed amid organized local opposition. As many as half the scheduled data centers meant to come online in 2026 could be delayed due to a combination of power constraints and political opposition. This directly constrains the compute buildout that the entire AI capability trajectory depends on.
sections.counterintuitive_claims:
**AI's most promising moment coincides with public support for its infrastructure collapsing.** The models are better than ever (Mythos found thousands of zero-days, GPT-5.4 is shipping, coding agents are production-ready), but the physical layer that powers them faces growing headwinds. The public can impede AI infrastructure in ways it never could with software or social media — because data centers require zoning, power, and local political approval.

**The tech industry's $710 billion datacenter spend forecast for North America in 2026 may be partially vaporware** if the political environment continues to deteriorate. Hyperscaler valuations depend on their ability to deliver on these commitments. The gap between committed capex and physically buildable capacity is a systemic risk that most AI investors are underweighting.
sections.steelman:
**Kantrowitz correctly identifies the fundamental bind.** AI companies need to massively scale infrastructure, but as their models get better, public awareness of AI's impacts grows — and that awareness often crystallizes around the most tangible, local manifestation: the humming building with no windows that appeared in your neighborhood, uses vast amounts of water and electricity, and employs almost nobody local.

The Pew Research finding (only 6% see positive impact on nearby communities) is devastating for the industry's social license argument. Data centers create fewer jobs per megawatt than almost any other industrial use. They consume water and electricity without generating the kind of community engagement that factories or offices do. The political economy is genuinely adverse.
sections.steelman_rebuttal:
**The article may overweight the political signal relative to the actual construction trajectory.** IDC data shows that equipment purchases have not slowed. The $156B in "blocked or stalled" projects may include many that were speculative or poorly sited to begin with. The projects with secured power and community buy-in are still proceeding. The backlash is real but its impact on aggregate capacity may be more marginal than the framing suggests.

**"Ultimately, the technology will likely win out"** — Kantrowitz's own conclusion undermines the alarm. If AI delivers even a fraction of its promised productivity gains, the economic incentives to build infrastructure will overwhelm local opposition through higher offers, better community benefit agreements, or relocation to more permissive jurisdictions.
sections.second_order_implications:
**For Tim's compute/scaling thesis:** The datacenter backlash is a second constraint on the capability trajectory alongside the technical ones (power, chip supply, cooling). Political risk should be modeled alongside technical risk in any AI infrastructure investment. Companies with secured sites and community relationships have a moat that gets wider as opposition grows.

**For the Restrepo framework:** Data center construction workers are the quintessential "bottleneck work" category — their wages are spiking ($260K/year for electricians on DC projects) precisely because the physical buildout is essential for AI scaling. The backlash threatens to make this bottleneck even tighter.

**For Anthropic specifically:** The Pentagon ban (see [blog-transformer-pentagon-anthropic-ban](blog-transformer-pentagon-anthropic-ban.md)) combined with data center backlash creates a dual political risk. Anthropic's Mythos/Glasswing strategy partially addresses this by positioning the company as a *defender* of critical infrastructure (patching bugs rather than just consuming power), which is politically smart.
sections.my_take:
**The datacenter backlash is real, politically bipartisan, and getting worse — but it's more likely to reshape the geography and political economy of AI infrastructure than to fundamentally constrain AI capability trajectories.** The industry will build the data centers; the question is where, at what cost, and with what political concessions. The companies that figure out community benefit agreements, co-location with power generation, and genuine local employment will have a durable advantage.

The Indianapolis shooting should not be normalized. It's a sign that the political temperature around AI infrastructure has reached a dangerous level that the industry's "lobbying blitz" approach is inadequate to address.
sections.talking_points:
> **$156 billion in AI data center projects blocked or stalled by community opposition.** This isn't NIMBYism — it's bipartisan, organized, and now violent. Only 6% of Americans think data centers are good for nearby communities. *(Best for: investor calls on AI infrastructure)*

> **The AI industry's bind: models get better → public awareness grows → infrastructure resistance increases.** The most promising AI moment coincides with collapsing public support for the physical layer. Data centers are the one part of the AI stack where the public can say no. *(Best for: VC roundtables)*

> **Secured sites with community buy-in are now a durable moat.** As opposition grows, the companies with locked-in locations, power, and local relationships have an advantage that gets wider. Geography becomes strategy. *(Best for: founder chats on infrastructure plays)*

title: MirrorCode: Evidence that AI can already do some weeks-long coding tasks
author: Tom Adamczewski, David Rein, David Owen, Florian Brand

metadata.author: Tom Adamczewski, David Rein, David Owen, Florian Brand
metadata.title: MirrorCode: Evidence that AI can already do some weeks-long coding tasks

sections.tldr: Epoch AI and METR present MirrorCode, a benchmark where AI must reimplement real CLI programs from scratch given only execute-only access to the original binary and tests. Claude Opus 4.6 autonomously reimplemented a 16,000-line bioinformatics toolkit (gotree) — estimated at 2-17 weeks of human work — consuming 280M tokens. The key finding: when AI has a detailed, checkable specification, its effective time horizon is dramatically longer than previously measured.
sections.whats_new:
The central contribution is a *methodological advance* in measuring AI coding capability. Existing benchmarks (SWE-bench) measure short tasks (~100-line diffs). Demo projects (Anthropic's C compiler, Cursor's browser) are impressive but uncontrolled — the human guidance is unknown and completeness is debatable. MirrorCode occupies the methodological sweet spot: real software, fully autonomous, rigorously graded.

The most striking finding: **the time-horizon gap is specification-dependent.** METR's general autonomous task horizon for Opus 4.6 is ~12 hours. MirrorCode shows weeks-long horizons *when the spec is precise and checkable*. This means "AI can do X hours of work" is an underspecified claim — the specification environment is a critical variable.
sections.counterintuitive_claims:
- **Older models submitted early because they hallucinated time pressure.** Opus 4.0 and 4.1 submitted at 8-23% completion, sometimes citing "time constraints" that didn't exist. Only Opus 4.6 persevered to completion. This suggests that *persistence* is a distinct capability that improved across model generations — not just raw coding skill.
- **AI can get the architecture right without articulating the choice.** Opus 4.6 chose the correct graph-with-edges data structure for phylogenetic trees without ever explaining why. Earlier models chose a simpler parent/children tree that caused cascading problems. The architectural instinct improved silently across generations.
- **AI can diagnose fundamental design flaws and still refuse to fix them.** On the unsolved Pkl task, Opus 4.6 identified the need for lazy evaluation at least 192 times across 9,000 messages but never implemented it, instead applying ad-hoc patches. It even briefly described the correct thunk-based architecture in words, then pivoted to a hack.
sections.technical_insights:
**Contamination methodology is exemplary.** They measure memorization by prompting models to reproduce original source functions, comparing against a baseline of post-cutoff codebases. The baseline similarity clusters at 0.34; target programs are at 0.31-0.41. This is the most rigorous contamination screen I've seen in a coding benchmark.

**Inference scaling curves are informative.** Gotree was solved in ~280M tokens. Pkl showed roughly linear progress through 1B tokens but wasn't solved — the curve hadn't plateaued. The implication: for sufficiently complex programs, the question is "how many tokens?" not "is it possible?" This changes the economics of AI coding from a capability question to a cost question.

**Code quality is mediocre despite functional correctness.** Opus 4.6's gotree solution had 36 copies of the same argument-parsing logic and used magic negative values in a node.depth field as metadata flags. Functionally correct but would fail human code review. This mirrors the generation-verification gap: the model can generate correct behavior but not clean code without explicit specification of "clean."
sections.key_assumptions:
1. **Precise specification availability.** The benchmark assumes a checkable oracle program exists. Most real software engineering operates against ambiguous, evolving requirements. The authors acknowledge this clearly.
2. **Cost-effectiveness.** The gotree solution cost ~$550 in inference. At ~2-17 weeks of human equivalent, that's $550 vs. $4,000-$34,000 in engineer salary. Already cost-effective even at current Opus pricing.
3. **Progress is monotonic.** The paper shows improvement across four model generations. If the Pkl lazy-evaluation failure mode persists in future models, that would challenge the "just throw more tokens/capability at it" thesis.
sections.second_order_implications:
- **The "time horizon" metric needs a specification-quality axis.** METR's 12-hour estimate for Opus 4.6 is for general tasks. MirrorCode shows weeks for spec-rich tasks. The gap suggests that investing in better specifications (tests, formal contracts, type systems) has multiplicative returns on AI productivity.
- **Inference cost will become the binding constraint on AI coding, not capability.** If Pkl requires 10-100B tokens at $0.55/B-token, the question becomes economic, not technical. This has implications for compute allocation and the inference-scaling investment thesis.
- **The "premature submission" failure mode is a form of the verification gap.** Older models couldn't accurately assess their own completion state. Opus 4.6's ability to track progress and persist is a verifier capability, not a generator capability. This connects directly to the generation-verification gap thesis (see `topics/verification-and-evaluation.md`).
sections.my_take:
This is the most rigorous evidence yet that AI coding capability extends far beyond short tasks. The methodological care (contamination screening, hidden test cases, cheating prevention via red-teaming) sets a new standard for coding benchmarks. The Pkl failure analysis is especially valuable — it's a detailed autopsy of *how* AI fails on complex tasks, not just *that* it fails.

For Tim's investment lens: the inference-scaling curve on Pkl is the chart to watch. If Pkl falls to 10B tokens, the implication is that most software reimplementation is solvable at current capability levels — it's just an inference cost problem. That changes the "sell work not software" thesis from aspirational to mechanistic.

Prior KB context: The tweet-kb-agent covered the MirrorCode announcement in `analyses/2026/04/10/` context. The Latent Space harness-engineering piece (`analyses/2026/04/11/blog-latentspace-extreme-harness-engineering.md`) discussed token economics at scale. MirrorCode provides the empirical grounding for both.
sections.talking_points:
- **"AI coding time horizons are specification-dependent, not fixed."** METR measures 12 hours for general tasks but MirrorCode shows weeks when there's a precise spec. Investing in better specifications has multiplicative returns on AI productivity. (Good for founder chats on AI coding tools)
- **"The binding constraint on AI coding is shifting from capability to inference cost."** MirrorCode's gotree solution cost $550 for work estimated at 2-17 human weeks. As inference gets cheaper, the question is 'how much compute?' not 'can it be done?' (Good for LP updates, compute investment thesis)
- **"Persistence is a distinct model capability that improved across generations."** Older models hallucinated time pressure and submitted at 8-23% completion. Only Opus 4.6 kept working to 100%. This is the verification-gap playing out in real time: the model needs to assess its own progress accurately. (Good for VC roundtables on model evaluation)
- **"AI can diagnose its own fundamental design flaws and still refuse to fix them."** Opus 4.6 identified lazy evaluation as the core issue 192 times in 9,000 messages but never rewrote the evaluator. That's the most realistic portrait of AI-as-engineer published yet — capable but risk-averse at architectural decisions. (Good for technical founder conversations)

title: EV #569: When the future is uncertain, what do you teach?
author: Azeem Azhar

metadata.author: Azeem Azhar
metadata.title: EV #569: When the future is uncertain, what do you teach?

sections.tldr: **Azhar's weekly wraps three threads: Mythos as a risk-repricing event for critical infrastructure, the "Is this AGI?" question as unhelpful distraction (citing Helen Toner), and education redesign in the AI era via a Cosmos Institute essay on Humboldt's *Bildung*.** The key through-line: when capability jumps make the future genuinely uncertain, institutions need to teach adaptability and whole-human development rather than specific skills.
sections.whats_new:
**Azhar's Mythos take centers on risk repricing, not capability.** His earlier piece ("Mythos and the mispricing of everything") argues that Mythos's most immediate implication is that critical infrastructure is the most exposed and systemically mispriced asset class. This is a financial framing that none of the other Mythos analyses have centered — it's the kind of take Tim can use in LP conversations.

**The Bildung connection is the surprise.** Referencing 1809 Prussia (a country in free fall, forced to reform its education system), Azhar surfaces the Cosmos Institute essay arguing for "designing an environment rather than a curriculum." When specific skills have uncertain half-lives, the correct educational response is general human development — not vocational training for jobs that may not exist. This connects to Restrepo's "supplementary work" category: if most knowledge work becomes economically supplementary, what do you teach?

**Helen Toner's push to abandon the AGI framing** is worth noting. She argues for "vivid, concrete milestones" over abstract capability labels. For Tim's purposes: talk about "AI that can find zero-days in every major OS" rather than "AGI."
sections.my_take:
**The newsletter is thin behind the paywall, but the three signals it curates are each valuable.** The Mythos-as-risk-repricing angle is Tim's most useful frame for investor conversations. The Bildung connection is a surprising and useful link between AI labor economics and education philosophy. And Toner's anti-AGI framing is tactically useful for Tim's own communications.

Cross-reference: Azhar's earlier Mythos piece is already in the KB via [blog-synthesis-morning](blog-synthesis-morning.md) references.
sections.talking_points:
> **Mythos reprices critical infrastructure risk.** The most immediate implication isn't capability — it's that critical infrastructure is the most exposed and systemically mispriced asset class in the AI era. *(Best for: LP updates)*

> **When the future is uncertain, teach Bildung, not Python.** If AI makes specific skills obsolete unpredictably, education should develop whole humans rather than train vocational specialists. 1809 Prussia had the same problem — and solved it by designing environments rather than curricula. *(Best for: conversations about AI in education)*

title: A Yale economist says AGI won't automate most jobs—because they're not worth the trouble
author: Nick Lichtenberg (covering Pascual Restrepo)

metadata.author: Nick Lichtenberg (covering Pascual Restrepo)
metadata.title: A Yale economist says AGI won't automate most jobs—because they're not worth the trouble

sections.tldr: **Restrepo's NBER paper "We Won't Be Missed" argues that AGI won't automate most jobs — not because it can't, but because most work isn't important enough for the economy to bother replacing.** He distinguishes "bottleneck" work (essential for growth: energy, infrastructure, science, national security) from "supplementary" work (everything else). Compute gets allocated to bottleneck tasks first. Supplementary jobs survive by economic irrelevance. But labor's share of GDP converges to zero.
sections.whats_new:
**The reframe is the contribution.** The standard AI-labor debate asks "which jobs can AI do?" Restrepo asks "which jobs is it *worth* AI doing?" — and the answer is: only the ones that are bottlenecks for growth. This inverts the usual fear hierarchy. Creative work doesn't survive because it's "uniquely human" — it survives because it's economically supplementary. Baristas survive not from irreplaceability but from irrelevance.

This directly extends the O-ring framework Tim tracks from Gans & Goldfarb and Imas (see [topic_taxonomy.md §8](../../topics/ai-labor-economics.md)). Where Imas asks "which tasks in a job get automated?" Restrepo asks "which *entire occupational categories* does the economy bother automating?" — a higher-level question with different policy implications.
sections.counterintuitive_claims:
**Wages go UP in the transition — then labor's share of GDP goes to zero.** Restrepo shows that total labor income is higher in the post-AGI world than pre-AGI (because the economy is bigger). But labor's *share* of GDP converges to zero. Workers aren't poorer in absolute terms — they're negligible in relative terms. The economy doesn't need them, but it doesn't punish them either.

**The title is literally true: we won't be missed.** If half the workforce stopped showing up today, the economy collapses. In the AGI world, Restrepo argues, it wouldn't. This is the starkest articulation of the "labor becomes economically marginal" thesis in the mainstream economics literature.
sections.steelman:
**Restrepo's bottleneck/supplementary distinction maps cleanly onto observed reality.** Data center construction workers earning $260K/year (32% premium over non-DC builds) is exactly what the model predicts: physical infrastructure is a bottleneck for AI expansion, so wages spike for tasks that are complementary to compute scaling. Meanwhile, knowledge workers whose tasks *are* compute-tractable face wage compression — the mid-career squeeze Tim has been tracking via Imas and Simon Willison.

The two modes of automation (compute-binding = gradual; algorithm-binding = jagged) correspond directly to the "jagged frontier" from the AISLE piece and the broader verification literature. Algorithm-binding transitions produce winners and losers unpredictably — consistent with empirical observations from METR (devs 19% slower with AI but think they're 20% faster).
sections.steelman_rebuttal:
**The bottleneck/supplementary distinction is unstable under capability improvement.** What counts as "bottleneck work" changes as AI capabilities expand. Today's bottleneck (physical infrastructure, energy production) may become supplementary once robotics and nuclear/fusion scale. Restrepo's categories are a snapshot, not a durable partition. The paper acknowledges this but doesn't model the dynamics of category migration.

**Labor share → 0 is a political impossibility, not an economic prediction.** Before labor's share actually approaches zero, democratic feedback loops (taxation, regulation, UBI, compute nationalization) would intervene. The model assumes a frictionless transition that ignores political economy — the very backlash we're already seeing with data center moratoriums (see today's Big Technology analysis).

**Restrepo sits on Anthropic's Economic Advisory Council and has been compensated by OpenAI.** This doesn't invalidate the research, but it positions him within the "AI is transformative" frame that both labs benefit from. An economist less embedded in the AI ecosystem might weight the "not worth automating" category differently.
sections.forward_looking_hypotheses:
- **Bottleneck work will shift from physical infrastructure to verification infrastructure** as AI agents become more autonomous. The scarce input isn't energy or compute — it's trusted evaluation of AI outputs.
- **The algorithm-binding transition mode** (sudden, jagged) is the one we're in now, which means the next 5-10 years will see sharp, unpredictable wage dislocations rather than gradual adjustment.
- **Compute ownership becomes the defining political economy question.** Restrepo explicitly states this. BlackRock's Larry Fink is already flagging it. Expect "compute as public utility" to become a policy position by 2028.
sections.key_assumptions:
- AGI is feasible and capable of all economically valuable work (strong assumption, taken as given for the model).
- Compute is the binding constraint (not data, not regulation, not social acceptance).
- Consumer preferences don't shift radically toward "human-made" goods (which could preserve labor demand via premium pricing).
- The transition happens on a timescale where the bottleneck/supplementary distinction is stable.
sections.second_order_implications:
**For venture investing:** The bottleneck category is where margin concentrates. Invest in companies solving bottleneck problems (energy, infrastructure, security, scientific research) and in companies building verification infrastructure for AI outputs. Supplementary-work businesses (many SaaS categories) face long-term margin compression even if they don't face automation.

**For the KB's labor economics thread:** This paper is the capstone that unifies the O-ring model (Imas/Gans-Goldfarb), the verification bottleneck (Catalini/Wei), and the mid-career squeeze (Willison) under a single growth-theoretic framework. Prior analyses were task-level; Restrepo operates at the economy-level. Cross-reference [ai-labor-economics topic](../../topics/ai-labor-economics.md).
sections.my_take:
**This is the most important AI labor economics paper Tim should be citing in 2026.** It's the rare academic work that changes the terms of the debate rather than adding another data point. The "not worth automating" frame is more honest than either "AI will take all jobs" or "AI will create more jobs than it destroys" — both of which assume the economy *cares* about human labor either way.

The weakness is political economy. Restrepo models a frictionless transition to AGI-dominance, but the path there goes through democratic institutions, union responses, data center moratoriums, and potential regulation. The paper is right about the endpoint but underspecifies the turbulence.

**Disclosure context is important:** Restrepo advises Anthropic and has been compensated by OpenAI. This is standard for top economists in this space but worth noting when citing him.
sections.talking_points:
> **Most jobs won't be automated — not because AI can't do them, but because they're not worth the compute.** Restrepo's "bottleneck vs. supplementary" framework is the cleanest way to think about which jobs survive and why. The barista survives by economic irrelevance, not by human magic. *(Best for: investor calls)*

> **Labor's share of GDP converges to zero.** Workers aren't poorer in absolute terms — but they become negligible relative to the overall economy. The defining question of the AGI era isn't "can AI do this job?" — it's "who owns the compute?" *(Best for: LP updates, macro discussions)*

> **The jagged transition is already here.** Data center electricians earning $260K/year while knowledge workers face compression — that's Restrepo's "algorithm-binding" transition in real time. The next decade is winners and losers, not gradual adjustment. *(Best for: founder chats on labor strategy)*

> **"We won't be missed" is the starkest title in AI economics.** If half the workforce vanished today, the economy collapses. In the AGI world, it wouldn't notice. That's not dystopia — it's the logical endpoint of compute abundance. *(Best for: X)*

title: Mythos isn't the end of the State
author: Andy Hall

metadata.author: Andy Hall
metadata.title: Mythos isn't the end of the State

sections.tldr: **Andy Hall pushes back on the dominant "Mythos proves the state is obsolete" narrative by proposing a third governance path: binding third-party oversight boards for frontier labs, rather than nationalization or corporate techno-dictatorship.** He also surfaces evidence that Anthropic itself is discussing transitioning Glasswing into a third-party-led consortium — which validates his earlier "Enlightened Absolutists" framework.
sections.whats_new:
**Hall's key move is rejecting the binary framing.** Noah Smith, Derek Thompson, and others reacted to Mythos by invoking Weber's monopoly on legitimate force and concluding either (a) governments must nationalize AI or (b) corporations will supplant the state. Hall argues this is a false dichotomy — there's a third path where binding third-party governance bodies oversee frontier lab decisions on safety and deployment, without the state needing to directly control the models.

This connects directly to his January piece "The Enlightened Absolutists" (see [kb/seed](../../../seed/) — Tim cited this piece in his KB seed doc), where he argued Anthropic's constitution is a policy memo, not a constitution, because it lacks credible self-binding. Now he has live evidence: Alex Heath reports that Anthropic's Logan Graham is discussing transitioning Glasswing into exactly the kind of multi-stakeholder consortium Hall proposed.
sections.counterintuitive_claims:
- **Mythos may not actually compromise the state's monopoly on force.** Hall maintains appropriate skepticism about the threat magnitude while acknowledging the capability advance. The state has survived previous capability diffusion (nuclear, cyber) through institutional adaptation, not prevention.
- **The right response to "who should control this?" isn't an answer — it's a structure.** Hall's question of the week — how should a safety board with binding powers be structured, who serves, how are they compensated — is a design problem, not a philosophical one.
sections.forward_looking_hypotheses:
- **Glasswing evolves into a permanent third-party consortium.** If the Alex Heath report is accurate, we may see a model governance body that includes all frontier labs plus critical infrastructure companies, with binding authority over deployment decisions for capability-tier models above some threshold.
- **Model cards become machine-readable.** Hall announces Free Systems is building a model card visualizer for cross-company comparison, which could become the standard for evaluating frontier model releases. This pairs with Vania Chow's "Dead Benchmarks" Substack on evals.
sections.key_assumptions:
- **The institutional capacity to build binding governance structures exists.** Hall's entire framework rests on the assumption that a credible third party can be convened quickly enough to matter — before the 12-18 month capability diffusion window closes.
- **Anthropic's willingness to submit to third-party authority is genuine.** The Glasswing-to-consortium transition could be genuine institution-building or it could be regulatory capture by another name.
sections.my_take:
**This is a short but strategically significant piece because it shifts the Overton window on AI governance from "nationalize or surrender" to "design the board."** Hall's Free Systems project is doing the actual institutional design work that most governance commentary only gestures at. His Dictatorship Eval (referenced at the end) is perhaps the most creative governance-specific benchmark being developed.

The piece's main weakness is brevity — the Mythos analysis is more of a weekly roundup entry than the deep treatment this topic deserves. For the deep version, see Hall's "Enlightened Absolutists" and the discussion in Tim's existing KB at [kb/seed/4ac7b809e66b-anthropics-constitution-as-policy-memo.md](../../../seed/4ac7b809e66b-anthropics-constitution-as-policy-memo.md).

Extends [kb/analyses/2026/04/12/blog-zvi-mythos-cybersecurity-glasswing.md](blog-zvi-mythos-cybersecurity-glasswing.md) — Zvi covers the capability case; Hall covers the governance implications.
sections.talking_points:
> **There's a third path between nationalization and techno-dictatorship: binding third-party governance boards for frontier labs.** Anthropic is already discussing transitioning Glasswing into a multi-stakeholder consortium. *(Best for: VC roundtables, founder conversations)*

> **The Overton window on AI governance just shifted.** A year ago, "binding oversight of model releases" was politically toxic. Post-Mythos, it looks moderate compared to the nationalization proposals now on the table. *(Best for: LP updates, policy conversations)*

> **Model cards have become unreadable.** Free Systems is building a cross-company visualizer that could become the standard. This is infrastructure for the governance layer. *(Best for: founder conversations on AI infra)*

title: "New Sages Unrivalled" — On Mythos
author: Dean W. Ball

metadata.author: Dean W. Ball
metadata.title: "New Sages Unrivalled" — On Mythos

sections.tldr: Dean Ball argues that Mythos represents a genuine inflection point for AI cybersecurity policy — not because the capability was unexpected, but because the decades-long accumulation of unfixed software vulnerabilities means even a moderate capability advance creates catastrophic exposure. His policy prescriptions center on compute buildout as the primary defense mechanism, not capability restriction.
sections.whats_new:
Ball's most original move is reframing Mythos not as an AI safety problem but as a *national infrastructure vulnerability* problem. The danger isn't the model — it's the millions of lines of legacy code that have been under-audited for decades. Mythos simply makes the existing vulnerability surface *visible* at scale. This shifts the policy lever from "restrict the model" to "harden the world," which is a fundamentally different framing than what most AI governance pieces offer.

He also names a specific competitive dynamic: the salient difference between the US and China isn't "innovation ecosystem" but *compute access*. Whoever has the GPUs to run Mythos-class vulnerability discovery first gets the defensive advantage. This connects directly to his FERC testimony on transmission siting — national security now depends on power permitting.
sections.counterintuitive_claims:
- **Adolescence is over.** Ball declares the era of treating AI risk discussion as "doomer" or "regulatory capture" suspicion is finished. Mythos forces everyone to drop the posturing.
- **Nonproliferation is impossible.** He explicitly states that Mythos-class capabilities will diffuse to adversaries within 1-2 years regardless of policy. The only viable strategy is defensive hardening, not prevention.
- **Internal deployments are the real frontier.** The best models may never be publicly released — they'll be used inside frontier labs for automated AI R&D. This creates a transparency crisis that Ball wants solved through private governance frameworks (auditing orgs).
sections.steelman: The strongest version of Ball's argument: We are in a transitional period where AI offensive capabilities outpace the world's ability to patch decades of accumulated software debt. The rational response is a Manhattan-Project-scale defensive cybersecurity effort that requires (a) compute infrastructure buildout at national-priority speed, (b) coordinated disclosure frameworks like Project Glasswing, (c) transparency mandates like CA SB 53, and (d) private governance bodies to audit internal deployments. The alternative — trying to keep the genie in the bottle — is not credible.
sections.steelman_rebuttal: Ball takes Anthropic's claims at face value. The critical question he doesn't engage: How much of the Mythos cybersecurity narrative is genuine unprecedented capability vs. very effective positioning? Project Glasswing makes Anthropic the center of a defensive coalition and deepens its relationships with every major tech company and the federal government — exactly the kind of moat-building that a $380B company needs. The vulnerability finds are real (CVEs are being patched), but the *magnitude* claim — that this fundamentally changes the cybersecurity landscape overnight — could be strategic framing that serves Anthropic's commercial interests.
sections.second_order_implications:
- **Compute buildout becomes a national security imperative, not just a commercial one.** This changes the politics of permitting, energy, and datacenter siting dramatically.
- **The DoD-Anthropic conflict looks increasingly self-destructive.** If Mythos is what Ball says it is, the government blacklisting its creator is strategically incoherent.
- **Open-source AI governance gets harder.** If Mythos-class capabilities can find zero-days, then open-weight models with similar capabilities present a genuine proliferation risk that the "open-source = good" coalition hasn't addressed.
sections.my_take:
This is Ball at his best: clear-eyed, historically grounded, unafraid to name what others tiptoe around. The piece is more manifesto than analysis — there's no technical deep-dive on *how* Mythos finds vulnerabilities, and the policy prescriptions are high-altitude. But the framing is exactly right: the era of pretending frontier AI doesn't have security implications is over. His insistence on compute as the binding constraint on defensive capability is the most investable insight here.

Prior KB context: The tweet-kb-agent's analyses on Mythos alignment risk (see `analyses/2026/04/07/2041584799929004045-sleepinyourhat-mythos-alignment-risk.md`) and interpretability (see `analyses/2026/04/07/2041588505701388648-jack-w-lindsey-mythos-interpretability.md`) cover the model's behavioral characteristics. Ball's piece is the macro-strategic complement — less about what Mythos *does* and more about what it *means* for national security and policy. Together they give Tim a complete picture.
sections.talking_points:
- **"Mythos isn't an AI safety problem — it's a technical debt reckoning."** Every line of unaudited legacy code is now a liability. The vulnerability isn't the model; it's the 27 years of unfixed bugs. (Good for VC roundtables, founder chats on security startups)
- **"The salient US-China AI gap isn't talent or innovation — it's GPUs."** Whoever can run Mythos-class vulnerability scans at scale wins the cyber-defense race. That makes datacenter permitting a national security priority. (Good for LP updates, policy discussions)
- **"The best models of the future may never be publicly released."** Internal deployments for automated AI R&D create a transparency crisis. Private governance frameworks — third-party auditors for frontier labs — are the missing institution. (Good for governance-focused conversations)
- **"Anthropic just made itself the center of a defensive cybersecurity coalition."** Project Glasswing deepens relationships with every major tech company and the federal government simultaneously. Whether that's altruism or moat-building is the trillion-dollar question. (Good for Anthropic equity discussions)

title: Your GPUs Just Got 6x More Valuable. No New Hardware Required.
author: Nate Parrott

metadata.author: Nate Parrott
metadata.title: Your GPUs Just Got 6x More Valuable. No New Hardware Required.

sections.tldr: **Google's TurboQuant paper (March 25) achieves 6x compression of KV cache memory during inference with zero accuracy loss, no retraining, and drop-in deployment.** Nate argues this is the most consequential development in AI infrastructure right now — not a new chip, not a new model, but a compression algorithm that turns existing GPU fleets into 6x more valuable assets overnight. A GPU that served 9 concurrent users now serves 50.
sections.whats_new:
**Nate reframes the AI infrastructure competition as a three-body problem — supply (chips), demand (agent workloads), and compression — and argues compression is the fastest-moving variable.** Most coverage of AI infrastructure focuses on the chip war (Nvidia vs. custom silicon) and demand growth (agent workloads consuming 10-100x more tokens). TurboQuant introduces a "third body" that moves on a completely different timescale: compression algorithms can be deployed in weeks, while new fabs take years.

The economic implication: a 6x reduction in KV cache memory translates into ~5x increase in revenue per GPU, because the bottleneck for concurrent inference was memory, not compute. This changes the concurrency math for every inference provider.

He also argues the KV cache is functionally RAM for a "transformer computer" — making compression not just an efficiency gain but an architectural insight about what inference actually is.
sections.forward_looking_hypotheses:
- **Compression becomes the primary competitive axis for inference providers.** Companies that deploy TurboQuant (or equivalents) first get a temporary but massive cost advantage.
- **Context windows expand rapidly.** If memory is 6x cheaper, the constraint on context length shifts from memory to attention computation. Expect 1M+ token contexts to become commodity.
- **The "compute squeeze" from Mythos-class models may be less severe than expected.** If compression continues at this pace, the demand-supply gap closes from the supply side via efficiency, not just from buildout.
- **This favors Google** (who published the research) over Nvidia (whose hardware pricing assumed memory scarcity).
sections.key_assumptions:
- **Zero accuracy loss holds at scale.** TurboQuant claims zero degradation, but edge cases in long-context or multi-turn agent workloads could surface. The "drop-in" claim needs production validation.
- **Compression gains compound.** Nate implies this is part of an ongoing trend. If true, the effective cost per token falls even faster than model improvements suggest.
sections.my_take:
**This is the most investment-relevant piece in this batch.** If TurboQuant's claims hold, it directly impacts the valuation of every company in the inference stack — from cloud providers to vertical AI startups that depend on inference costs. The piece's strength is its clear economic framing (revenue per GPU is the metric that matters). Its weakness is that the paywall prevents me from evaluating Nate's analysis of who wins and loses in the competitive landscape.

The connection to Tim's existing KB: this directly updates [kb/topics/compute-and-scaling.md](../../../topics/compute-and-scaling.md) and relates to the Diligence Stack's compute infrastructure coverage. Also relevant to Zvi's point in the Mythos piece that "limitless demand for compute" makes every efficiency gain valuable — TurboQuant is a concrete mechanism by which that demand gets partially satisfied.
sections.talking_points:
> **The most important variable in the AI infrastructure war isn't a chip — it's a compression algorithm.** Google's TurboQuant gives every existing GPU fleet 6x more inference capacity overnight, with zero accuracy loss. *(Best for: investor calls, LP updates)*

> **Revenue per GPU is the metric that matters for inference providers.** TurboQuant turns a 6x memory compression into ~5x revenue per GPU by unlocking concurrent users. This changes the compute economics for every AI company. *(Best for: founder conversations)*

> **The "compute squeeze" from Mythos-class models may be less severe than feared.** Compression algorithms deploy in weeks; new fabs take years. The supply side is moving faster than the hardware cycle. *(Best for: VC roundtables)*

title: Executive Briefing: Valve Got Lord of the Flies. Zappos Got Paralysis. Your Reorg Is Next.
author: Nate

metadata.author: Nate
metadata.title: Executive Briefing: Valve Got Lord of the Flies. Zappos Got Paralysis. Your Reorg Is Next.

sections.tldr: **Every management layer contains three functions bundled together: routing (moving information), sensemaking (interpreting it for decisions), and accountability (feedback and growth). They're on completely different automation timelines.** Routing is automatable now. Sensemaking is 18-36 months out. Accountability may never be fully automatable. Companies that removed all three at once (Valve, Zappos, Medium, GitHub) hit the same wall. The 44% of companies currently cutting management layers are reproducing those failures at AI-era scale.
sections.whats_new:
**The three-function decomposition of management is the original contribution.** Most AI-and-labor discussions operate at the task level (which tasks can AI do?) or the job level (which jobs get automated?). Nate operates at the *function* level within a role: the manager's job isn't one thing but three bundled services, each with distinct properties. This is a genuinely useful analytical framework that I haven't seen articulated this cleanly elsewhere.

The key insight: when companies flatten org charts, they think they're removing one function (overhead/coordination). They're actually removing three, and the one they meant to remove (routing) is the one AI already handles. The functions they didn't intend to remove (sensemaking, accountability) are the ones whose absence causes the real damage — but the symptoms (misalignment, six incompatible responses to the same memo) *look* like a routing problem, so companies add more Slack channels instead of addressing the sensemaking vacuum.
sections.counterintuitive_claims:
**The sensemaking vacuum looks exactly like a communication problem, but isn't.** Six people reading the same strategy memo and proposing six incompatible responses is not a routing failure — the information got routed fine. It's a sensemaking failure: no one has the authority or context to resolve interpretive conflicts. Adding routing (more meetings, Slack channels, all-hands) is the wrong fix. This is a diagnostic trap that most org design frameworks miss.

**Your best people leave not because of the reorg — they leave because of the feedback void.** The accountability function is the highest-stakes one to lose. Mid-tenure performers with options stop waiting for feedback that isn't coming and start interviewing. By the time attrition data surfaces, you've lost the hardest-to-replace people.
sections.steelman:
**The three-function framework explains why some flat orgs work and others don't.** The article argues that successful flattening (Meta's stock tripling after layer cuts; Shopify's "prove AI can't do it" hiring gate) preserved sensemaking and accountability while automating routing. Failed flattening (Valve's "Lord of the Flies" dynamics; Zappos's holacracy paralysis) removed all three simultaneously. The consistency of the pattern across very different companies — Valve (games), Zappos (retail), Medium (media), GitHub (dev tools) — suggests a structural finding, not a management fad.

**The automation timeline stagger is credible.** Routing (moving information between teams) is already handled by AI agents, scheduling tools, and workflow automation. Sensemaking (interpreting ambiguous signals for context-dependent decisions) requires the kind of judgment that current AI handles poorly but will improve at with better long-context models and domain-specific fine-tuning. Accountability (telling humans whether they're on track and helping them grow) requires trust, relational continuity, and emotional intelligence that may be permanently human-essential.
sections.steelman_rebuttal:
**The three-function decomposition may be too clean.** In practice, routing, sensemaking, and accountability are deeply entangled. A good manager's "routing" decision (who should get this information?) is itself a sensemaking act. The decomposition is analytically useful but may mislead leaders into thinking they can cleanly separate the functions.

**The "18-36 months" timeline for sensemaking automation is suspiciously precise.** This is a claim about AI capability trajectories that isn't grounded in specific technical analysis. It could be 6 months or 5 years — the uncertainty is much wider than the article implies.

**The paywall hides the most actionable content.** The free preview lays out the thesis beautifully but the actual playbook (three companies hollowing out now, the sequence that works, what to do this week) is behind the Executive Circle paywall.
sections.second_order_implications:
**For AI agent design:** If the management bundle can be decomposed, then AI agents should be designed for specific functions rather than "replacing the manager." An AI routing agent, an AI sensemaking assistant, and a human accountability structure is the correct hybrid architecture — not a single "AI manager."

**For the labor economics thread:** This connects directly to Restrepo's bottleneck/supplementary distinction at a finer grain. Routing is supplementary (AI handles it now). Sensemaking may be bottleneck work for organizational function. Accountability is socially intensive work that survives by being hard to replicate with compute. The three functions map onto three different automation trajectories from the NBER paper.

**For Anthropic's enterprise strategy:** Conway/Cowork/Managed Agents are routing infrastructure. The platform play succeeds to the extent it solves routing (and it clearly does). The next competitive frontier is sensemaking assistance — which is where long-context models, decision traces, and institutional memory matter. See [Anthropic platform strategy](../../topics/claude-managed-agents.md) and prior Nate analyses (e.g., [blog-natesnewsletter-gpus-6x-turboquant](blog-natesnewsletter-gpus-6x-turboquant.md)).
sections.my_take:
**This is Nate's best analytical piece in weeks.** The three-function decomposition is genuinely original and immediately useful. Tim can apply it in any conversation about org design in the AI era — it's the kind of framework that makes a founder pause and rethink their flattening strategy.

The weakness is the paywalled playbook. The free preview is excellent theory; the actionable "sequence that works" (replace routing → protect feedback → concentrate sensemaking) is behind the Executive Circle tier. Worth the paywall for Tim given Nate's track record as the #1 Anthropic ecosystem source.
sections.talking_points:
> **Every manager is three services in a trench coat: routing, sensemaking, and accountability.** The companies flattening their orgs are removing all three when they only meant to remove routing — which AI already handles. That's why 44% of companies cut a management layer last year, and most of them are about to add it back. *(Best for: founder chats on org design)*

> **The sensemaking vacuum looks exactly like a communication problem.** Six people read the same strategy memo and propose six incompatible responses — that's not a routing failure, it's a sensemaking failure. Adding Slack channels to fix it is like treating a broken arm with a bandaid. *(Best for: VC roundtables)*

> **AI agents should be designed for specific management functions, not "replacing the manager."** An AI routing agent + AI sensemaking assistant + human accountability structure is the correct hybrid. This is the org-design analog of harness engineering. *(Best for: enterprise AI discussions)*

title: Research on AI and the labor market is still in the first inning
author: PIIE Realtime Economics

metadata.author: PIIE Realtime Economics
metadata.title: Research on AI and the labor market is still in the first inning

sections.tldr: **The academic consensus on AI's labor market impact is: we don't know yet.** PIIE surveys the entire landscape and finds contradictory signals: Brynjolfsson et al. find job posting declines correlate with AI exposure, but Iscenko & Millet (2026) argue the timing corresponds better to rising interest rates than ChatGPT's launch. Individual productivity studies find mixed results — one study found AI made developers *slower*, another found consultants over-relied on AI beyond its capabilities. The most reliable finding: AI creates entirely new occupations, consistent with historical patterns.
sections.whats_new:
**The "first inning" framing is the contribution.** This isn't a specific finding — it's a meta-finding about the state of the field. The research base is too young, the data too noisy, and the technology changing too fast for anyone to claim confident predictions about AI's labor impact. This is useful precisely because it tempers the certainty of both optimists (Restrepo, Goldman) and pessimists (Citrini, Acemoglu on displacement).

**The Iscenko & Millet finding is the most important challenge to the standard narrative.** If the decline in AI-exposed job postings started in 2022 (before ChatGPT), then interest rates — not AI — may be the primary driver. This is a confound that most AI-labor commentary ignores.

**Imas (2026) is cited as the survey source** for productivity studies: "many look at coding or customer service. Most find productivity benefits, with notable exceptions." This positions Imas as a meta-analyst, not just an O-ring theorist — consistent with his growing role in Tim's intellectual framework.
sections.my_take:
**Essential background reading for calibrating confidence levels in AI-labor claims.** Tim should cite this piece whenever someone presents AI labor predictions with excessive certainty. The "first inning" metaphor is the right corrective to both techno-optimist and techno-pessimist certainty.

Pairs with the Restrepo analysis: Restrepo is the theoretical endpoint; PIIE is the empirical reality check that says "we're nowhere near testing these models yet."
sections.talking_points:
> **Research on AI and labor is in the first inning.** The data is noisy, the studies contradict each other, and the technology is changing faster than researchers can study it. Anyone claiming confidence about AI's labor impact is overselling. *(Best for: tempering overconfident claims in any setting)*

> **The interest rate confound.** Job posting declines in AI-exposed occupations may be driven by rising interest rates, not AI adoption. The timing matches the macro cycle better than the ChatGPT launch. *(Best for: nuanced macro discussions)*

title: 2026.15: Myth and Mythos
author: Ben Thompson

metadata.author: Ben Thompson
metadata.title: 2026.15: Myth and Mythos

sections.tldr: **Thompson frames Anthropic's Mythos moment through the "Boy Who Cried Wolf" parable — with a critical twist: the wolf *did come* in the end.** Anthropic's growth trajectory has been exponential for nearly two years, and now it has "undoubtedly the most powerful model in the world." There's reason for cynicism about Anthropic's safety messaging given its history, but the part of the fable everyone forgets is that the wolf was real. The weekly newsletter wraps Mythos, the NYT interview (human expertise as moat), and broader AI competitive dynamics.
sections.whats_new:
**The "Boy Cries Wolf" reframe cuts through the Mythos discourse.** Thompson's observation is that Anthropic has repeatedly warned about AI danger while also building the dangerous thing. The cynical read is that safety messaging is marketing. But the Wolf fable's actual lesson isn't "the boy was lying" — it's "eventually the wolf shows up, and nobody believes it." If Mythos's cybersecurity capabilities are real (and the AISLE analysis suggests at least the direction is, even if exclusivity is overstated), then the industry is in the uncomfortable position of having normalized exactly the kind of warning that now needs to be taken seriously.

**The "once-barely-visible trajectory" observation is the most important for investors.** Thompson notes that Anthropic's exponential growth includes the early part of the curve that everyone missed. The company has been on this trajectory for nearly two years — it just became visible. This is a structural point about exponential growth detection that applies broadly to AI company evaluation.
