1. **Pets → cattle for both containers AND harnesses.** The initial architecture (everything in one container) created debugging nightmares — the WebSocket event stream couldn't distinguish harness bugs from container failures from network drops. After decoupling, both containers and harnesses are stateless and replaceable. Session state lives in the append-only event log.

2. **Security via structural separation, not scoping.** Rather than limiting what tokens can do (which "encodes an assumption about what Claude can't do with a limited token — and Claude is getting increasingly smart"), they ensure credentials never enter the sandbox at all. Git tokens are baked into repo clones during init. OAuth tokens live in a vault accessed through a proxy. The agent's generated code physically cannot read credentials.

3. **`getEvents()` as the context management primitive.** The session log is a positional event stream that the brain can interrogate with slices — rewinding, replaying, skipping. This is fundamentally different from the "compaction + trimming" approach most agent platforms use. It preserves optionality: no irreversible context decisions until the harness explicitly makes them.
sections.key_assumptions:
- That the brain/hands/session decomposition is the right factoring for agent systems. If future paradigms require tighter coupling (e.g., agents that need sub-millisecond access to execution state), the abstraction leaks.
- That models will continue to outgrow their harnesses, making harness churn the dominant engineering cost. If models plateau, specific harnesses become durable and the meta-harness adds unnecessary indirection.
- That enterprises will accept running their agent infrastructure on Anthropic's platform rather than self-hosting. The VPC peering story (now solved by decoupling) suggests this was a real objection.
sections.second_order_implications:
- **Harness companies become harness-on-Managed-Agents companies.** The "many different harnesses" framing sounds open, but the gravitational pull is toward Anthropic's interfaces. LangChain, CrewAI, and every other orchestration framework will need to decide whether to integrate with Managed Agents or compete against it.
- **Session-hour pricing ($0.08/hr) becomes the unit of agent economics.** If agents become long-running background processes (the daemon trajectory Tim has been tracking), session-hours are more natural than token counts as the billing unit. This reprices the entire agent infrastructure market.
- **The "many brains, many hands" architecture enables agent-of-agents patterns at platform level.** Brains can pass hands to other brains. This is Anthropic building the coordination substrate that third parties were trying to build (see `2026/03/23/2036189486175101055-aakashgupta-four-ways-autonomous-claude.md`).
sections.my_take:
**This is the most architecturally rigorous piece Anthropic has published on agent infrastructure.** The OS analogy isn't just rhetoric — the specific patterns (append-only session logs, lazy container provisioning, structural credential separation) are well-chosen and defensible. The meta-harness concept resolves the tension between the harness-maximalist position (OpenAI, Fowler) and the bitter-lesson position (models will absorb harness features): you need harnesses today, but you should design your infrastructure to survive harness churn.

The piece notably doesn't mention pricing, competitive positioning, or the OpenClaw saga. It reads like internal engineering documentation that was published. That's a signal — Anthropic is competing on architectural credibility, not marketing.

The KB already has 200+ analyses touching agent infrastructure and Managed Agents. This piece is the **canonical primary-source document** for how the platform actually works under the hood. It should be the reference for every future CMA-related analysis.
sections.talking_points:
> **Managed Agents is an OS, not a product.** Anthropic virtualized agents into session/harness/sandbox the same way Unix virtualized hardware into process/file. The interfaces are designed to outlast any specific harness implementation. *(Best for: founder chats, VC roundtables)*

> **Every harness is a depreciating asset.** Context resets built for Sonnet 4.5 became dead weight on Opus 4.5. Anthropic's bet is that harness churn is the dominant cost, so the durable investment is the meta-harness — the stable interfaces. *(Best for: investor calls)*

> **Security through structural separation, not policy.** Agent-generated code physically cannot access credentials because they're never in the sandbox. This is a fundamentally different security model than scoping or filtering. *(Best for: enterprise conversations)*

> **60% TTFT drop from lazy container provisioning.** Most agent platforms pay container setup cost up front. Anthropic starts inference immediately and provisions containers only when code execution is needed. *(Best for: technical founder chats)*

title: Cybersecurity Looks Like Proof of Work Now
author: Drew Breunig

metadata.author: Drew Breunig
metadata.title: Cybersecurity Looks Like Proof of Work Now

sections.tldr: **Security economics under Mythos-class models reduce to a proof-of-work equation: spend more tokens discovering exploits than attackers spend exploiting them.** The UK AI Safety Institute's independent evaluation confirms Mythos finds exploits with no diminishing returns as token budgets increase. Open-source software becomes *more* valuable (not less) because security token spending is shared across all users. Breunig predicts a three-phase agentic coding cycle: develop → review → harden.
sections.whats_new:
**The novel contribution is the economic framing.** Others have analyzed Mythos's capabilities (Zvi's three-part series, AISLE's jagged frontier, PostQuantum's cost model). Breunig is the first to connect the AISI evaluation's token-budget data to a clean economic model. The key chart from the AISI report shows Mythos completing "The Last Ones" — a 32-step corporate network attack simulation that takes humans ~20 hours — in 3/10 attempts at 100M tokens per run (~$12,500/attempt). Crucially, no model showed diminishing returns at 100M tokens. More spend = more exploits found.

This transforms cybersecurity from a skill problem into a capital allocation problem. The "proof of work" analogy is structurally precise: success is tied to raw computational expenditure, not cleverness.
sections.counterintuitive_claims: **Open-source libraries become MORE valuable, not less.** This directly contradicts the "yoink" thesis that AI coding agents should reimplement dependencies to avoid supply-chain risk (Karpathy's position). Breunig's argument: if security is purely a function of token expenditure, Linus's law expands to include tokens. A widely-used OSS library benefits from pooled security spending across all its corporate dependents. A one-off reimplementation only gets whatever budget a single organization allocates. The collective security spend on OpenSSL will always dwarf what any team spends hardening their bespoke replacement.
sections.steelman: **If you accept that (a) Mythos-class vulnerability discovery scales with tokens without diminishing returns, and (b) attackers and defenders have access to comparable models, then security economics become a pure spending race.** The defender's advantage is that they can invest in hardening once and share the result across all users/deployments, while the attacker must find novel exploits that haven't been patched. This is structurally favorable to defenders — especially open-source ecosystems where security investment is collective. The "proof of work" frame makes an implicit prediction: organizations that systematically allocate token budgets to security hardening will have measurably fewer exploitable vulnerabilities.
sections.steelman_rebuttal:
**The "no diminishing returns" finding is based on a single evaluation at a single budget ceiling.** AISI tested up to 100M tokens. Real-world codebases are vastly larger and more complex than CTF simulations. Diminishing returns may emerge at higher budgets or against already-hardened systems. More importantly, the asymmetry between finding and exploiting matters enormously — Bruce Schneier's point (see `2026/04/14/blog-schneier-mythos-glasswing-pr.md`) that "finding for the purposes of fixing is easier for an AI than finding plus exploiting" suggests the economics may be more favorable to defenders than Breunig's zero-sum framing implies.

Also: the "proof of work" analogy breaks down at the margin. In crypto, proof of work has no external benefit — the compute is pure waste. Security token expenditure produces real defensive value. This is proof of *useful* work, which has different equilibrium dynamics.
sections.forward_looking_hypotheses:
**Three-phase agentic coding cycle:** Breunig predicts software development evolves to development → review → hardening, with human input as the limiter for phase 1 and money as the limiter for phase 3. This is a testable prediction: we should see dedicated hardening-phase tooling emerge within 6 months. Anthropic's $15-20/PR code review product is already phase 2; phase 3 tools are the next market.

**Embedded bet:** "Code remains cheap, unless it needs to be secure." This implies a bifurcation in the software market between low-stakes vibe-coded applications and high-stakes systems where security token budgets dominate total cost. The security premium could become the primary cost driver, not development itself.
sections.technical_insights:
**The AISI data is the strongest independent validation of Mythos's capabilities so far.** The UK's AI Safety Institute is a government body, not an Anthropic partner. Their finding that Mythos completed a 32-step attack simulation in 3/10 attempts — while no other model completed it at all — is rigorous. The $12,500/attempt cost ($125K for 10 runs) provides the first real pricing benchmark for Mythos-class security auditing.

The "token budget" framing connects directly to the verification-and-evaluation theme in Tim's KB: security hardening is a special case of verification where the verifier (Mythos) searches for counterexamples (exploits) and the budget determines search depth.
sections.second_order_implications:
1. **Cybersecurity becomes a capital expenditure, not a headcount expense.** CISOs will argue for token budgets alongside headcount budgets. This changes how boards evaluate security investment — it becomes measurable ROI.

2. **Open-source foundations gain new fundraising logic.** "We need $X to run Y tokens against critical libraries" is a much cleaner ask than traditional security audit funding.

3. **The security premium creates a new moat for infrastructure providers.** Anthropic/AWS can offer "pre-hardened" APIs as a service, charging for the token expenditure they've already made. This directly connects to the Metalayer/Agent Unit pricing model from d'Ornano's analysis (see `2026/04/14/blog-decodingdisc-digital-labor-tax.md`).
sections.my_take:
**This is the cleanest economic framing of Mythos's security implications yet.** The proof-of-work analogy will stick because it's simple and directionally correct, even if the details break down at the margin. The open-source counterargument to Karpathy's "yoink" thesis is particularly sharp and timely — it reframes OSS from a supply-chain liability into a security asset precisely because of AI's capabilities.

The piece is short but load-bearing. It connects the AISI evaluation (empirical data), the economic model (token budgets as security investment), and the market prediction (three-phase coding cycle) in a way that's immediately actionable for investor conversations.

**One gap:** Breunig doesn't address the attacker-side economics. If Mythos-class models become available to adversaries (which Schneier argues is inevitable), the equilibrium shifts from "defenders can outspend" to "it's a continuous arms race where the cheapest model that finds the exploit wins." The defender's structural advantage (fix once, deploy everywhere) helps, but doesn't eliminate the race.
sections.talking_points:
> **Cybersecurity is now a capital allocation problem, not a skills problem.** AISI shows Mythos finds exploits without diminishing returns as you increase token spend. Security reduces to: spend more on finding bugs than attackers spend on exploiting them. *(Best for: investor calls)*

> **Open-source is a security asset, not a liability.** Pooled token spending across all users of a library will always exceed what any single team spends hardening a bespoke reimplementation. Karpathy's "yoink and replace" thesis gets weaker, not stronger, under Mythos-class models. *(Best for: founder chats)*

> **The three-phase coding cycle is coming: develop, review, harden.** Human intuition limits phase 1, money limits phase 3. Anthropic's code review product is phase 2. Phase 3 hardening tools are the next market opportunity. *(Best for: enterprise SaaS conversations)*

> **Code is cheap unless it needs to be secure.** The security premium may become the dominant cost driver for high-stakes software. This creates a bifurcation between vibe-coded prototypes and properly hardened production systems. *(Best for: VC roundtables)*

title: Anthropic's Digital Labor Tax
author: Raphaëlle d'Ornano

metadata.author: Raphaëlle d'Ornano
metadata.title: Anthropic's Digital Labor Tax

sections.tldr: **Anthropic's Claude Managed Agents creates what d'Ornano calls the "Metalayer" — a managed runtime that bundles compute, intelligence, and execution into a single "Agent Unit" priced by the session-hour.** This transforms Anthropic from a model API company into a "tax collector of digital labor," where every synthetic colleague running on the platform pays a per-hour toll regardless of who builds the application layer. The paradox: the better this works, the faster it consumes the compute Anthropic doesn't own, making success and vulnerability the same mechanism.
sections.whats_new:
**The conceptual leap is reframing Managed Agents as an economic instrument, not just a product feature.** d'Ornano introduces two precise definitions: the "Metalayer" (the managed runtime for persistent, long-running, multi-agent workloads) and the "Agent Unit" (the bundled cost of running an autonomous agent — compute + intelligence + execution, billed hourly). The session-hour is "not a software metric; it is a headcount metric — the cost of an autonomous worker, billed hourly."

This reframing is load-bearing: it connects Anthropic's pricing ($0.08/session-hour + tokens) directly to the $60 trillion global labor market rather than the ~5% of enterprise spend that goes to software. The TAM shifts from IT budgets to labor budgets.
sections.counterintuitive_claims:
**The Metalayer's success intensifies the very constraint it depends on.** This isn't the usual "growth is good" narrative. d'Ornano argues that every unit of adoption creates more compute demand, that Managed Agents create consumption patterns "categorically more compute-intensive than the API calls they replace," and that the advisor tool actually multiplies model calls per task. The flywheel accelerates demand faster than supply can scale. This is a "combinatorial explosion of inference demand."

**The advisor pattern may be as much defensive as innovative.** d'Ornano reads the Opus-advises-Haiku strategy not just as cost optimization but as a response to the compute crunch: "When you are capacity-constrained, the most valuable innovation is the one that delivers comparable intelligence at lower intensity."
sections.steelman: **The strongest version: Anthropic is building AWS for digital labor.** The AWS parallel is precise: EC2's per-hour pricing removed friction so effectively that it accelerated the adoption it was taxing. Fifteen years of compounding followed. The Metalayer could replicate this if session-hour stickiness functions like DBU stickiness at Databricks — enterprises that deploy persistent agents with accumulated state face meaningful switching costs. The moat isn't the model; it's the operating environment and the accumulated agent configuration state.
sections.steelman_rebuttal: **The AWS analogy breaks at the critical point: AWS owned its infrastructure.** Anthropic's Metalayer runs on rented compute from landlords (Google, Amazon) who operate competing runtimes. The leaked OpenAI memo from CRO Denise Dresser — "Their strategic misstep to not acquire enough compute is showing up in the product. Customers feel it through throttling" — may be competitive propaganda, but the underlying geometry is real. The Broadcom TPU deal is contingent on "Anthropic's continued commercial success" — the landlord put that clause there for a reason. And CoreWeave, the landlord with no competing runtime, is itself capital-constrained with aggressive leverage.
sections.technical_insights:
**The advisor pattern's economics are mechanistically elegant.** Haiku with Opus advisor delivers >2x its solo BrowseComp score at 85% less cost. SWE-bench Multilingual improves 2.7% at 11.9% lower cost per task. The trick is dynamic intelligence allocation — knowing when to think hard vs. act fast. This isn't just a cost optimization; it's an architectural pattern that decouples revenue from the linear compute-to-megawatt equation that defines the rest of the industry.

**The three commercial positions are structurally distinct.** (1) Anthropic moves up-stack into verticals (captures full value chain), (2) ISVs like Salesforce build on the Metalayer (Anthropic becomes the engine), (3) enterprises build directly on the runtime (Anthropic sells digital headcount to the C-suite). In all three, the "tax" flows to Anthropic.
sections.key_assumptions:
- That session-hour stickiness actually materializes (no execution proof yet, as d'Ornano acknowledges)
- That hyperscaler landlords won't deprioritize Anthropic's workloads when compute binds
- That the advisor pattern's cost savings scale across diverse workloads
- That enterprises will shift agent budgets from IT (2-5% of spend) to labor (~60% of spend)
- That the October 2026 IPO timeline holds despite compute constraints
sections.second_order_implications:
**If the Agent Unit becomes the standard billing primitive for digital labor, it creates a new macroeconomic category.** Bureau of Labor Statistics doesn't track session-hours. Tax policy doesn't address them. The Brookings framework on AI taxation (also surfaced today) assumes robot-tax logic; session-hour billing creates a more natural unit for such taxation than token consumption.

**The "sorting" thesis accelerates.** The Metalayer "kills the wrapper whose value proposition was technical and not strategic" — companies that differentiated on "we built the agent infrastructure" lose that moat instantly at $0.08/session-hour. What survives: context depth, regulatory embeddedness, proximity to the business outcome. This directly extends the [prior KB analysis of the Orchestration Graph](../12/blog-stratechery-myth-and-mythos.md) and the [Conway/Cowork platform thesis](../../topics/anthropic-platform-strategy.md) Tim has been developing since February.
sections.my_take:
**This is the most important Anthropic strategy piece since d'Ornano's own Claude Code leak analysis.** The "Metalayer" and "Agent Unit" concepts are immediately useful vocabulary for investor conversations. The paradox framing (success = vulnerability) is the right level of sophisticated bearishness — not a takedown, but a serious structural risk analysis that should be in every pre-IPO diligence deck.

The piece's weakness is that it treats the compute constraint as more binding than it may turn out to be. The Google-Broadcom deal (3.5 GW from 2027) and the CoreWeave agreement may provide enough runway. But d'Ornano's core insight is sound: Anthropic is building a flywheel on rented ground, and the flywheel's speed is inversely correlated with the ground's stability.

For Tim: this directly extends the Anthropic platform strategy arc (topic 5) from "intelligence utility" to "labor utility." The session-hour reframing connects to AI labor economics (topic 8) in a way that the token-level conversation didn't. Worth citing in any conversation about Anthropic's IPO valuation.
sections.talking_points:
> **Anthropic isn't just selling intelligence — it's taxing digital labor at $0.08/session-hour.** Every synthetic colleague, regardless of who builds it, pays the Anthropic toll. The TAM shifts from IT budgets to the $60T global labor market. *(Best for: investor calls)*

> **The Metalayer paradox: the better it works, the faster it breaks.** Success accelerates compute demand on infrastructure Anthropic doesn't own. It's a flywheel on rented ground. *(Best for: VC roundtables)*

> **The advisor pattern is both product innovation and compute triage.** Opus-advises-Haiku delivers near-Opus quality at 85% less cost. When you're capacity-constrained, the most valuable innovation is the one that delivers comparable intelligence at lower intensity. *(Best for: founder chats)*

> **The Metalayer kills the "we built the agent infrastructure" wrapper companies.** When Anthropic gives away the runtime at $0.08/hr, the only surviving moat is context depth, regulatory embeddedness, and proximity to the business outcome. *(Best for: enterprise SaaS discussions)*

> **Watch for the session-hour to become the unit of digital labor economics.** Just as Databricks' DBU became the consumption unit for data, the Agent Unit could become the billing primitive that policymakers, analysts, and CFOs use to price AI labor. *(Best for: X posts)*

title: Neoclouds and the Three Business Models
author: Ben Bajarin

metadata.author: Ben Bajarin
metadata.title: Neoclouds and the Three Business Models
metadata.note: Preview/intro only — full report is paywalled

sections.tldr: **The "neocloud" category is actually three distinct businesses with different economics, risk profiles, and durability.** Full-stack AI platforms (CoreWeave, Nebius) capture $10-12M revenue per megawatt but carry hardware refresh, financing, and utilization risk. Bare-metal GPU clouds (IREN) monetize owned power and hardware with less software differentiation. Power Landlords (Core Scientific, Cipher, TeraWulf) — former bitcoin miners — may have the most durable economics because they sit lowest in the stack, avoid technology-refresh cycles, and generate ~$1.4M/MW from long-duration infrastructure hosting. The constraint is shifting from GPUs to deliverable power.
sections.whats_new:
**The novel contribution is the three-model taxonomy and the revenue-per-megawatt comparisons.** Previous coverage of neoclouds (including Data Gravity's earlier analysis that Tim has tracked) treated them as a single category competing for the same opportunity. Bajarin argues this is wrong. CoreWeave at $10-12M/MW and Core Scientific at $1.4M/MW aren't in the same business — one owns the technology stack and refresh risk, the other owns the dirt, power, and cooling. The 7-8x revenue spread reflects fundamentally different positions in the value chain, not different performance levels.

**The constraint-shift thesis is particularly sharp:** power is becoming the strategic asset that's hardest to replicate. Switchgear procurement takes a year. Transformers take 2+. High-voltage substations: 3-5 years. ERCOT reports 137 new large-load submissions totaling ~140,000 MW of potential demand by 2036. Companies that secured power early have advantages that capital alone cannot replicate.
sections.counterintuitive_claims:
**Lower in the stack may mean better on duration.** This inverts the conventional wisdom that capturing more of the value chain is always better. CoreWeave captures 7x more revenue per megawatt than Core Scientific, but also carries GPU depreciation risk on hardware whose economic life (3-4 years) is shorter than its accounting life (6 years). That duration mismatch is a "hidden fault line" per Bajarin. The Power Landlords avoid this entirely — their asset (power + cooling) doesn't depreciate the same way GPUs do.

**The hyperscaler paradox:** the same customers funding the neocloud buildout (Microsoft is 67% of CoreWeave's 2025 revenue, up from 62%) are the entities most capable of internalizing that demand. Microsoft outsources today because it's faster, but it's also building internal capacity. Concentration + renewal dynamics are the real risk, not demand.
sections.steelman:
**If AI demand is durable (and the backlog data suggests it is — $66.8B CoreWeave, $27B Nebius, $9.7B IREN with Microsoft), then the question is which business model converts that demand into sustainable returns.** The Power Landlord model is structurally superior on durability: power assets have 20-30 year lifespans, bitcoin miners already proved these sites work at scale, tenant credit quality is hyperscaler-grade, and there's no technology-refresh cycle to manage.

The full-stack model wins on revenue capture and optionality — CoreWeave's software stack and orchestration layer create stickiness and pricing power that a landlord can't match. But that stickiness comes with the risk that the technology you've built your stack around becomes obsolete in 2-3 years.
sections.key_assumptions:
1. **AI demand is durable at current levels for 3+ years.** The contracted backlog numbers support this, but contracts can be renegotiated or cancelled if the AI investment thesis weakens.
2. **Power remains the binding constraint.** If GPU supply catches up (post-Blackwell ramp), power replaces GPUs as the bottleneck. If GPU supply doesn't catch up, the GPU-owning neoclouds retain pricing power.
3. **Hyperscalers don't fully internalize neocloud demand.** Microsoft bringing capacity in-house would compress the entire category. The 67% revenue concentration is a structural risk.
sections.second_order_implications:
1. **The GPU-to-power constraint shift changes where value accrues.** If power is the bottleneck, Nvidia's leverage diminishes and energy companies/utilities gain strategic importance. This connects to Stratechery's April 13 analysis (already in KB: `2026/04/13/blog-stratechery-mythos-muse-compute.md`) where Thompson argued opportunity cost of compute is the binding constraint.

2. **Former bitcoin miners have an asymmetric advantage.** They already own permitted, powered, cooled sites that can be repurposed for AI inference. The bitcoin-to-AI infrastructure conversion is a real asset-light strategy with proven sites. This is an investable thesis for Tim.

3. **Token production optimization becomes the next competitive frontier.** Bajarin flags a key question: "which of these models is best positioned to deliver better customer economics as the market shifts from securing capacity to optimizing token production?" This connects to the session-hour economics from this morning's Decoding Discontinuity analysis.
sections.my_take:
**This is the sharpest infrastructure taxonomy I've seen for the neocloud category.** The three-model framework (full-stack platform / bare-metal GPU / Power Landlord) will become the standard analytical frame. The revenue-per-megawatt comparisons provide the quantitative backbone that most infrastructure analyses lack.

The bitcoin-miner-to-AI-infrastructure pipeline is particularly interesting for Tim's VC lens. Core Scientific, TeraWulf, and Cipher have proven power assets, hyperscaler-grade tenants, and long-duration contracts. They've done the hard work (permitting, power procurement, construction) that takes 3-5 years. The AI industry needs their sites now. That's a classic infrastructure-reuse play.

**One concern:** The preview doesn't address how Anthropic's Metalayer/Agent Unit pricing (from d'Ornano's analysis this morning) changes the demand picture. If Anthropic is pricing compute as session-hours rather than raw tokens, the "optimizing token production" question may matter less than "optimizing outcome-per-session." Different optimization targets favor different infrastructure models.
sections.talking_points:
> **"Neocloud" is three businesses, not one.** Full-stack platforms at $10-12M/MW, bare-metal at mid-range, and Power Landlords at $1.4M/MW. They look the same from the outside but have completely different risk profiles and durability. *(Best for: investor calls)*

> **Power is the new strategic moat.** GPUs can be manufactured; 3-5 year power procurement timelines cannot be accelerated with capital. The companies that secured power early have advantages that money can't buy. *(Best for: LP updates)*

> **Former bitcoin miners may have the most durable economics.** They already own the dirt, power, and cooling. They avoid GPU depreciation risk. Their assets last 20-30 years vs. 3-4 years for GPUs. And their tenants are hyperscalers with investment-grade credit. *(Best for: VC roundtables)*

> **Watch the 67% number.** Microsoft is 67% of CoreWeave's revenue and building internal capacity. The same customer funding the buildout could compress the opportunity. Contract renewal dynamics, not demand, are the real risk. *(Best for: due diligence conversations)*

title: When the AI Did It, Who Did It?
author: Carlo Iacono

metadata.author: Carlo Iacono
metadata.title: When the AI Did It, Who Did It?

sections.tldr: **A comprehensive legal-philosophical framework for AI governance, arguing that AI will require six new "legal primitives": digital replica rights, authenticity/provenance mandates, a law of machine delegation, due process for consequential AI decisions, cognitive liberty protections, and labor rights for algorithmic management.** The sharpest claim: "the AI did it" must never become a complete sentence in a court of law — responsibility must run uphill to builders, deployers, and profiteers, not downhill into the system.
sections.whats_new:
**The "legal primitives" framing is the most useful governance taxonomy published since Andy Hall's "Enlightened Absolutists."** Rather than arguing for or against a single AI statute, Iacono maps six distinct legal categories that will emerge piecemeal, each in response to specific scandals, and each retrofitted onto existing law. The taxonomy:

1. **Digital replica rights** — protection against unauthorized identity simulation (not style, which is too broad)
2. **Authenticity as traceability** — chain of custody for media, analogous to food labeling or court evidence
3. **Law of machine delegation** — a power-of-attorney rewrite for systems that act at machine speed across domains
4. **Due process for consequential AI decisions** — real rights to explanation, correction, and human appeal
5. **Cognitive liberty** — limits on systems optimized to exploit loneliness, grief, or cognitive decline
6. **Labor transition rights** — notice before substitution, contestable AI management decisions, portable retraining

**The camera analogy is structurally precise.** Warren and Brandeis wrote their foundational privacy article in 1890 because photography made an old moral intuition impossible to ignore. AI creates the same forcing function, but across six dimensions instead of one: fabricating, impersonating, deciding, persuading, delegating, and scaling become cheap simultaneously.
sections.counterintuitive_claims:
**AI personhood is a trap, not a solution.** It seems to solve the accountability problem by giving the machine a legal home, but actually "pushes responsibility downhill into the system, where it dissolves." The smarter direction is the opposite: responsibility runs uphill to builders, deployers, and profiteers. This directly contradicts the corporate-veil analogy in the thoughtful comment from a reader — but Iacono's point is that creating the entity *before* the accountability structures exist is the mistake.

**"Cognitive liberty" will be the defining legal fight of the decade, not copyright or deepfakes.** AI companion systems that are "always available, endlessly patient, emotionally adaptive, and optimised by people whose interests are not identical to yours" create a new asymmetry. A TV ad didn't know when you were lonely. A sales email didn't adapt to your grief in real time. Existing consumer protection law assumed roughly symmetrical persuasion.
sections.second_order_implications:
**The "law of machine delegation" connects directly to Anthropic's Managed Agents.** If agents can buy, book, sign, file, negotiate, and move money, then every session-hour on the Metalayer (see [today's Decoding Discontinuity analysis](blog-decodingdisc-digital-labor-tax.md)) is an act of delegation that needs a legal framework. Iacono gives 18 months before this becomes "operationally urgent." That timeline aligns with Anthropic's IPO and agent scaling roadmap.

**The training-data reckoning will produce a "mixed regime, not total prohibition or total freedom."** Licensing for some corpora, consent rules for sensitive material, documentation duties for major sources, and an unlearning right for personal data. This maps cleanly onto the EU AI Act's phased implementation.
sections.my_take:
**This is the strongest governance essay in the KB since Andy Hall's "Enlightened Absolutists" (see [prior analysis](../12/blog-freesystems-mythos-end-of-state.md)).** Where Hall focused on the political theory of AI lab governance, Iacono maps the legal infrastructure that society needs regardless of lab behavior. The six-primitive taxonomy is immediately useful for any governance conversation.

The weakness is that it's long on framework and short on political economy — who actually builds these legal primitives, and in what order, given Congressional dysfunction? Iacono's prediction (digital replica rights, provenance mandates, and due process arrive first; agent liability and cognitive liberty arrive later) is plausible but undefended.
sections.talking_points:
> **"The AI did it" must never become a complete sentence in a court of law.** Responsibility runs uphill to builders, deployers, and profiteers — not downhill into the system. *(Best for: governance discussions)*

> **We need six new legal primitives for AI, not one giant statute.** Digital replica rights, provenance mandates, machine delegation law, due process for AI decisions, cognitive liberty, and labor transition rights. *(Best for: policy conversations)*

> **Cognitive liberty is the defining legal fight of the decade.** AI companions that exploit loneliness and grief at zero marginal cost create an asymmetry that existing consumer protection law can't handle. *(Best for: X posts)*

> **Every agentic session-hour is an act of delegation that needs legal infrastructure.** If your agent agrees to something, is that your agreement? We have 18 months before this becomes operationally urgent. *(Best for: founder chats with enterprise companies)*

title: Lossy self-improvement
author: Nathan Lambert

metadata.author: Nathan Lambert
metadata.title: Lossy self-improvement

sections.tldr: **Lambert coins "Lossy Self-Improvement" (LSI) as an alternative to Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI), arguing that models are becoming core to their own development loop but friction breaks down all three RSI assumptions.** Three specific frictions: (1) automatable research is too narrow — agents optimize single metrics but can't navigate the multi-objective complexity that defines leading model development, (2) Amdahl's law caps the value of more agents — from 1 to 4 is huge, from 30 to 300 gives diminishing returns, and (3) resource bottlenecks and organizational politics introduce irreducible human friction. The bottom of every sigmoid feels like an exponential; we're on a sigmoid, not an exponential.
sections.whats_new:
**The Amdahl's law analogy for AI agent scaling is the sharpest contribution.** Lambert walks through the progression: hand-coding → AI autocomplete → autonomous agents → 3-4 agents on subtasks (huge gain) → 30-40 agents (manageable for some people) → 300-400 agents (who can generate that many tasks per day?). The parallelization ceiling is set by the human capacity to decompose problems and evaluate results, not by compute availability. This connects directly to the generation-verification gap: as you add more agents, the verification bottleneck tightens proportionally.

**The AutoML precedent is well-chosen.** During Lambert's PhD (2017-2022), AutoML (Bayesian Optimization for architectures and hyperparameters) was hyped as the thing that would replace ML researchers. "The hype never translated into changing my job." LLMs will do more than AutoML, but the pattern of "local optimization doesn't replace systemic insight" may repeat.
sections.counterintuitive_claims:
**"The bottom of every sigmoid feels like an exponential."** This is the central claim that cuts against the prevailing narrative. In Lambert's telling, GPT-4 (2023), reasoning models (2025), and AI-automated workflows (2026) are all S-curves, each delivering massive value but each with a ceiling. Stacking S-curves creates the *impression* of exponential progress without the underlying dynamics of a true self-amplifying loop.

**"Over 90% of the challenge in post-training is getting the last 1-3% of performance."** This is an insider claim that reframes the difficulty of model improvement. Agents can probably get the first 97% — that's the easy part. The gap between "good model" and "leading model" is where human intuition, multi-objective navigation, and taste dominate.
sections.steelman:
**The three RSI assumptions Lambert identifies are precise and testable.** For RSI to occur: (1) the loop must be closed (models improve models), (2) the loop must be self-amplifying (each generation yields bigger improvements), (3) the loop must run without losing efficiency. Lambert argues all three leak:

1. The loop is partially closed — models help optimize narrow metrics but can't design new paradigms (continual learning, world models).
2. The loop is not self-amplifying — the early gains are massive but the marginal value of the Nth agent declines sharply (Amdahl's law).
3. Friction accumulates — organizational politics, resource allocation decisions, and the complexity brake (Paul Allen) all introduce loss at each step.

The "lossy" framing is precise: information and value are lost at each step of the self-improvement cycle, preventing the exponential compounding that RSI requires. Self-improvement is real; its lossiness prevents takeoff.
sections.steelman_rebuttal:
**The complexity brake argument assumes AI research stays as complex as it currently is.** If a future model discovers a simplifying paradigm — the equivalent of transformers replacing LSTMs — the complexity brake releases. Lambert assumes the current optimization landscape is representative; a paradigm shift could flatten the landscape.

**Amdahl's law applies to fixed task decompositions, but AI might discover new decompositions.** If agents can not only work on sub-tasks but also discover new ways to decompose problems, the parallelization ceiling rises. This is speculative, but it's exactly the scenario that makes RSI proponents nervous.

**"The hype never translated into changing my job" is survivorship reasoning.** Lambert's job survived AutoML. Many ML engineering jobs did not — AutoML automated feature engineering and hyperparameter tuning at scale, eliminating entire categories of work. The frontier researchers survived; the median practitioners were affected.
sections.forward_looking_hypotheses:
- **2026 will feel like a huge step but won't exhibit fundamentally different dynamics** from 2023 or 2025. Each year adds a new S-curve; none produces a self-amplifying loop.
- **"Lossy self-improvement" is the operating regime for "a few years."** Lambert implicitly predicts that if takeoff doesn't happen by ~2028-2029, the case for RSI weakens substantially.
- **The colloquial AGI threshold (drop-in replacement for remote workers) may be crossed during the LSI era.** Models won't look like human replacements but will be "far more effective than trying to work with a human" for many tasks.
sections.key_assumptions:
- That the complexity brake holds — complexity continues to increase faster than AI's ability to manage it. If not, the friction Lambert identifies evaporates.
- That human taste and multi-objective navigation remain irreducible bottlenecks. If models develop emergent "taste" for what makes a good model, the AutoML precedent breaks.
- That organizational politics and resource allocation are structural, not contingent. A sufficiently well-organized lab might eliminate friction #3.
sections.second_order_implications:
- **Investment thesis: the "LSI economy" rewards infrastructure, not moonshots.** If self-improvement is real but lossy, the value accrues to companies that make the self-improvement loop more efficient (better harnesses, better verification, better agent coordination) rather than companies betting on RSI takeoff.
- **The verification bottleneck is the loss function.** Every loss in Lambert's framework is a verification failure — the agent optimizes the wrong metric, the parallel agents duplicate work, the org allocates resources suboptimally. This connects directly to Tim's generation-verification gap thesis: the "loss" in lossy self-improvement *is* the verification gap.
- **The Karpathy autoresearch pattern is the current ceiling.** Karpathy's autoresearch (optimizing a single loss on GPUs) represents the maximum current automation of AI research. Everything above it — multi-objective optimization, paradigm selection, taste — remains human-bottlenecked.
sections.my_take:
**Lambert is one of the few people with both the technical depth and the intellectual honesty to make this argument stick.** He's not dismissing RSI from the outside — he's an AI researcher who uses these tools daily and sees their limitations firsthand. The "lossy" framing is genuinely useful: it captures the reality that self-improvement is happening (not a myth) while identifying specifically where and how it degrades (not magic).

The connection to Tim's KB is rich. The generation-verification gap (topic #1 in the taxonomy) is essentially the mechanism that makes self-improvement lossy — agents generate improvements they can't fully verify. The Amdahl's law argument extends Tim's thinking on agent reliability (topic #3): adding more agents doesn't help if each additional agent needs proportionally more verification.

The piece is from March 22 — before the Mythos release and the current RSI discourse peak. It reads as prescient in hindsight: Mythos demonstrated exactly the kind of narrow capability improvement (93.9% SWE-bench) that Lambert would classify as an S-curve gain, not an RSI signal.
sections.talking_points:
> **"The bottom of every sigmoid feels like an exponential."** Three S-curves in three years (GPT-4, reasoning models, AI-automated research) create the illusion of takeoff. It's stacked S-curves, not RSI. *(Best for: LP updates, VC roundtables)*

> **Amdahl's law for AI agents: from 1 to 4 is huge, from 300 to 400 is nothing.** The parallelization ceiling for AI research isn't compute — it's human capacity to decompose problems and evaluate results. The verification bottleneck *is* the loss in lossy self-improvement. *(Best for: investor calls, founder chats)*

> **The LSI economy rewards infrastructure, not moonshots.** If self-improvement is real but lossy, invest in companies that reduce the loss — better harnesses, better verification, better agent coordination — not companies betting on takeoff. *(Best for: investment committee)*

> **90% of post-training difficulty is the last 1-3% of performance.** Agents can get you to "good." Getting from "good" to "leading" requires human taste, multi-objective navigation, and intuition that no current model has. *(Best for: technical founder chats)*

title: Notion's Token Town: 5 Rebuilds, 100+ Tools, MCP vs CLIs and the Software Factory Future
author: swyx, Alessio Fanelli, Simon Last, Sarah Sachs

metadata.author: swyx, Alessio Fanelli, Simon Last, Sarah Sachs
metadata.title: Notion's Token Town: 5 Rebuilds, 100+ Tools, MCP vs CLIs and the Software Factory Future

sections.tldr: **Notion rebuilt their agent harness five times over 3.5 years, and the history of those rebuilds is a masterclass in what "agent lab" engineering actually looks like at enterprise scale.** Simon Last (co-founder) and Sarah Sachs (head of AI) reveal that the key lessons weren't about waiting for better models — they were about giving models what they want (markdown over custom XML, SQL over JSON query formats), progressive tool disclosure at 100+ tools, and distributing tool ownership across the entire engineering org rather than gatekeeping a single system prompt file.
sections.whats_new:
**The five rebuilds tell a story most agent companies won't share publicly.** Version 1 was a JavaScript coding agent (2022) — models were too bad at code. Version 2 was custom XML tool-calling before tool-calling existed — models hated the custom format. Version 3 switched to markdown and SQL-like abstractions — breakthrough in model compatibility. Version 4 moved from few-shot prompting to tool definitions — enabled distributed ownership across teams. Version 5 (shipping now) adds progressive disclosure over 100+ tools with agent-to-agent invocation.

The non-obvious insight: **the transition from few-shot to tool definitions was the biggest organizational unlock**, not just a technical one. When the agent harness was a single few-shot prompt file, only 5-6 people could touch it. Tool definitions let every product team own their own tools and evals. This is the "platform team" transformation that most agent startups haven't hit yet.
sections.counterintuitive_claims:
**"Coding agents are the kernel of AGI"** — Simon Last argues that everything converges to coding agents because an agent that can write, debug, and maintain code can bootstrap its own capabilities. This inverts the usual framing where coding agents are just one vertical.

**Notion deliberately does NOT optimize for ease of use in Custom Agents.** Sarah Sachs: "We're not trying to build the user experience that anyone can figure out how to use. The more we do that, the more we diminish its capabilities." They explicitly build for power users ("teach the top of the class") rather than abstracting away capability. This cuts against the typical product-led-growth playbook.

**Memory is just pages and databases — no special memory abstraction.** Rather than building a bespoke agent memory system, Notion gives agents edit access to a page. The agent writes its own memory there. Humans can edit it too. This is radically simple compared to the vector-store-backed memory architectures most agent frameworks use.
sections.technical_insights:
**Progressive tool disclosure is the scaling bottleneck they solved.** At 100+ tools, showing all tools in the system prompt was both token-expensive ("saying hello was thousands of tokens") and quality-degrading (any engineer adding a niche tool could nerf overall performance). Their solution: tool search and progressive disclosure — the agent discovers tools as needed rather than seeing everything upfront.

**MCP vs CLI — a nuanced position.** Simon is bullish on CLI because: (1) it lives in a terminal environment with pagination and progressive disclosure built in, (2) it's self-debugging (if a tool breaks, the agent can fix it in the same environment), (3) it can bootstrap new capabilities (an agent without a browser built itself one in 100 lines). MCP's advantage: strong permission model (tools only), simpler for narrow/lightweight agents. Sarah adds the cost angle — repeated MCP token costs for deterministic tasks that should just be code.

**Model Behavior Engineer is a real role at Notion** — not software engineers, not PMs. They come from diverse backgrounds (linguistics PhDs, new grads) and combine qualitative judgment with eval engineering. They triage failures, define headroom evals, and write LLM judges. Notion has a conviction that this is "its own career path" that doesn't require an engineering background.

**Three-tier eval system:** (1) Regression tests in CI with stochastic pass-rate thresholds, (2) Launch-quality evals as a product report card, (3) "Frontier/headroom" evals intentionally at ~30% pass rate to track where model capabilities are heading. They call this "Notion's Last Exam."
sections.steelman: **The strongest version of Notion's thesis:** Notion is becoming the Datadog of knowledge work — an expert observation and orchestration layer that sits on top of foundation model infrastructure, the way Datadog sits on top of cloud infrastructure. AWS has CloudWatch, but Datadog understands how engineers actually want observability. Similarly, every model provider offers agents, but Notion understands how enterprise teams actually collaborate. The 100+ tools, the progressive disclosure, the distributed ownership model, the three-tier eval system — these are the "secret sauce" that a model provider can't replicate because they're built from understanding millions of real workflows, not from model capability alone.
sections.steelman_rebuttal:
**The counter-thesis:** Notion's agent strategy depends on remaining the "system of record" for knowledge work. But if coding agents (which Simon himself calls "the kernel of AGI") continue improving, the locus of work moves from Notion pages to code repositories and agent-native environments. The "software factory" vision — agents that spec, code, test, debug, review — may end up living in GitHub/VS Code/Cursor rather than Notion databases. Notion risks being the collaboration layer for humans while the actual work happens elsewhere.

Additionally, the "teach the top of the class" strategy explicitly sacrifices breadth. If a simpler competitor (even a model provider's built-in agents) captures the 80% of users who don't want 100+ tools and progressive disclosure, Notion's agent product could end up as a power-user niche.
sections.second_order_implications:
- **Agent-to-agent invocation without special protocols** — Notion's approach (shared databases as coordination primitives, webhook triggers) suggests that multi-agent coordination may not need fancy new protocols. Existing data infrastructure (databases, webhooks, task queues) may be sufficient.
- **"Manager agents" as the natural abstraction layer** — When one user built 30 custom agents and got 70 notifications/day, the answer was a manager agent that reduced it to 5. This pattern (agent hierarchy with human-in-the-loop at the top) will likely emerge in every enterprise agent deployment.
- **The Model Behavior Engineer role signals a new labor category** — Notion is creating a career path that doesn't exist at most companies. If this role scales across the industry, it could absorb some of the "mid-career squeeze" displacement from traditional engineering roles.
sections.my_take:
**This is the most substantive "how we actually build agents" interview published in 2026.** Most agent content is either abstract (frameworks, benchmarks) or surface-level (product announcements). This goes deep on the organizational and engineering decisions that actually determine whether an agent product works at enterprise scale. The five-rebuild history is genuinely instructive — every rebuild taught a lesson that applies broadly.

The MCP vs CLI nuance is particularly valuable. Simon's point about self-debugging (CLI agents can fix their own tools; MCP agents can't fix a broken transport) is an underappreciated insight that will influence how harness architectures evolve. Sarah's cost-alignment point (repeated LLM calls for deterministic tasks is wasteful) is the kind of pragmatic insight that separates real operators from demo builders.

The "Notion's Last Exam" concept — headroom evals intentionally at 30% pass rate — deserves its own KB topic. It's the most sophisticated eval strategy I've seen from a non-lab company, and it directly connects to the [generation-verification gap](../../topics/verification-and-evaluation.md) theme Tim has been tracking.
sections.talking_points:
> **Notion rebuilt their agent harness five times in 3.5 years. The lesson isn't patience — it's that the transition from few-shot prompting to distributed tool definitions was a bigger unlock than any model improvement.** When only 5 people can touch the system prompt, you can't scale. *(Best for: founder chats)*

> **"Coding agents are the kernel of AGI" — Notion's co-founder argues everything converges there because code-writing agents can bootstrap their own capabilities.** The software factory (agents that spec, code, test, review, deploy) is the endgame, not a vertical. *(Best for: investor calls)*

> **MCP vs CLI isn't a religious war — it's a cost-and-capability tradeoff.** CLI wins on self-debugging and bootstrapping. MCP wins on permissions and lightweight agents. The real question is whether you're paying repeated token costs for tasks that should be deterministic code. *(Best for: VC roundtables)*

> **Notion invented a new role: "Model Behavior Engineer." It doesn't require a CS degree.** Linguistics PhDs and new grads who combine qualitative judgment with eval writing. This may be the first new enterprise job category created by the agent era. *(Best for: X)*

title: The Most Important Ideas in AI Right Now (April 2026)
author: Daniel Miessler

metadata.author: Daniel Miessler
metadata.title: The Most Important Ideas in AI Right Now (April 2026)

sections.tldr: **Miessler identifies five interlocking ideas reshaping AI: autonomous component improvement, intent-based engineering, transparency, the scaffolding revelation (75-99% of knowledge work is overhead), and expertise diffusion into public knowledge.** The core claim is that these five dynamics are compounding — improvement speed itself is accelerating — and the entities that adopt the define→execute→log→improve cycle first will compound so fast that laggards can't catch up.
sections.whats_new:
**The "scaffolding revelation" is the strongest original contribution.** Miessler's claim is precise and falsifiable: 75-99% of knowledge work is scaffolding overhead — the maintenance of tooling, workflows, templates, knowledge bases, and contextual understanding required for work to happen. The actual hard thinking is "a tiny percentage, done by a tiny percentage of people, a tiny percentage of the time." AI crushes the scaffolding part, not the thinking part.

This connects powerfully to Tim's existing KB themes:
- **Agent architecture / harness design** (see [topics/agent-infrastructure.md](../../topics/agent-infrastructure.md)): Miessler's scaffolding insight is the labor-economics corollary of the "harness > model" thesis. The harness IS scaffolding — and if AI can automate it, the remaining human contribution is intent and judgment.
- **Generation-verification gap** (see [topics/verification-and-evaluation.md](../../topics/verification-and-evaluation.md)): Miessler frames verification as "evals for everything" — a universal measurement layer. This echoes Karpathy's Software 2.0 framing (future of software is verification, not generation).
- **AI labor economics**: The scaffolding revelation predicts which workers are most vulnerable — not those doing the hardest thinking, but those maintaining the most complex scaffolding (legal workflows, dev environments, consulting templates).
sections.counterintuitive_claims:
**The articulation gap is the new bottleneck, not model capability or compute.** Miessler argues that the scarce skill isn't coding, prompting, or even domain expertise — it's being able to articulate what you actually want in terms precise enough for AI to verify and optimize against. "Ask a CEO what their ideal security program looks like and you'll get hand-waving." The companies that figure out intent specification first get to point all the optimization tools at real targets while everyone else is still hand-waving about OKRs.

**Expertise becomes public infrastructure.** The one-way ratchet: "Humans take 20-30 years to develop deep expertise in a single domain. They forget things, they retire, they leave companies. AI absorbs all captured expertise instantly, never forgets, and can be duplicated infinitely." Once knowledge is extracted into skills, SOPs, and context files, it permanently enters the collective knowledge base. This is the mechanism behind the scaffolding commoditization.
sections.steelman:
**Miessler's strongest argument is the compounding loop.** The five ideas aren't parallel trends — they feed each other:

1. Transparency reveals that most work is scaffolding
2. AI commoditizes the scaffolding, freeing resources
3. Freed resources go to intent specification and measurement
4. Better measurement enables autonomous improvement (autoresearch for X)
5. Autonomous improvement accelerates all of the above

The critical insight: "the speed of the improvement itself will improve." This is a recursive self-improvement argument, but framed at the organizational level rather than the model level. It's RSI for companies, not for AI systems. The Karpathy Autoresearch connection makes it concrete — this isn't speculative; people are already running autonomous optimization loops on their workflows.
sections.steelman_rebuttal:
**The 75-99% scaffolding claim is unfalsifiable as stated and likely overfitted to Miessler's domain (cybersecurity).** In security testing, yes — 99% of the work is tooling, environment setup, and workflow maintenance. But in surgery, therapy, teaching, or political negotiation, the scaffolding-to-substance ratio is very different. Miessler's examples (security, development, consulting) are all domains where the work product is digital and the context is machine-readable. For domains where the work product is embodied, relational, or requires real-time judgment under uncertainty, the scaffolding fraction is much lower.

**The "articulation gap" thesis has a circularity problem.** If the hardest part of leveraging AI is articulating intent precisely, and AI is supposed to replace the scaffolding around that articulation, then who does the articulation? Miessler's answer (humans do, but with AI help) doesn't fully resolve this — it just moves the bottleneck one level up. At some point, the articulation itself becomes the scaffolding.

**The autonomous improvement loop assumes verifiability.** Miessler's entire framework depends on being able to define what "good" looks like for any workflow. But many of the highest-value knowledge work outputs — strategy documents, investment memos, product visions — are precisely the ones where "good" is subjective, contextual, and only knowable in retrospect. The generation-verification gap that Tim tracks extensively in this KB applies to Miessler's framework too: autonomous improvement only works in domains where verification is cheap.
sections.technical_insights:
**The "universal improvement cycle" is a concrete architecture.** Miessler proposes: Map goals → Execute with agents → Log everything → Collect failures → Improve autonomously → Update SOPs → Repeat. This maps cleanly to the RL loop (state → action → reward → policy update) applied at the organizational level. The connection to Karpathy's Autoresearch is apt — Autoresearch runs this loop for ML hyperparameter search; Miessler is generalizing it to any measurable workflow.

**The RLHF supply chain data is a useful aside.** Miessler documents the scale of the human expertise extraction industry: Scale AI (700K+ experts, Meta's 49% stake for $14.3B), Surge AI ($1B+ revenue), and several smaller players. This is the economic infrastructure behind the "expertise diffusion" thesis — these companies are literally extracting human knowledge into training data at industrial scale.
sections.second_order_implications:
**If scaffolding is 75-99% of knowledge work and AI commoditizes it, the labor market implications are massive.** The O-ring model predicts displacement is worst where tasks are *chainable* and *independently automatable*. Scaffolding tasks are both. This means the mid-career professionals whose value comes from maintaining complex scaffolding (senior developers who "know the codebase," consultants who "know the templates," lawyers who "know the process") are more exposed than the commonly cited "entry-level" targets.

This directly extends the mid-career squeeze thesis already tracked in the KB via the Imas O-ring framework and the Pragmatic Engineer's AI impact analysis (see [blog-pragmaticengineer-ai-impact-swe-2026.md](blog-pragmaticengineer-ai-impact-swe-2026.md)).

**The transparency thesis implies a new competitive moat: measurability.** Companies that can describe their workflows precisely enough for AI to verify and optimize will compound faster than those that can't. This is a variant of the "decision traces as moat" thesis from the Diligence Stack (see [topics/agent-infrastructure.md](../../topics/agent-infrastructure.md)) — but Miessler frames it as an offense rather than defense. You don't just accumulate traces; you run autonomous improvement loops on them.
sections.my_take:
**This is the most compelling practitioner-level synthesis of how AI changes work that I've seen in the KB to date.** Miessler isn't an economist or a theorist — he's a cybersecurity veteran who built his own AI infrastructure (PAI) and is reasoning from direct experience about what breaks when you automate real workflows.

The scaffolding insight is genuinely powerful. It reframes the AI labor debate from "which jobs get automated?" to "which parts of jobs were never really the job?" That's a subtler and more actionable question. It also explains why the macro statistics on AI displacement are still flat despite obvious capability gains — the scaffolding is being automated first, and it's invisible in job-level data because the job title stays the same even as 80% of the actual work changes.

The piece's weakness is ambition: five big ideas in one post means none gets fully developed. The autonomous improvement loop deserves a 5,000-word treatment on its own. The scaffolding claim needs empirical grounding beyond cybersecurity anecdotes. But as a map of the territory — a sketch of how all these AI trends connect — it's excellent.

**New source: danielmiessler.com.** Not in Tim's subscription list or url_sources, but covers agent architecture, scaffolding/harness design, verification, and labor economics from a practitioner angle. The PAI (Personal AI Infrastructure) framework he's building is architecturally interesting and maps to several KB themes. Worth adding to discovered sources.
sections.talking_points:
> **75-99% of knowledge work is scaffolding, and AI crushes scaffolding.** The actual hard thinking is a tiny fraction of the work. The rest — tooling, templates, workflows, context maintenance — is overhead. AI doesn't need to be smarter than experts; it needs to be better at maintaining the infrastructure experts need to do their jobs. *(Best for: founder conversations about product strategy)*

> **The new scarce skill is articulating intent, not coding.** If AI handles scaffolding, the bottleneck moves to: can you describe what "good" looks like precisely enough for AI to verify and optimize? Most leaders can't. The "articulation gap" is the next competitive frontier. *(Best for: VC roundtables, LP updates)*

> **Autonomous improvement loops are the new operating model.** Define goals → execute with agents → log everything → collect failures → improve autonomously → repeat. Karpathy's Autoresearch proved this for ML; Miessler is generalizing it to every measurable workflow. The entities that adopt this first compound so fast that laggards can't catch up. *(Best for: X, investor calls)*

> **The mid-career squeeze is worse than the entry-level one.** If scaffolding is the part being automated, the most exposed workers aren't juniors — they're the senior developers who "know the codebase," the consultants who "know the templates," the lawyers who "know the process." Their value was maintaining scaffolding, not doing the hard thinking. *(Best for: AI labor economics discussions)*

title: Sora Died. Atlassian Cut 1,600 Engineers. Anthropic Got Blacklisted.
author: Nate

metadata.author: Nate
metadata.title: Sora Died. Atlassian Cut 1,600 Engineers. Anthropic Got Blacklisted.

sections.tldr: **The AI industry is leaving the capability phase and entering the economics phase.** Nate threads five seemingly unrelated March 2026 events — Sora's death ($15M/day inference vs $2.1M lifetime revenue), Criteo's 1.5x conversion rates in ChatGPT, Atlassian cutting 1,600 engineers while cloud revenue grew 26%, data center infrastructure blockades across 12 states, and Anthropic's Pentagon blacklisting — into a single argument: the question is no longer "what can we build?" but "what can we sustain?"
sections.whats_new:
**The Sora economics are the sharpest data point on inference cost reality published this year.** $15 million/day in inference costs against $2.1 million in total lifetime revenue. That's a >2,500:1 cost-to-revenue ratio. Nate argues the "physics of why" apply to every AI product being built, not just video generation. This is the hardest evidence yet for the inference economics thesis that Data Gravity and the Diligence Stack have been developing (see [prior KB coverage](../../topics/compute-and-scaling.md)).

**The Atlassian data point crystallizes the SaaS repricing thesis.** Cloud revenue up 26% and stock down 84% from peak. Wall Street isn't pricing the present — it's pricing a future where AI agents don't need software seats. The per-seat model, the most durable business model in enterprise tech for 20 years, is being repriced in real time before seat counts even decline. This is the leading indicator for the SaaS disruption Tim has tracked since the Bessemer/Newcomer "legacy SaaS is dead" piece in March.
sections.counterintuitive_claims:
**Anthropic's Pentagon blacklisting was net positive for its commercial position.** Getting blacklisted by the U.S. government for refusing to build autonomous weapons, then watching the Claude app go to #1 on the App Store the same week, demonstrates that "safety posture became a market position." Enterprise and government buyers are now using the lab's disposition on weapons as a real procurement criterion.

**The first real ad dollar in an AI interface may be more consequential than any model release.** Criteo's ChatGPT integration produced 1.5x the conversion rate of search — "the first credible threat to Google's $300 billion ad model." If AI interfaces capture ad intent better than search, the economics of the entire digital advertising stack shift.
sections.key_assumptions:
- That inference cost physics generalizes from video (Sora) to text/agent workloads
- That per-seat SaaS repricing is structural, not cyclical
- That safety posture creates durable market differentiation (not just a news cycle)
- That the data center infrastructure blockade (12 states, 50+ local governments, Iranian drone threats) will meaningfully constrain supply
sections.second_order_implications:
**The "economics phase" framing suggests a transition from a model capability race to a unit economics race.** This reorients the competitive landscape: the winners aren't whoever has the best model, but whoever can serve it profitably. This directly supports d'Ornano's "Metalayer" analysis (see [today's Decoding Discontinuity analysis](blog-decodingdisc-digital-labor-tax.md)) — Anthropic's advisor pattern is an economics-phase product, not a capability-phase one.

**Atlassian's 26%-growth-yet-84%-decline pattern is the template for SaaS repricing.** If the market prices AI-driven seat compression before it shows up in revenue, every incumbent SaaS company with per-seat pricing faces the same dynamic. The Menlo VC "Software Finally Gets to Work" thesis and the Bessemer "legacy SaaS is dead" narrative both predict this, but Atlassian puts hard numbers on it.
sections.my_take:
**Nate's core framing — capability phase → economics phase — is the single most useful lens for understanding March/April 2026.** It explains why Mythos matters (economics of restricted access), why Sora died (inference economics), why Atlassian got crushed (business model economics), and why Anthropic's Pentagon standoff was net positive (brand economics). Every other analyst is still covering the capability race; Nate has correctly identified that the game has shifted.

Note: This analysis is based on the free preview; the full post is paywalled. The five signal threads described in the preview are sufficiently detailed for the analysis above.
sections.talking_points:
> **The AI industry just entered its economics phase.** The question is no longer "what can we build?" — it's "what can we sustain?" Sora's $15M/day inference costs are the proof point. *(Best for: investor calls)*

> **Atlassian: 26% cloud growth, stock down 84%.** The market is pricing AI-driven seat compression before it shows up in the numbers. Every per-seat SaaS company faces this. *(Best for: enterprise SaaS discussions)*

> **Sora died on unit economics, not capability.** $15M/day inference against $2.1M total lifetime revenue. The physics of why apply to every AI product. Inference cost is the new bottleneck. *(Best for: founder chats)*

> **Safety posture is now a procurement criterion.** Anthropic got blacklisted by the Pentagon for refusing autonomous weapons — and went to #1 on the App Store the same week. *(Best for: governance conversations)*

title: The Impact of AI on Software Engineers in 2026: Key Trends
author: Gergely Orosz

metadata.author: Gergely Orosz
metadata.title: The Impact of AI on Software Engineers in 2026: Key Trends

sections.tldr: **A 900+ response survey of software engineers reveals that AI tools are creating three distinct archetypes — Builders, Shippers, and Coasters — with divergent impacts on each.** The headline findings: ~30% of engineers hit usage limits regularly, AI tool costs are viewed as unsustainable by leadership, European companies are more cost-conscious than US ones, and the most unexpected trend is "identity loss" among senior engineers who can no longer justify hands-on coding.
sections.whats_new:
**The Builder/Shipper/Coaster taxonomy is the most useful segmentation of AI's labor impact published this year.** Builders (quality-focused senior engineers) get value from large refactors and "quality of life" tasks, but suffer from reviewing AI slop and experiencing identity loss. Shippers (outcome-focused product engineers) are the most enthusiastic. Coasters (adequate-but-undifferentiated engineers) are upleveling faster but generating the most AI slop, frustrating Builders.

**The cost data is the sharpest empirical evidence of the inference economics squeeze.** Companies pay ~$200/month per engineer for max plans, but heavy users regularly blow through budgets. One CTO ran up $600/month on Cursor alone. The pattern: subsidies keep things at bay for now, but the AI hype cycle is "dampening awkward conversations about budgets." When subsidies end, the same vendor lock-in playbook from cloud pricing will apply.

**Identity loss among Builders is an underreported psychological effect.** Senior engineers report "a sense of identity loss and even some grief" because they can no longer justify hands-on coding when agents generate decent code faster. This is the *qualitative* face of the mid-career squeeze that Simon Willison and Lenny described in quantitative terms (see [prior KB coverage of the mid-career squeeze](../../topics/ai-labor-economics.md)).
sections.counterintuitive_claims:
**The engineering manager role is becoming more similar to the engineer role, not more different.** As engineers shift to orchestrating and context-switching (away from writing code), and managers can be more hands-on (using AI tools directly), the two roles converge. This inverts the traditional assumption that AI widens the gap between technical and managerial tracks.

**EU/UK companies are significantly more cost-sensitive to AI tools than US companies.** Finance teams in Europe push back on even £25/month per engineer, while US companies adopt "invest first, measure later" approaches. If AI tool costs rise (as most respondents expect), the transatlantic gap in AI adoption could widen.
sections.second_order_implications:
**The Coaster problem creates a verification bottleneck at team level.** If less-skilled engineers generate more AI slop while Builders spend more time reviewing it, the effective output of the team may not improve as much as the raw code volume suggests. This is the O-ring model at the team level: automating code generation increases the value of the remaining bottleneck task (code review and architectural judgment).

**The DHH anecdote about P1 optimization is the clearest example of "expanding the pie."** An engineer used agents to optimize the fastest 1% of requests — a project that would never have been prioritized pre-AI. 12 PRs, 2,500 lines changed, done as a side project in days. This is the augmentation thesis in action: AI doesn't replace the engineer, it lets them do work that was previously below the economic threshold.
sections.talking_points:
> **AI tools create three types of engineer: Builders, Shippers, and Coasters. Each is affected differently.** Shippers love it, Builders are grieving, Coasters are generating slop. The team-level question is whether the slop overwhelms the speed. *(Best for: founder chats)*

> **30% of engineers regularly hit AI usage limits — and the response is to switch tools, not stop working.** The modal engineer in 2026 has 2-3 AI tools and rotates between them based on which has quota left. *(Best for: enterprise AI discussions)*

> **The most surprising finding: senior engineers are experiencing identity loss.** They can no longer justify writing code by hand when agents do it faster. The craft of software engineering is being redefined in real time. *(Best for: X posts)*

> **AI tool costs are unsustainable at current subsidized rates.** Most respondents expect prices to rise. When they do, the cloud vendor lock-in playbook repeats: subsidize → lock in → raise prices. *(Best for: investor calls)*

title: Components of A Coding Agent
author: Sebastian Raschka

metadata.author: Sebastian Raschka
metadata.title: Components of A Coding Agent

sections.tldr: **Raschka decomposes coding agent harnesses into six components and argues that "a lot of apparent model quality is really context quality."** The six: (1) live repo context, (2) prompt shape and cache reuse, (3) structured tools with validation and permissions, (4) context reduction and output management, (5) structured session memory (dual-layer: working memory + full transcript), and (6) delegation with bounded subagents. He backs this with a minimal open-source implementation (Mini Coding Agent) in pure Python. The headline claim: drop a top open-weight model like GLM-5 into a comparable harness and it likely matches GPT-5.4 in Codex or Opus 4.6 in Claude Code.
sections.whats_new:
**The dual-layer memory architecture (working memory vs. full transcript) is the most precisely articulated component.** Most discussions of agent memory blur the distinction between "what goes back into the prompt" (compact transcript — for prompt reconstruction) and "what the agent explicitly maintains as task state" (working memory — for task continuity). Raschka separates them cleanly: the compact transcript is a compression strategy for the next model call; working memory is a persistent, curated summary of what matters across turns. Both are stored as JSON on disk, both contribute to the prompt, but they serve different purposes and have different update cadences.

**The "context quality > model quality" thesis is stated more boldly than anyone else.** By claiming that putting GLM-5 into the right harness would match GPT-5.4 in Codex, Raschka is saying that the model is approximately 0% of the differential between good and bad coding agents — the harness is ~100%. This is further than even the OpenAI harness engineering team goes (see `2026/04/13/blog-openai-harness-engineering.md`), where they focused on harness *alongside* the model.
sections.technical_insights:
**The six components, concretely:**

1. **Live repo context** — workspace snapshot (git branch, status, README, AGENTS.md) collected before any work starts. "Stable facts" that ground every subsequent prompt.

2. **Prompt shape and cache reuse** — stable prefix (instructions + tools + workspace summary) separated from changing state (recent transcript + working memory + user request). The stable prefix is designed for API prompt cache reuse — the provider skips re-processing tokens that haven't changed.

3. **Structured tools with validation and permissions** — pre-defined named tools with input validation, path sandboxing (files must be inside workspace), and approval gates for risky operations. "The harness is giving the model less freedom, but it also improves usability."

4. **Context reduction and output management** — clipping (cap any single output to prevent one verbose result from consuming the budget), transcript reduction (compress older events, keep recent events richer), and deduplication (don't re-insert the same file content read multiple times).

5. **Structured session memory** — dual-layer: working memory (small, curated, modified rather than appended) + full transcript (append-only, resumable). The distinction between these and the compact transcript (section 4) is subtle but important: the compact transcript is for prompt construction, session memory is for task continuity across turns and sessions.

6. **Delegation with bounded subagents** — spawn subtasks that inherit context but run in tighter boundaries (read-only, recursion depth limits). Key design problem: "not just how to spawn a subagent but also how to bind one."
sections.counterintuitive_claims:
**"If we dropped GLM-5 into a similar harness, it could likely perform on par with GPT-5.4 in Codex."** This is a strong empirical claim. It implies that harness-specific post-training (the difference between GPT-5.3 and GPT-5.3-Codex) adds relatively little compared to the harness itself. Counter-evidence: Terminal Bench 2.0 shows Opus 4.6 drops from #5 in an open harness to #33 in Claude Code specifically — suggesting harness-model coupling matters more than Raschka implies.

**Context management is "one of the underrated, boring parts."** Raschka argues that clipping, deduplication, and transcript compression drive more user-perceived quality improvement than model upgrades. This connects to Anthropic's Managed Agents argument that "irreversible decisions to selectively retain or discard context can lead to failures" (see `2026/04/14/blog-anthropic-scaling-managed-agents.md`).
sections.key_assumptions:
- That the six components are relatively stable across coding agent paradigms. If a new paradigm emerges (e.g., agents that operate on ASTs rather than text files, or agents that use formal verification rather than test execution), the component decomposition may shift.
- That prompt cache reuse is a first-order performance driver. This depends on provider-side caching behavior — if the model provider doesn't offer prompt caching (or changes its caching policy), this optimization evaporates.
