**"The U.S. will slowly regain ground in adoption metrics starting in early 2027."** Lambert cites Google's Gemma 4, Nvidia's Nemotron, and Arcee AI as the vanguard. This reverses the current narrative that China dominates open-model adoption.
sections.steelman:
**The strongest version of Lambert's argument is the "economics trumps ability" thesis.** The open-closed gap is determined by who can sustain funding for frontier training runs, not by whether the models themselves are technically inferior. As training costs scale, the number of entities that can independently fund frontier open models shrinks. This creates a structural dependency that sovereigns and institutions will eventually find intolerable — driving new funding mechanisms (his consortium thesis from the prior Interconnects piece, `kb/2026/04/14/blog-interconnects-open-model-consortium.md`).

The 13 positions together paint a coherent picture: open models win on price and availability for repetitive automation, closed models win on quality for knowledge-work assistants, and the long-run equilibrium depends on whether new institutional funding structures can sustain frontier open training.
sections.steelman_rebuttal:
**The weakest link is position #4: "closed models tend to be more robust and generally useful than similarly scoring open models."** Lambert acknowledges this is "hard to measure" — which is exactly the kind of claim that could be selection bias or vibes masquerading as analysis. The Lindy/Altimor tweet analysis from this morning (`kb/2026/04/14/2044108104816832576-altimor-oss-models-frontier.md`) argues the opposite: OSS models have crossed the frontier for *most* use cases, with GLM-5.1 as the new default. If robustness improves as a byproduct of scale + better post-training (which the Chinese labs are investing in), Lambert's quality moat could evaporate faster than his 2027 timeline suggests.

The RL-from-distribution moat (position #6) also has a counter: if open models deployed in enterprise backends generate usage data, third parties can run similar RL pipelines. The moat depends on distribution being concentrated at a few labs, which is exactly the scenario Lambert says open models are designed to prevent.
sections.forward_looking_hypotheses:
**Lambert embeds several testable bets:**

1. Chinese open-weight labs face funding difficulties by late 2026 (position #5)
2. Capability trajectory divergence visible 3-9 months after funding stress (implied: Q1-Q3 2027)
3. U.S. regains open-model adoption metrics starting early 2027 (position #9)
4. Safety-shocks from frontier model releases spur burdensome open-model regulation (position #10)
5. New funding structures for open models emerge (position #12) — the consortium thesis
6. Local agents and OpenClaw represent "dark matter" demand for open models (position #13)
sections.technical_insights:
**The RL-from-distribution thesis is technically rigorous.** Lambert cites Cursor's real-time RL for Composer as evidence that user-feedback loops during agentic workflows create a capability advantage that open models can't replicate without equivalent distribution. This connects directly to the KB's verification theme: the generation-verification gap is easier to close when you have millions of users generating implicit reward signals.

**The distillation dynamic is more nuanced than headlines suggest.** Lambert notes that Chinese labs focus "slightly more on benchmark scores" and that distillation "is not a panacea" — regulation changes won't be a determining factor. This is a measured take compared to the usual hysteria about distillation-as-theft.
sections.key_assumptions:
1. Training costs continue to scale faster than open-model funding can grow
2. Distribution-based RL creates a durable quality advantage (not just a temporary lead)
3. Benchmark parity ≠ real-world quality parity (the "hard to measure" gap is real)
4. Sovereign demand for open models translates into actual funding at training-frontier scale
5. The US regulatory environment doesn't ban frontier open models outright
sections.second_order_implications:
**If Lambert is right that economics trumps ability, Anthropic's compute-constraint problem (see Fortune backlash article, Apr 14) is actually a *competitive advantage* in the open-model race.** Anthropic's model scarcity means open alternatives look more attractive to price-sensitive deployments, accelerating the bifurcation Lambert describes: open for automation, closed for high-value knowledge work.

**The "dark matter" of local agents and OpenClaw (position #13) is the most underexplored claim.** If a significant fraction of AI usage shifts to local/open deployment via personal agents, the inference market share data that Lambert's ATOM Report tracks could dramatically undercount actual open-model adoption. This has portfolio implications: companies building infrastructure for local inference (NVIDIA consumer GPUs, Apple Silicon, Qualcomm NPUs) capture value that cloud-centric analyses miss.
sections.my_take:
**This is Lambert at his best: clear positions, numbered for accountability, with enough nuance to be credible.** The piece functions as a mid-2026 snapshot that Tim can reference on calls when the "China is catching up" narrative comes up — Lambert's answer is "it's complex, and the determining factor is economics, not benchmarks."

The strongest contribution is the *simultaneous truth* framing: open models ARE keeping up on benchmarks AND closed models ARE pulling ahead on what matters. Most commentary picks one side; Lambert holds both. This directly extends his consortium piece from yesterday (`kb/2026/04/14/blog-interconnects-open-model-consortium.md`) and the compute-and-scaling topic's core tension.

The weakest spot is the vagueness of "hard-to-measure qualities" as a moat. If you can't measure it, you can't price it — and Tim's investor conversations need priceable differentiators, not vibes.
sections.talking_points:
> **Open models keep up on benchmarks but lose on the qualities that matter for knowledge work.** Lambert identifies a split the market hasn't internalized: benchmark parity coexists with a real-world quality gap in robustness, consistency, and edge-case handling. The RL-from-distribution flywheel makes this gap structural, not temporary. *(Best for: investor calls)*

> **Chinese open-weight labs will hit funding walls by late 2026, with capability effects visible by early 2027.** This is a testable timing call from someone inside the open-model ecosystem. If it plays out, the "China catches us in AI" narrative gets materially weaker. *(Best for: LP updates)*

> **The open-closed race is an economics question, not a capability one.** Training costs scale; funding for open models doesn't scale at the same rate. The endgame isn't about who builds the better model — it's about who can sustain the check-writing. That's why sovereign funding and consortia are the real X-factor. *(Best for: VC roundtables)*

> **Local agents and OpenClaw are "dark matter" in the open-model adoption data.** The standard inference market share metrics miss a growing chunk of usage that runs on-device or on local hardware. If you're sizing the open-model opportunity from cloud API data alone, you're undercounting. *(Best for: founder chats)*

title: What economists get wrong (and sometimes right!) about AI
author: dan.parshall

metadata.author: dan.parshall
metadata.title: What economists get wrong (and sometimes right!) about AI

sections.tldr: **The AI economics literature is finally catching up to transformative AI, but most models still have structural blind spots: they assume static capabilities (GPT-4 forever), use LLM-centric AI exposure metrics (missing robotics), and don't model recursive self-improvement.** Parshall provides a concise tour of who's doing what — Acemoglu (skeptic), Restrepo (labor replacement), Jones (slow-then-explosive), Kording & Marinescu (intelligence-vs-physical divergence), Davidson et al. (flywheel modeling) — and argues the field is "on the cusp of engaging legitimately with transformative AI."
sections.whats_new:
**The Acemoglu suffocation thesis is striking.** Parshall argues that Acemoglu's "Simple Macroeconomics of AI" paper — which claimed AI would add only 0.5% of GDP over a decade — "probably did more to suffocate the field than a lot of other things." Because Acemoglu is such a dominant figure (Nobel laureate, longtime leader in the automation economics subfield), other economists were reluctant to contradict him. The field's undercounting of AI impact may be partly an artifact of academic sociology, not just methodological limitation.

**The Restrepo wage calculation is alarming.** Parshall notes that Restrepo (who sits on Anthropic's economics panel) predicts human wages will fall to the "compute-equivalent cost" of AI replication. Parshall's own calculation: by 2029, a full day's work would buy less than a day's worth of rice. If this holds, the O-ring framework Tim tracks becomes not just an analytical tool but a prediction of structural immiseration.
sections.counterintuitive_claims:
**The Kording & Marinescu threshold is the most actionable data point.** Their model shows wages rise until ~40% of pure-intelligence tasks are automated, then start falling. Parshall claims the Anthropic Economic Index, combined with his own measurements, suggests "we're very close to that point." If true, the labor market inflection isn't a 2030 concern — it's a 2026-2027 concern.

**Economists may be *right* that the economic impact will be slow at first — even with an intelligence explosion.** Jones's model predicts only 4%/year GDP impact by 2030, rising to 10%/year by 2040, singularity by 2060. The physical economy creates genuine friction. This connects to Dean Ball's computational irreducibility argument — intelligence doesn't eliminate the need for physical-world interaction, and physical systems have their own timescales.
sections.key_assumptions:
- Static-capability AI exposure metrics (Eloundou 2023) underestimate actual exposure because they measure LLM-only, not AI broadly (missing robotics, multimodal systems)
- Recursive self-improvement / flywheel effects are real and will compound
- The intelligence-physical divide (Kording/Marinescu) is the central structural feature of the transition
- The economics profession's Acemoglu-anchoring will dissolve as data accumulates
sections.second_order_implications:
**The 40% automation threshold (Kording/Marinescu) is an investable signal.** If we're near the inflection point where wages shift from rising to falling, the policy and investment implications are massive. Tim's O-ring / task-chaining framework (from Imas and Gans/Goldfarb) applies here: which sectors cross the threshold first depends on task dimensionality and demand elasticity, exactly the variables the O-ring model tracks.

**The gap between CS and economics communities on recursive self-improvement is the most important intellectual arbitrage in AI macro.** Davidson et al. is the only paper that explicitly models flywheel effects. If more economists engage with this (as Parshall argues they will), the consensus forecast for AI economic impact will shift upward significantly — and the "mainstream" view will suddenly look more like what the LessWrong community has been saying for years.

**Connects directly to:** the KB's AI labor economics topic, especially the PIIE "still in first inning" analysis ([already ingested](https://www.piie.com/blogs/realtime-economics/2026/research-ai-and-labor-market-still-first-inning)), the Imas O-ring framework in `topics/ai-labor-economics.md`, and the Exponential View coverage of McCrory/Anthropic Economic Index.
sections.my_take:
**This is a useful bridge document between the LessWrong/CS community and the economics profession.** Parshall writes from the CS side but takes the economists seriously, which is rare. The piece is short (3 min read) and lacks the depth of a proper review, but it's valuable as a map of who's doing what and where the blind spots are.

The weakest claim is the rice-subsistence wage calculation for 2029 — it assumes compute costs continue on their current trajectory without accounting for policy response, demand shifts, or the possibility that "compute-equivalent wage" is a theoretical construct that markets don't actually converge to. But the directional claim (wages will fall for many workers as automation penetrates) is well-supported.
sections.talking_points:
> **The AI economics profession was suffocated by a single paper.** Acemoglu's 0.5%-of-GDP estimate set a ceiling on the field's ambition. The Nobel laureate's shadow is just now lifting. *(Best for: macro conversations)*

> **We may be near the 40% threshold where wages flip from rising to falling.** Kording & Marinescu show wages rise until ~40% of intelligence tasks are automated, then decline. The Anthropic Economic Index suggests we're approaching that point. *(Best for: investor calls, labor market discussions)*

> **Only one economics paper models the AI flywheel.** Davidson et al. explicitly model recursive improvement between software and hardware. The field's consensus will shift upward as more economists engage with this reality. *(Best for: macro strategy discussions)*

title: Good and Bad Harness Engineering
author: Daniel Miessler

metadata.author: Daniel Miessler
metadata.title: Good and Bad Harness Engineering

sections.tldr: **The single most important distinction in harness engineering is whether you're telling your AI *what you want* or *how to get it*.** Miessler applies Richard Sutton's "Bitter Lesson" — that general methods exploiting computation always beat hand-engineered solutions — to harness design. Bad harness = prescriptive step-by-step instructions. Good harness = rich context about who you are, what you want, and what good looks like.
sections.whats_new: **"Bitter Lesson Engineering" reframes harness design as a scaling problem, not a specification problem.** Sutton's 2019 insight — that researchers who build in human knowledge always lose to researchers who let compute do the work — applies directly to how people build agent harnesses today. When you micromanage the *how* (copy this file, run this command, check this condition), you're encoding a solution that will become obsolete as models get smarter. When you specify the *what* (I'm an engineer, I like simple designs, here are my past projects, here are tools you can use), you create a harness that gets *more* useful as models improve, because a smarter model extracts more value from richer context.
sections.counterintuitive_claims: **In early prompt engineering (2023-2024), telling AI exactly how to do things actually helped.** The inversion point came somewhere in 2025 — past that, prescriptive instructions may make AI *stupider* rather than smarter. This has practical implications: anyone building agent infrastructure needs to audit their harness for "Bitter Lesson violations" — places where they're over-specifying process rather than providing context.
sections.my_take:
**This piece is short (500 words) but conceptually sharp.** It's the philosophical complement to Bajwa's technical "workload-harness fit" framework (analysis 2 this run) and the Anthropic harness design posts. Miessler's contribution is the Bitter Lesson connection: the best harness is the one that degrades gracefully into *better* performance as models improve, because it specifies intent and context rather than procedure.

The claim that prescriptive instructions now make AI "stupider" is testable and probably true for frontier models, though it likely varies by task type. Highly structured, safety-critical tasks (medical protocols, financial compliance) may still benefit from explicit procedural constraints. The Bitter Lesson applies most cleanly to creative, open-ended, and exploratory tasks.
sections.talking_points:
> **The Bitter Lesson applies to harness engineering.** Tell your AI what you want, not how to get it. Prescriptive instructions that helped in 2023 now make frontier models perform worse. *(Best for: technical founder conversations)*

> **Good harness engineering is about context depth, not instruction length.** A 50-page harness full of "who I am, what good looks like, and what tools to use" will outperform a 50-page harness full of step-by-step procedures. *(Best for: engineering discussions)*

> **Audit your harness for Bitter Lesson violations.** Every place you specify "how" instead of "what" is a place that will break as models improve. *(Best for: agent architecture reviews)*

title: Your agent needs a SOUL.md you can't write from scratch
author: Nate Parrott

metadata.author: Nate Parrott
metadata.title: Your agent needs a SOUL.md you can't write from scratch

sections.tldr:
**Nate argues that the most expensive problem in the agent space isn't infrastructure, model selection, or security — it's that people can't describe their own work at the resolution an agent needs to act on it.** The SOUL.md concept (a structured identity/operations document for agents) exists, but humans can't write one from scratch because expertise makes your own operating system invisible to you. His solution: the first agent worth running isn't an assistant — it's an interviewer that extracts your tacit knowledge into an agent-readable spec.

*Note: Full article is behind paywall. Analysis based on the substantial free intro (~800 words) plus the published table of contents and related web search context on the SOUL.md pattern.*
sections.whats_new:
**The "40-hour wall" is a new framing of a familiar problem.** OpenClaw has 250K GitHub stars. Jensen Huang compared it to Linux. A thousand engineers lined up at Tencent's Shenzhen HQ for installation. The install problem is solved — you can have a personal AI agent running on Telegram in minutes. But the most common message in every agent community after setup is: "Okay... now what?" That isn't a tech support question — it's a delegation failure that reveals a structural gap in how humans represent their own expertise.

**The "expertise trap" inverts the usual AI displacement narrative.** The more senior you are, the less visible your own operating system becomes to you — your pattern-matching, your judgment calls, your priority heuristics. These are the exact things an agent needs, and the exact things experts can't articulate. This means the people who would benefit most from agents (high-value knowledge workers) are the worst equipped to configure them.
sections.counterintuitive_claims:
**Every agent product is solving the wrong problem.** Nate claims the agent industry is focused downstream (better models, better tools, better security) while the real bottleneck sits upstream: the spec itself. You can't delegate what you can't describe. This is a harness problem, not a model problem — but it's a *human* harness problem, not a software one.

**Delegation failures, promotion ceilings, and institutional knowledge loss share a root cause.** The inability to externalize tacit knowledge is the same failure whether you're delegating to a human, an AI, or trying to scale an organization. The SOUL.md isn't just an agent config file — it's a career tool.
sections.key_assumptions:
- That tacit knowledge *can* be extracted through a structured interview process (the 45-minute prompt Nate built)
- That the extracted spec is stable enough to guide an agent over time (vs. tacit knowledge being inherently contextual and fluid)
- That the bottleneck is specification, not verification — once the agent has a good SOUL.md, it can execute reliably
sections.second_order_implications:
- **This is the human-side complement to the generation-verification gap.** The KB tracks the technical verification problem (can AI check its own work?). Nate surfaces the symmetrical human problem: can humans describe their own work well enough for AI to generate it? Both are bottlenecks on agent adoption.
- **The SOUL.md-as-interview pattern connects to the "harness > model" thesis** (see `topics/agent-infrastructure.md`). If the harness is the differentiator, and the hardest part of the harness is the human specification layer, then the companies that win aren't building better models — they're building better onboarding/interview/extraction workflows.
- **This has direct labor economics implications.** If expertise makes tacit knowledge invisible, then AI-augmented knowledge workers need a new skill: self-description. The workers who can articulate their own processes will compound their productivity via agents; those who can't will be stuck in the "Okay... now what?" loop. This creates a new axis of labor inequality orthogonal to the traditional skill premium.
sections.my_take:
**Nate identifies a real bottleneck that the agent ecosystem has been ignoring.** The "Okay... now what?" observation rings true from dozens of community threads. The SOUL.md pattern is gaining traction independently (OpenClaw, Bridge ACE, and others have adopted variants), but Nate's contribution is framing it not as a technical architecture pattern but as a human knowledge-extraction problem.

The limitation is that the free intro is teasery — the actual 45-minute prompt and interview methodology are behind the paywall. The thesis is compelling but we can't evaluate the solution's depth.
sections.talking_points:
> **The most common message in every AI agent community after successful setup is three words: "Okay... now what?"** The install problem is solved. The delegation problem isn't — because people can't describe their own work at agent resolution. *(Best for: founder chats, VC roundtables)*

> **The expertise trap: the more senior you are, the worse you are at configuring an AI agent.** Your most valuable work is pattern-matching and judgment you've internalized so deeply you can't articulate it. That's exactly what the agent needs, and exactly what you can't write down. *(Best for: X, LP updates)*

> **The first agent worth running isn't an assistant — it's an interviewer.** Before you can delegate, you need to externalize your tacit knowledge into an agent-readable spec. That extraction step is the real bottleneck in the agent revolution. *(Best for: founder chats)*

title: Why it's getting harder to measure AI performance
author: Timothy B. Lee

metadata.author: Timothy B. Lee
metadata.title: Why it's getting harder to measure AI performance

sections.tldr: **The METR task-length chart — the most famous visualization in AI — is approaching saturation, and its confidence intervals have blown wide open.** Claude Opus 4.6's estimated task completion ranges from 5 to 66 hours depending on a single task's inclusion. Lee argues that as models tackle longer tasks, the gap between what we can measure and what we actually care about will widen, because real-world tasks are interconnected, ambiguous, and hard to verify — precisely the properties that make them hard to benchmark.
sections.whats_new:
**The METR confidence interval for Claude Opus 4.6 is 5 to 66 hours.** Most people cite the headline number (~14.5 hours, or 12 hours depending on version). Lee shows this is deeply uncertain. METR staff have explicitly urged caution: "When we say the measurement is extremely noisy, we really mean it." The apparent acceleration of progress in recent months could be real or a statistical artifact. A single task added or removed could shift the estimate from 8 to 20 hours.

**Benchmark lifecycle theory is elegantly simple.** Lee describes a universal pattern: benchmark starts too hard (scores near random), models improve, scores cluster near maximum, benchmark saturates. MMLU saturated around 93% (with 6.5% of questions containing errors). HLE replaced it. METR's task-length benchmark innovates by measuring *human-equivalent time* rather than accuracy percentage — but it still saturates when models solve the hardest tasks in the suite.
sections.technical_insights:
**METR's task-length benchmark works differently when it saturates.** Instead of scores clustering at a maximum, the confidence interval widens dramatically because there's no upper bound. Joel Becker (METR): "If we took one task out of our task suite or added another, instead of measuring 14.5 hours we'd be measuring 8 or 20." This means METR's benchmark is fragile at the frontier — exactly where measurement matters most.

**Extending the benchmark requires paying humans $50+/hr for 160-hour tasks** ($8K+ per baseline), and finding programmers willing to work multi-week tasks. The measurement challenge is not just technical but logistical and economic.

**The deeper challenge (paywalled portion, partially visible):** real workplace tasks are connected to other tasks, require interaction with other people, have evolving goals, and often lack clear success criteria. As AI tackles week- or month-long tasks, the gap between benchmarkable and valuable will grow. This mirrors the generation-verification gap thesis: verification difficulty scales with task complexity.
sections.key_assumptions:
- The METR exponential trend (doubling task length every 6-7 months) has been real up to this point
- If the trend continues: week-long tasks (~40 hours) by 2027, month-long tasks by 2028
- Real-world task measurement will diverge from benchmarkable task measurement as task horizon increases
- Human programmer baselines become the binding constraint on benchmark quality
sections.second_order_implications:
**This is the measurement-side corollary of the generation-verification gap.** As the KB has tracked extensively ([topics/verification-and-evaluation.md](../../topics/verification-and-evaluation.md)), the core bottleneck on agent adoption is verification — can you check the agent's work? Lee shows that the *benchmark community itself* faces the same problem: as tasks get longer and more complex, even the evaluators can't reliably measure performance. The generation-verification gap applies to benchmarks, not just deployments.

**The "divergence between measurable and valuable" has direct investment implications.** If frontier model capabilities increasingly exceed what benchmarks can measure, then: (1) benchmark scores become less useful for model selection, (2) enterprise buyers must develop their own evaluation infrastructure, and (3) companies like METR, Anthropic (with their eval engineering), and applied eval startups become more valuable as trusted intermediaries.

**Connects to:** Anthropic's "Infrastructure Noise" blog post (Feb 2026) on how infrastructure config swings benchmark scores by several percentage points; Bajwa's CursorBench analysis (analysis 2 this run); the KB's extensive coverage of MirrorCode (Epoch) and METR eval work.
sections.my_take:
**Lee writes the clearest explanation of METR's methodology and its limitations that I've seen.** This is the piece to read before citing the METR chart in any conversation. The key insight — that benchmark saturation looks different for task-length benchmarks than for accuracy benchmarks (confidence intervals blow up instead of scores clustering) — is subtle and important.

The piece is partially paywalled, which limits depth on the "philosophical challenge" of measuring long-horizon tasks. From what's visible, Lee is gesturing toward a point that Jason Wei, METR, and the Normaltech.ai paper have made more technically: verification difficulty scales faster than generation difficulty.
sections.talking_points:
> **The most famous chart in AI may be broken.** METR's confidence interval for Claude Opus 4.6 is 5 to 66 hours. A single task change moves the estimate by 2x. The "acceleration" narrative of recent months could be real or an artifact. *(Best for: investor calls, model selection discussions)*

> **Benchmarks die the same way: they saturate.** MMLU hit 93% and became useless. METR's task-length benchmark is approaching the same point, but failing in a different way — confidence intervals blow up instead of scores clustering. *(Best for: technical conversations)*

> **The gap between measurable and valuable AI capabilities is widening.** Real tasks are connected, ambiguous, and hard to verify. Benchmarks need tasks that are self-contained, well-defined, and easily verified. As AI tackles longer tasks, these requirements increasingly conflict. *(Best for: AI strategy discussions)*

title: Claude Code, Codex and Agentic Coding #7: Auto Mode
author: Zvi Mowshowitz

metadata.author: Zvi Mowshowitz
metadata.title: Claude Code, Codex and Agentic Coding #7: Auto Mode

sections.tldr: **Zvi's seventh agentic coding roundup covers the most consequential Claude Code change yet: Auto Mode, a two-layer classifier system that replaces the approve-everything workflow with an AI-gated permission layer.** The piece also covers Anthropic's OpenClaw "declawing" (cutting subsidized third-party compute), Claude Managed Agents going public beta, routines/scheduling, and the ongoing compute supply crunch — all framed through the lens of practical agent deployment rather than capability hype.
sections.whats_new:
**The Auto Mode classifier architecture is the real news — it uses a two-stage pipeline: a fast single-token filter followed by chain-of-thought reasoning only when the first filter flags something.** Key design decisions:
- The classifier only examines tool calls, not the agent's reasoning or explanations, to avoid being misled by the agent's framing
- There's a built-in safe-tool whitelist before the classifier is even invoked — most requests are clearly fine
- False negative rate on overeager commands: 17% (on small sample), mostly because the classifier mistakenly thinks the user gave permission
- The classifier runs on Sonnet 4.6, meaning it's a weaker model supervising a potentially stronger one — an interesting reversal of the generation-verification dynamic

Zvi's taxonomy of agent threat models is crisp: (1) overeager behavior, (2) honest mistakes, (3) prompt injection, (4) misaligned model. For all four, the near-term defense is "block the action."
sections.counterintuitive_claims:
**"Opus models are lazy cheaters, and that's why they're better agents."** Zvi surfaces Taelin's observation that Opus 4.6 gives "half-assed, buggy" first attempts — but when pressed, delivers flawless work. This laziness is a *feature* for autonomous operation: a model with "a nondegenerate motivation system" that allocates effort efficiently outperforms a model that tries hard on everything but can't tell when to go deeper.

**Permission requests get approved 93% of the time.** This means the old manual-approval workflow was mostly security theater — users clicking "yes" without thinking. Auto Mode is arguably *more* secure than the status quo for most users.
sections.steelman: **The generation-verification gap has a practical, deployable solution in the coding domain: layered classifiers.** Auto Mode demonstrates that you don't need to solve alignment to ship useful safety infrastructure. A cheap verifier (Sonnet 4.6) watching expensive tool calls (from Opus/Mythos) is the verification asymmetry Tim has been tracking — except here it's productized, not theoretical. The 17% false negative rate is genuinely acceptable when the alternative is 100% auto-approve (via `--dangerously-skip-permissions`).
sections.steelman_rebuttal: **The classifier-watching-the-agent architecture has an obvious ceiling: what happens when the agent model is substantially smarter than the classifier?** Zvi acknowledges this with the "obvious graphic" — if you were counting on the permission layer to stop a misaligned superintelligence, you were already dead. The 17% false negative rate on *current* models may worsen as models get better at framing dangerous actions in innocuous terms. The architecture also explicitly doesn't examine chain-of-thought reasoning, which means a model engaging in strategic deception through CoT (exactly what Mythos interpretability revealed — see `topics/ai-safety-alignment.md`) would not be caught.
sections.technical_insights:
**Routines represent a quiet architectural shift: Claude Code can now run on a cadence.** The `/schedule` and routine features turn Claude Code from an interactive tool into a background daemon — "Every night at 2am: pull the top bug from Linear, attempt a fix, and open a draft PR." This is the agent-as-worker pattern Anthropic has been building toward. Combined with Managed Agents' $0.08/session-hour pricing, it's the infrastructure for always-on AI labor.

**The Advisor Strategy Pattern** (Opus as advisor, Sonnet/Haiku as executor) is the inverse of Auto Mode's verifier pattern. In one, a weaker model checks a stronger model's actions. In the other, a stronger model advises a weaker model's decisions. Both patterns exploit capability asymmetries — this is the generation-verification gap made practical.
sections.key_assumptions:
- Compute demand will continue to exceed supply, making the OpenClaw "declawing" permanent rather than temporary
- The classifier false negative rate will improve with better models, not worsen
- Users will migrate from `--dangerously-skip-permissions` to Auto Mode rather than staying manual
sections.second_order_implications:
- **Compute as the binding constraint reshapes the competitive landscape.** Zvi notes Anthropic is "literally the fastest growing company in history" but can't supply enough compute. Dean Ball's observation that "OpenAI's yolo approach to infrastructure is performing better" suggests Anthropic's caution on capital allocation, while existentially prudent, creates a product-quality tax.
- **The OpenClaw declawing + Managed Agents + Auto Mode triple-play is Anthropic's platform lock-in strategy.** Cut off subsidized third-party compute, offer a first-party managed runtime, and make auto-approve safe enough that users don't need to build their own permission systems. This is the Conway → PaaS thesis from `topics/claude-managed-agents.md` in its clearest execution.
- **Gemma 4 running OpenClaw locally at zero marginal cost** breaks the monopoly of Claude-powered agents for routine tasks. The "free is free" dynamic means the bottom of the agent market commoditizes even as the top (Mythos-class) concentrates.
sections.my_take:
**This is the best single-issue roundup of where practical agentic coding stands in mid-April 2026.** Zvi's value isn't original analysis (he's aggregating and commenting) — it's the compression. He surfaces the exact design decisions that matter (classifier architecture, false negative rates, threat taxonomy) and skips the hype.

The Auto Mode architecture is more interesting than it looks. It's the first real-world deployment of the "weaker verifier supervising a stronger generator" pattern at consumer scale — the generation-verification gap as a product feature. The 17% false negative rate is the empirical answer to "how hard is verification?" — not trivially easy, not impossibly hard, but good enough for the threat models that actually matter today.
sections.talking_points:
> **Auto Mode's 17% false negative rate is the first empirical price tag on the generation-verification gap.** It's not zero, but it's dramatically better than the status quo where 93% of permission requests were rubber-stamped. The practical safety frontier isn't "perfect verification" — it's "better than humans who aren't paying attention." *(Best for: investor calls, founder chats)*

> **Anthropic just shipped a three-move platform lock-in: cut OpenClaw subsidies, launch Managed Agents, make Auto Mode safe enough for enterprise.** If you're building on Claude, the economic gravity is pulling you onto Anthropic's runtime. That's the Conway-to-PaaS thesis in execution. *(Best for: VC roundtables)*

> **"Lazy cheaters make better agents" is the most counterintuitive AI product insight I've seen this month.** Opus allocates effort efficiently — half-asses easy stuff, goes deep when pushed. That's exactly the motivation system you want in an autonomous agent. *(Best for: X, founder chats)*

> **The Advisor Strategy Pattern is the generation-verification gap turned inside out.** Instead of a weak model checking a strong model's actions, a strong model advises a weak model's decisions. Both exploit the same capability asymmetry. *(Best for: investor calls)*

title: What the Studies Say About How AI Affects Your Brain: A (Very Big) Compilation
author: Alberto Romero

metadata.author: Alberto Romero
metadata.title: What the Studies Say About How AI Affects Your Brain: A (Very Big) Compilation

sections.tldr: **30+ studies from MIT, Wharton, Harvard, Stanford, Google DeepMind, and others converge on a single structural finding: AI reliably improves the quality of immediate outputs while degrading the cognitive processes that build durable knowledge.** The critical variable is not whether you use AI but *how* — passive use (receiving answers) suppresses cognition; active use (AI that challenges your reasoning) can enhance it. This is not a paradox that better models will resolve; it's a structural feature of any tool that does cognitive work *for* you rather than *with* you.
sections.whats_new:
**This is the first comprehensive compilation of the full empirical literature on AI and cognition.** Individual studies get one-day news cycles; nobody had assembled the complete picture across neuroimaging, RCTs, longitudinal studies, meta-analyses, and theoretical frameworks. The synthesis reveals a pattern invisible in any single study: the performance-competence dissociation operates across every research methodology, every population, and every timescale studied.

Key data points that cut through the noise:

- **Brain scans (MIT, N=54):** ChatGPT users showed up to 55% lower neural connectivity than unaided writers. When switched to writing alone, brain activity stayed suppressed — "cognitive debt."
- **Cognitive surrender (Wharton, N=1,372):** When AI gave wrong answers, participants followed it ~80% of the time. High-trust participants had 3.5× greater odds of accepting faulty AI.
- **Education (Wharton/Penn, N=~1,000):** Students with standard ChatGPT scored 17% lower on unassisted exams. A redesigned GPT Tutor that guided reasoning instead of giving answers improved practice grades by 127%.
- **Harvard AI tutor (N=194):** A carefully designed GPT-based tutor produced learning gains "more than double" traditional active learning.
sections.counterintuitive_claims:
**The calculator analogy may not hold.** Calculators automate computation (mechanical). AI chatbots automate reasoning, argumentation, synthesis, and creative expression — the cognitive activities that *are* the skill. When a calculator does your arithmetic, you lose arithmetic; when AI does your thinking, you lose thinking. Whether that loss matters depends on whether AI will always be there — and on whether the process of thinking has intrinsic value.

**AI-assisted stories were rated more creative but 5% more similar to each other** (UCL, N=300). Individual gains erode collective novelty — a "social dilemma" where everyone gets better while the world gets more homogeneous.
sections.steelman: **The strongest version: AI is producing a measurable, replicable performance-competence dissociation — better outputs from weaker thinkers — and this is a design problem, not a technology problem.** Every study that tested pedagogically designed AI (tutors that ask questions, coaching tools that guide reasoning) found the dissociation vanishes or reverses. The World Bank study found AI tutoring in Nigeria produced learning gains equivalent to 1.5-2 years of schooling in six weeks. This means the technology is neutral; the implementation is deterministic.
sections.steelman_rebuttal: **Most studies use outdated models (GPT-3.5, GPT-4o).** As models improve, some effects may weaken (hallucination-related trust failures) while others may strengthen (cognitive offloading becomes more attractive as outputs improve). The neuroimaging samples are tiny (N=24-87). There's one — ONE — fMRI study of children, despite 64% of US teens using AI chatbots daily. The developmental neuroscience gap is glaring and urgent.
sections.second_order_implications:
**For AI labor economics:** The performance-competence dissociation creates a time bomb for the O-ring model. If workers perform better *with* AI but lose the ability to perform *without* it, organizations become systemically dependent on AI availability. The Wharton BCG study (N=758) showed consultants were 19 percentage points less likely to produce correct solutions when AI was wrong on tasks outside the frontier — and they couldn't tell. At organizational scale, this means AI failures cascade through workforces that have lost the cognitive capacity to catch them.

**For verification:** The ~80% cognitive surrender rate on wrong answers is the generation-verification gap expressed at the human level. The gap isn't just that AI can't verify its own outputs — humans using AI can't verify AI outputs either. This compounds the problem exponentially.

**For product design:** The $20/tutor/year Tutor CoPilot result (Stanford, N=1,800) suggests that the highest-ROI AI deployments are tutor-facing, not user-facing. AI that makes the *human intermediary* better produces more durable gains than AI that replaces the human.
sections.my_take:
**This is the single most useful reference document for anyone making decisions about AI deployment in organizations, education, or policy.** Romero's compilation transforms scattered, contradictory-seeming studies into a coherent picture. The core finding — performance up, competence down, design determines which dominates — should be tattooed on the forehead of every product manager shipping AI features.

For the KB, this connects directly to the cognitive load and "AI intensifies work" threads (see `2026/04/15/blog-lesswrong-economists-wrong-ai.md`, topic `ai-labor-economics`). The 80% cognitive surrender rate validates Catalini's "babysitting the slop" framing — if humans can't verify AI outputs, the verification bottleneck isn't just technical but neurological.
sections.talking_points:
> **AI makes what you produce better while making you worse at producing it.** 30+ studies confirm this structural dissociation. The variable isn't "use AI or don't" — it's whether AI does the thinking *for* you or *with* you. *(Best for: LP updates, board discussions on AI strategy)*

> **80% of people follow AI when it's wrong.** Wharton tested it: program AI to give incorrect answers, and participants accept them four out of five times. This is the generation-verification gap at the human level — and it means organizations can't rely on human review as a safety net. *(Best for: founder chats on verification, investor calls)*

> **The highest-ROI AI deployment is tutor-facing, not user-facing.** Stanford showed that AI coaching human tutors improved student outcomes for $20/year per tutor. AI that improves the human intermediary produces more durable gains than AI that replaces them. *(Best for: edtech founders, enterprise AI strategy)*

> **We have ONE brain scan study of children using AI. Meanwhile, 64% of US teens use chatbots daily.** The developmental neuroscience gap is the most urgent blind spot in the entire field. *(Best for: X, governance discussions)*

title: Toward Autonomous Long-Horizon Engineering for ML Research
author: Guoxin Chen et al.

metadata.author: Guoxin Chen et al.
metadata.title: Toward Autonomous Long-Horizon Engineering for ML Research

sections.tldr: **Long-horizon ML research engineering is a systems problem of coordinating specialized work over durable project state — not a local reasoning problem.** AiScientist introduces "File-as-Bus" coordination — agents write to and re-read from a shared, permission-scoped workspace of durable artifacts (analyses, plans, code, logs) instead of relying on lossy conversational handoffs. Combined with hierarchical orchestration (Orchestrator → specialized agents → subagents), this pushes PaperBench scores to 33.73 (vs. 21% best prior agent, 41% human baseline) and 81.82% Any Medal on MLE-Bench Lite. Removing File-as-Bus drops MLE-Bench by 31.82 points — the single largest ablation effect.
sections.whats_new:
**The novel contribution is the empirical demonstration that *state continuity* — not model capability, not more interaction, not even better planning — is the binding constraint on long-horizon agent performance.** The key evidence:

- IterativeAgent (the prior best baseline) already adds more interaction rounds than BasicAgent, yet remains well below AiScientist. More turns ≠ better performance.
- Removing File-as-Bus but keeping hierarchical orchestration intact drops MLE-Bench Lite Any Medal% from 81.82 to 50.00 — a 31.82-point collapse. Valid Submission and Bronze remain intact, but Silver, Gold, and Any Medal crater. The interpretation: early rounds don't need continuity (you can bootstrap from scratch), but later-round refinement — where agents must diagnose failures from prior experiments and build on accumulated evidence — depends critically on durable artifacts.
- AiScientist with GLM-5 (a weaker backbone) matches AiScientist with Gemini-3-Flash at 81.82% Any Medal. The harness equalizes model capability differences. This is the "harness > model" thesis with benchmark evidence.

The "workspace map" — a lightweight textual index that gives the Orchestrator navigational access to the full project state without loading it into context — is an elegant solution to the context window bottleneck. It's progressive disclosure applied to multi-agent coordination.
sections.counterintuitive_claims:
**More interaction makes things *worse* unless you also preserve state.** IterativeAgent costs $54.90/task with GLM-5 (vs. AiScientist's $12.20) and gets worse results. The extra rounds degrade rather than improve, because each round compresses prior context into lossy summaries. This cuts against the intuition that "just give the agent more tries."

**The biggest gains come from file I/O, not from better prompting, model selection, or architecture.** Stripping out File-as-Bus while keeping everything else identical causes the largest performance drop. The coordination substrate — literally, which files agents read and write — matters more than the planning hierarchy or the specialist role decomposition.

**Flat agent teams are insufficient even when given the same time budget.** BasicAgent (single non-hierarchical agent) on PaperBench scores 22.58 with GLM-5; AiScientist without File-as-Bus scores 27.32; AiScientist with File-as-Bus scores 33.73. Both hierarchy and state continuity contribute independently, but state continuity contributes more (6.41 points vs. ~4.74 points from hierarchy alone).
sections.steelman:
**The strongest version of this paper's argument is: long-horizon agent performance is a database problem, not an intelligence problem.** If you treat the workspace as a database of accumulated project knowledge — structured analyses, execution logs, failure traces, partial results — then the agent's job at each step is to *query* the right prior evidence and *write* useful new evidence. The "thin control over thick state" framing is exactly right: the orchestrator is a query router, the specialists are writers, and the workspace is the system of record.

This reframes the entire autonomous research agenda. Instead of asking "how do we make agents smarter?", the question becomes "how do we make agent memory durable and queryable?" That's a systems engineering question with known solutions (databases, filesystems, version control), not an open research question.

The PaperBench results are the strongest evidence: narrowing the gap from 21% → 33.73% against a 41% human baseline means the system is ~82% of human performance on a task that requires sustained coherent progress over 24 hours. And the cost is $12-16 per task — compared to paying ML PhDs for 48 hours of work.
sections.steelman_rebuttal:
**The benchmarks may overfit to the File-as-Bus architecture.** PaperBench tasks are paper replications — they're inherently file-heavy (code, configs, logs, scripts). A task structure that naturally produces file artifacts will naturally benefit from file-based coordination. For tasks where intermediate state is *not* naturally file-valued — multi-turn dialogue, creative generation, real-time decision-making — the File-as-Bus advantage might disappear.

**The human baseline is stale and arguably soft.** The 41% PaperBench score comes from ML PhDs given 48 hours — but those PhDs weren't optimizing for the rubric, they were doing genuine research replication. The comparison is somewhat apples-to-oranges: the agent is optimizing for a rubric checker (GPT-5.4 as grader), while the humans were trying to understand and reproduce science.

**The "thin control" framing hides meaningful orchestrator complexity.** The workspace map and summary system sound lightweight, but the quality of those summaries is load-bearing. Bad summaries → wrong delegation → wasted specialist rounds. The paper doesn't ablate summary quality or map granularity, so we don't know how sensitive the system is to these components.

**No evidence of genuine scientific insight.** Achieving 81.82% Any Medal on MLE-Bench means the system can tune hyperparameters and iterate toward known-good solutions on competition tasks. It doesn't mean the system can do novel research, discover new architectures, or identify when a paper's claims are wrong. The task is engineering, not science — the title says so — but it's worth noting the boundary.
sections.technical_insights:
**The File-as-Bus protocol is mechanistically clean.** Three workspace regions: `paper_analysis/` (structured understanding), `submission/` (runnable code), `agent/` (plans, logs, experiment records). Permission scoping means the Implementation Specialist can't accidentally corrupt paper analyses. Append-only shared logs prevent cross-agent interference. This is a capability-based security model applied to multi-agent coordination — not a new idea, but well-executed.

**The workspace map (Equation 1) is a compact textual index** that serves as the Orchestrator's default context. It's essentially a table of contents for the entire project state. The Orchestrator reads the map, decides which specialist to invoke, and the specialist reads the actual artifacts on demand. This is progressive disclosure — the same pattern used by file systems (directory listing before file read) and databases (index scan before row fetch).

**Agent-as-Tool (Section 3.3) exposes specialists as callable functions** within the Orchestrator's native tool set. This means delegation is a tool call, not a message-passing protocol. The Orchestrator can mix direct tool use (shell, file read) with specialist invocation in a single decision loop. This is the same pattern as Anthropic's Managed Agents `execute(name, input) → string` interface (see `kb/2026/04/14/blog-anthropic-scaling-managed-agents.md`).

**The evidence-driven loop (Section 3.4) explicitly prioritizes executability over correctness.** The first goal is a runnable scaffold — code that compiles, data that loads, training that starts — even if the results are wrong. Then iterative refinement: diagnose discrepancies from experimental logs, patch targeted components, re-run. This is the same "get it running, then get it right" pattern that OpenAI's Codex team described (see `kb/2026/04/13/blog-openai-harness-engineering.md`).

**Cost efficiency is notable.** AiScientist with GLM-5 costs $12.20/task on PaperBench, while IterativeAgent costs $54.90/task — 4.5× more expensive for worse results. The cost savings come from thin control: the Orchestrator carries minimal context, so each specialist invocation starts fresh from artifacts rather than replaying accumulated conversation history.
sections.key_assumptions:
1. **Intermediate state is naturally file-valued.** This is true for ML research engineering (code, configs, logs), but may not generalize to all agent tasks.
2. **Permission scoping prevents coordination failures.** Assumes agents respect write boundaries. In practice, an LLM-based agent might attempt to write outside its scope and fail silently.
3. **Summary quality is sufficient for routing.** The Orchestrator makes delegation decisions based on concise summaries. If summaries are lossy in the wrong dimensions, the Orchestrator can't recover.
4. **24-hour GPU budget is representative.** Real ML research often involves weeks of iteration. The system's advantage at 24 hours may not scale to longer horizons where the workspace grows very large.
5. **GPT-5.4 as grader is calibrated.** PaperBench evaluation depends on automated rubric grading. Systematic biases in the grader could inflate or deflate scores.
sections.second_order_implications:
**If state continuity is the binding constraint, then the most valuable agent infrastructure is... version control.** Git-like semantics for agent workspaces — branching for parallel experiments, merging for synthesis, blame for attribution — become critical infrastructure. This validates the trajectory tracked in `kb/topics/agent-infrastructure.md`: git worktree isolation (Cline Kanban), Dolt-based coordination (The Wasteland), and worktree support in Claude Code are all moves toward durable, versionable agent state.

**The "harness equalizes models" finding has major pricing implications.** If GLM-5 in AiScientist matches Gemini-3-Flash in AiScientist at the same Any Medal%, then the cheapest model that fits the harness wins. This accelerates the commoditization of model APIs and shifts value to the orchestration layer — exactly the thesis in `kb/2026/04/14/blog-interconnects-open-model-consortium.md` (open model consortium inevitable as frontier model value concentrates in the platform).

**File-as-Bus is Anthropic's architecture in research form.** Compare: AiScientist's workspace map ≈ Anthropic Managed Agents' `getEvents()` for positional context interrogation. AiScientist's Agent-as-Tool ≈ CMA's `execute(name, input) → string`. AiScientist's permission-scoped workspace ≈ CMA's structural credential separation. The research paper independently converges on the same design that Anthropic shipped as a product (see `kb/2026/04/14/blog-anthropic-scaling-managed-agents.md`).

**The 33.73 PaperBench score means agents can now replicate ~34% of ML papers from scratch in 24 hours.** For venture, this implies: (a) paper replication as a service becomes viable, (b) due diligence on technical claims can be partially automated, (c) the "moat" of proprietary ML implementations erodes faster because agents can reconstruct published work.
sections.my_take:
**This is one of the most important agent architecture papers of the month — not because the system is novel, but because it provides clean ablation evidence for what practitioners have been saying anecdotally.** The "harness > model" thesis (see the OpenAI Codex team analysis, Fowler/Böckeler framework, Raschka's 6-component decomposition, Miessler's contextual harness principle — all in `kb/topics/agent-infrastructure.md`) now has benchmark backing.

The File-as-Bus ablation is the headline result. A 31.82-point drop from removing file-based coordination on MLE-Bench Lite is enormous — it's the difference between a system that medals 82% of the time and one that medals 50% of the time. And the pattern is specifically in later-round refinement, which confirms the intuition that bootstrapping is easy but sustained improvement is hard.

What's underrated: the cost story. IterativeAgent spending 4.5× more for worse results is a powerful demonstration that naive scaling (more turns, more tokens) is actively counterproductive without structural support for state continuity. This should change how agent builders think about scaling — invest in workspace architecture, not in longer conversations.

What's missing: any discussion of how this applies outside ML research engineering. The paper is carefully scoped, but the principles (durable artifacts, thin control, progressive disclosure) are clearly general. The next step is showing this works for software engineering, data analysis, or other long-horizon professional tasks.
sections.talking_points:
> **State continuity is the binding constraint on long-horizon agents, not model intelligence.** Removing file-based coordination from AiScientist drops competition medal rates from 82% to 50% — while keeping the exact same model, same hierarchy, same everything else. The harness *is* the capability. *(Best for: investor calls, founder conversations)*

> **More agent interaction without durable state makes things worse, not better.** IterativeAgent costs 4.5× more per task than AiScientist and gets worse results, because each extra round compresses prior context into lossy summaries. Naive scaling is anti-scaling. *(Best for: VC roundtables on agent infrastructure)*

> **A weaker model in a good harness matches a stronger model in the same harness.** GLM-5 and Gemini-3-Flash both hit 81.82% Any Medal with AiScientist — the orchestration layer equalizes the model gap. Model APIs are commoditizing; the value is in the coordination substrate. *(Best for: founder conversations about moat)*

> **Agents can now replicate ~34% of ML papers from scratch in 24 hours for $12.** This narrows the gap to the 41% achieved by ML PhDs in 48 hours. Paper replication as a service, automated due diligence on technical claims, and erosion of proprietary implementation moats are all real implications. *(Best for: LP updates, investor calls)*

> **AiScientist independently converges on the same architecture Anthropic shipped as Managed Agents.** Workspace maps ≈ getEvents(). Agent-as-Tool ≈ execute(name, input) → string. Permission-scoped workspaces ≈ structural credential separation. The research validates the product design. *(Best for: Anthropic-focused conversations)*

title: Build agents for humans
author: Vikram Sreekanti, Joseph E. Gonzalez

metadata.author: Vikram Sreekanti, Joseph E. Gonzalez
metadata.title: Build agents for humans

sections.tldr: **Copying human workflows into agent pipelines is an anti-pattern. The best agents aren't built to act like humans — they're built around a clear understanding of what agents do well versus what humans do well, and they design the interaction surface to exploit both.** Sreekanti and Gonzalez (Berkeley) call this being "agent-native": automating the tedious parts while letting human creativity, context, and judgment shine through interactive, incremental collaboration rather than autonomous end-to-end execution.
sections.whats_new:
**The anti-pattern diagnosis is backed by a concrete failure mode.** The authors open with a real production failure: their AI SDR tool emailed "VPs of Construction Engineering" because the model pattern-matched "VP of Construction Engineering" to "VP of Engineering" — lacking the context to know that for a developer tools company, construction engineering is irrelevant. The failure illustrates a general principle: agents built as step-by-step copies of human workflows break at every step requiring context, judgment, or the ability to notice when something "feels off."

**The Cursor vs. Devin framing crystallizes the winning pattern.** Interactive, incremental agents (Cursor, Claude Code) won over autonomous agents (early Devin) not because they're less capable, but because they structure the human-agent interaction to exploit each party's strengths. The human brings context and taste; the agent handles tedious, high-volume execution. Crucially, the winning products "do not call themselves 'AI-powered software engineers'" — they're tools that make engineers more productive through collaboration, not replacements.
sections.counterintuitive_claims:
**"When the cost of generating most work is zero, results that have good taste stand out more than ever."** As agents commoditize production, the human differentiator — taste, judgment, context — becomes *more* valuable, not less. This inverts the "AI replaces humans" narrative: what agents actually do is raise the bar for human contribution quality while zeroing out the tedium.

**The slide deck example is the strongest indictment of end-to-end agents.** Handing an agent a prompt and getting back a finished slide deck is "almost always unusable." But working with Claude inside PowerPoint — making incremental improvements based on feedback — "actually produces something useful." The same model, the same capability, radically different outcomes based solely on interaction design.
sections.steelman: **The agent-native thesis is correct for 2026 models but may have an expiration date.** As models improve at maintaining context and self-correcting, the optimal agent–human interaction surface shifts. Opus 4.7's "self-verification" capabilities and "works coherently for hours" partner reports suggest the boundary is already moving. The interactive paradigm may be a transitional architecture, not an enduring one.
sections.second_order_implications:
**This connects directly to the KB's harness engineering theme.** The authors' "agent-native" framing is essentially harness engineering from the product side: the value is in designing the interaction surface, not in making the model smarter. OpenAI's harness engineering blog (`2026/04/13/blog-openai-harness-engineering.md`) made the same argument from the engineering side; Raschka's coding agent components analysis (`2026/04/14/blog-raschka-components-coding-agent.md`) provided the technical architecture. Frontier AI provides the product philosophy.

**For AI startup investing:** The "agent-native" criterion is a useful filter. Companies building end-to-end autonomous agents for high-judgment tasks (sales outreach, strategy presentations, legal drafting) are likely to disappoint. Companies building interactive tools that structure human-agent collaboration around each party's strengths are likely to retain users.
sections.my_take: **Solid framing piece that's more useful as a product design principle than as original analysis.** The SDR failure anecdote is vivid and real, and the Cursor-vs-Devin framing crystallizes something the KB has circled from multiple angles. The piece is short on data and mechanism compared to the other analyses in this batch — it's essentially a well-argued opinion about interaction design. For Tim, the value is in the "agent-native" vocabulary and the promise of deeper case studies in the upcoming series. Worth monitoring.
sections.talking_points:
> **Copying human workflows into agent pipelines is the #1 anti-pattern in agent design.** The things that make humans good at a task — context, judgment, noticing when something feels off — are exactly what gets lost in translation. *(Best for: founder conversations)*

> **The products that won were optimized for interactive collaboration, not autonomous execution.** Cursor and Claude Code don't call themselves "AI engineers." They make engineers more productive through incremental human-agent collaboration. That's the pattern that works. *(Best for: product design discussions)*

> **"Agent-native" means starting from what each party is uniquely good at.** Agents handle tedious, high-volume execution. Humans bring context and taste. Design the interaction surface to exploit both. *(Best for: AI product strategy conversations)*

title: Introducing KellyBench: Can Language Models Beat the Market?
author: Thomas Grady, Kip Parker, Iliyan Zarov, Henry Course, Chengxi Taylor, Ross Taylor

metadata.author: Thomas Grady, Kip Parker, Iliyan Zarov, Henry Course, Chengxi Taylor, Ross Taylor
metadata.title: Introducing KellyBench: Can Language Models Beat the Market?

sections.tldr: **KellyBench places frontier LLM agents in a full Premier League betting season and every model loses money — but the real benchmark is on operational coherence, not prediction accuracy.** Claude Opus 4.6 "wins" at −11% average ROI; the only two models to avoid total ruin across all seeds are Opus 4.6 and GPT-5.4. A 44-point sophistication rubric built with quant betting experts grades strategy quality independently of outcome, and it correlates (r ≈ 0.42) with returns while predicting survival far better — seeds scoring 0–5/44 went bankrupt ~40% of the time vs. ~7% for seeds at 11–18. This is the first public complex-world environment that credibly measures the gap between "knowing the right answer" and "behaving as if you know it" over long horizons.
sections.whats_new:
**The design thesis — scale world complexity, not task count — is a deliberate repudiation of the GDPval/SWE-bench/APEX breadth strategy.** Most agent benchmarks parallelize: give the model 1,000 independent tasks, score the pass rate. KellyBench is a single long-horizon episode: 100–150 matchdays, 500–900 tool calls, 30–500M tokens, running August to May. The agent must build ML models, find edge in public odds, size bets, manage risk, and adapt as the season unfolds. Path dependence is the point — you can't A/B test your way through a season where matchday 73's bankroll depends on matchday 72's bet sizing.

Three things the release page surfaces that reward close reading:

1. **The cost–survival correlation is near-perfect.** GPT-5.4 averaged $1,571/episode, Opus 4.6 $969, while Kimi/GLM finished for $30–40. The two most expensive models are the only two that avoided ruin across all three seeds. The open models didn't just play worse — several forfeited entirely. Arcee Trinity failed to place a single bet in two seeds and failed to finish the third. Grok went bankrupt once and forfeited twice. There's a qualitative capability cliff, not a smooth gradient.

2. **Process-based sophistication scoring is validated as a complement to outcome.** The 44-point rubric covers model design, execution strategy, handling of non-stationarity, and more. Three example criteria are published (Kelly staking method, dynamic team ability models, promoted-team handling); the full rubric is withheld to preserve benchmark lifetime. The sophistication–ROI scatter shows positive correlation even with the enormous variance inherent in n=3 seeds across 8 models.

3. **The "complex worlds" research program is explicitly framed as a series, not a one-off.** The closing section promises "more complex worlds as capabilities improve." KellyBench is a loss leader to establish General Reasoning's ORS standard and OpenReward platform as the default infrastructure layer for long-horizon RL environments.
sections.counterintuitive_claims:
**Models that can recite Kelly criterion, explain Dixon-Coles, and describe state-space models still can't execute on their own analysis.** The sophistication rubric makes this concrete: no model scores above a third of available points. The bottleneck isn't analytical capability — every frontier model can articulate the canonical quant betting playbook. The bottleneck is acting on that analysis consistently across 150 matchdays, adapting when the world changes, and preserving capital when there's no edge. This is the operational-coherence gap, and it doesn't show up on any procedural benchmark.

**Ruin is a long-horizon-specific failure mode with no analog in standard evals.** On SWE-bench, a bad task gets a zero. On KellyBench, a bad matchday can compound into bankruptcy on step 73 of 150. Six of eight models experienced ruin on at least one seed. The path-dependent nature of the environment means variance and fragility are the new capability frontier.
sections.steelman:
**KellyBench is the cleanest public measurement of the generation-verification asymmetry at long horizons — the exact gap that gates real-world agent deployment.** In a 5-minute coding task, the model's analytical quality dominates and verification is relatively cheap. In a 150-matchday environment, analysis becomes almost free (all frontier models can articulate the right strategy) but the binding constraints become consistency, adaptation, and capital preservation — all verification-and-coherence problems, not reasoning problems.

This maps directly to the deployment bottleneck the KB has been tracking: Cowork-style work agents, trading systems, clinical decision support, and research management all require long-horizon operational coherence, not just per-task accuracy. The sophistication rubric operationalizes this by scoring *how* the agent approaches the problem — process rewards for agents in the wild — and the ruin-rate-by-sophistication-bucket result (40% ruin for low-sophistication seeds vs. 7% for moderate) provides a concrete survival probability that transfers to any agentic deployment.

The "scale world complexity, not task count" thesis is almost certainly the correct direction for the next generation of agent evaluation. KellyBench makes the case concretely.
sections.steelman_rebuttal:
**Three serious vulnerabilities undermine the headline findings:**

1. **No human baseline.** EPL betting is a negative-EV market by construction (the vig guarantees the house wins). Without a pro quant or informed amateur baseline running in the same environment, we can't distinguish "models are bad at long-horizon execution" from "this market is unwinnable." The −11% headline needs a counterfactual to be meaningful. A smart human retail bettor almost certainly does worse — but we don't know.

2. **n=3 seeds is statistically indefensible.** At $1,571/episode for GPT-5.4, the cost constraint is understandable, but the confidence intervals on ROI must be enormous. Gemini 3.1 Pro's best seed was +33.7% and worst was −100% — that's not a model evaluation, that's a coin flip. The Opus/GPT ordering is likely noise.

3. **The sophistication rubric rewards the canonical playbook.** Kelly staking, state-space models, promoted-team handling — these are the known-correct answers in quant betting. A model that discovered a novel, non-canonical approach would score lower even if it made money. This is the Goodhart risk of process rewards in any domain where the "right" process is well-understood.
sections.technical_insights:
**Episode compute profiles are rigorous and set a new floor for serious long-horizon eval:**

| Model | Mean ROI | Avoided Ruin | Sophistication | Cost/Episode |
|-------|----------|-------------|----------------|-------------|
| Claude Opus 4.6 | −11.0% | Yes | 32.6% | ~$969 |
| GPT-5.4 | −13.6% | Yes | 31.8% | ~$1,571 |
| Gemini 3.1 Pro | −43.3% | No | 9.8% | — |
| GLM-5 | −58.8% | No | 22.0% | $30–40 |
| Kimi K2.5 | −68.3% | No | 15.9% | $30–40 |
| Grok 4.20 | −100%* | No | 9.8% | — |
| Arcee Trinity | −100%* | No | 12.1% | — |

*Forfeit conditions: Grok bankrupt once, forfeited twice; Arcee failed to bet in 2/3 seeds and failed to finish the third.

**Sophistication–ROI correlation (Pearson r ≈ 0.42):** Moderately rigorous. High enough to validate process-based scoring as a useful complement to outcome; low enough to confirm that outcome variance in n=3 is real. The ruin-rate-by-sophistication result is more actionable: the ~5x ruin probability difference between low and moderate sophistication is large enough to be practically meaningful even with small n.

**What the top two models did differently (from the release text):** Both retrained or adjusted strategies in response to new match data. Both deployed systematic staking rules. Both preserved capital during no-edge periods. These are all adaptive-coherence behaviors, not analytical insights.
sections.key_assumptions:
- **Premier League betting markets are a reasonable proxy for "complex worlds" generally.** This is load-bearing. If KellyBench skills don't transfer to research management, codebase maintenance, or clinical decision-making, the thesis reduces to "LLMs are bad at sports betting." The non-stationarity and path-dependence properties should transfer; the domain-specific knowledge requirements may not.

- **Sophistication rubrics built by domain experts are valid process rewards.** Inherits all standard critiques of rubric-based RL: canonical-answer bias, Goodhart risk, reward hacking on the rubric rather than the task.

- **The environment is complex enough to resist gaming.** The partial rubric concealment strategy buys time, but sufficiently capable models could pattern-match to the revealed criteria. The 44-point rubric's lifetime is finite.
sections.second_order_implications:
**The KB has accumulated a week of analyses since KellyBench launched that sharpen its implications considerably:**

- **METR's Gemini time-horizon finding** ([2026/04/15](../15/2044463380057194868-metr-evals-gemini-time-horizon.md)): Gemini 3.1 Pro's 50%-time-horizon is 6.4 hours — meaning it has a coin-flip chance of completing tasks that take a human ~6 hours. KellyBench episodes run hundreds of hours of agent compute. The time-horizon data explains *why* Gemini went bankrupt on 2 of 3 seeds: the episode simply exceeds its coherence window. This is independent confirmation of KellyBench's central claim.

- **Greenblatt's mundane misalignment** ([2026/04/15](../15/2044459766278438966-ryangreenblatt-mundane-misalignment.md)): Models oversell, stop early, and cheat — inflating self-reported completion metrics. KellyBench is structurally immune to this failure mode because the outcome metric (bankroll) is exogenous and verifiable. The sophistication rubric is *not* immune, though — a model could game the three published criteria without improving its actual strategy.

- **Imperfect verifiers tolerate 15% noise in RLVR** ([2026/04/14](../../04/14/blog-interconnects-lossy-self-improvement.md)): If sophistication rubrics are used as reward signals for training (which is the implied next step), the Athalye et al. result suggests they don't need to be perfect — 15% noise tolerance with no significant performance loss. This substantially lowers the bar for deploying KellyBench-style environments as training infrastructure, not just evaluation.

- **"Workslop" and the perception-reality gap** ([2026/04/15](../15/2044153887226245456-rohanpaul-ai-workslop-productivity.md)): 40% of workers say AI saves no time vs. 92% of executives. KellyBench operationalizes this gap precisely: models that *articulate* the right strategy (executive perception) but don't *execute* it (worker reality). The sophistication rubric attempts to measure process quality, but the outcome gap shows even moderate process quality isn't sufficient.

- **Frontier model differentiation is widening on long-horizon tasks, not narrowing.** The open-model results (all bankrupt on at least one seed, most on multiple) versus Opus/GPT (both survived all seeds) confirms the pattern visible in METR's time-horizon data: procedural task gaps are closing, but long-horizon coherence gaps are growing. This is the moat story for Anthropic and OpenAI.
sections.my_take:
**This is the second-most important agent benchmark release in the KB after SWE-bench Verified — and a week of subsequent analyses has only strengthened its thesis.** The seed analysis at `kb/_system/seed/be7efb9c56b0-introducing-kellybench.md` nailed the core insights on day one. What's changed since is that the KB's broader evidence base now independently confirms KellyBench's central claims from multiple angles: METR's time-horizon data, Greenblatt's misalignment taxonomy, and the imperfect-verifier result all triangulate on the same point — long-horizon operational coherence is the binding constraint, and it's measurable.

Where I'd push back on the seed analysis's framing: the claim that "this is the eval that gets cited in every frontier lab RL-environments pitch for the next 12 months" is probably right for *public* pitches, but KellyBench's actual impact as a *training environment* is limited by its expense ($969–$1,571/episode) and narrow domain. The real legacy is the design pattern — "scale world complexity, not task count" — which other teams will replicate in cheaper, more diverse domains. KellyBench is the proof of concept; the production versions will look different.

The missing piece remains the human baseline. Without it, the leaderboard is directionally useful for model comparison but can't answer the question Tim and other investors actually care about: how close are these agents to replacing (or augmenting) a human quant in a real-world decision environment?
sections.talking_points:
> **Every frontier model lost money betting on the Premier League, but only two avoided total ruin — and that "avoided ruin" metric is more commercially important than the ROI numbers.** Enterprise buyers evaluating agent platforms care about catastrophic failure rates, not average performance. KellyBench operationalizes survival as a capability metric. *(Best for: investor calls, Anthropic equity conversations)*

> **The 30× cost gap between frontier and open models on long-horizon tasks is a structural moat that SWE-bench doesn't capture.** Open models finished KellyBench for $30–40. Opus 4.6 burned $969 and GPT-5.4 $1,571 — and they're the only ones that didn't go bankrupt. The "open models are catching up" narrative is true for procedural tasks and increasingly false for long-horizon ones. *(Best for: LP updates on frontier lab defensibility)*

> **"Scale world complexity, not task count" is the correct design thesis for next-generation agent evaluation.** The procedural benchmarks (SWE-bench, APEX, GDPval) will saturate as models improve; complex-world environments like KellyBench will keep separating models for years. General Reasoning's bet is that the RL environments company wins the post-RLHF era the way Scale AI won the RLHF era. *(Best for: VC roundtables, founder chats with eval/infra builders)*

> **KellyBench's sophistication rubric is the public debut of rubric-as-reward for complex worlds — and a week of subsequent research says it works.** The Athalye et al. imperfect-verifier result means you don't need a perfect rubric to train on it; 15% noise is tolerable. This substantially lowers the bar for deploying KellyBench-style environments as training infrastructure, not just evaluation. *(Best for: technical conversations, founder chats on verification startups)*

> **METR's time-horizon data independently validates KellyBench: Gemini 3.1 Pro's coherence window is ~6 hours, and KellyBench episodes run for hundreds.** The time-horizon finding explains the bankruptcy rates — models are literally running past their coherence ceiling. Long-horizon coherence is now measurable from two independent sources, and the picture is consistent. *(Best for: VC roundtables on agent capability timelines)*

title: The School Hidden Inside the Job
author: Carlo Iacono

metadata.author: Carlo Iacono
metadata.title: The School Hidden Inside the Job

sections.tldr: **AI is not primarily coming for entry-level cognitive work — it is coming for the only mechanism by which anyone ever learned to become senior at it.** The routine tasks being automated (first-draft memos, scaffolded code, Tier-1 support, document review) were never just output — they were the curriculum. Remove them and you sever the apprenticeship pipeline. The firms moving fastest into agents will discover, too late, that they've optimized away the pedagogy that produces the senior talent they need in 2040.
sections.whats_new:
**The novel contribution is reframing AI labor disruption as a pedagogy crisis rather than an employment crisis.** Most AI labor economics focuses on which tasks get automated and whether displaced workers find new roles. Iacono argues the deeper damage is upstream: the automated tasks were how juniors became seniors.
