The token inflation (up to 1.35x for the same input) makes the "same pricing" claim technically true but economically misleading — Anthropic addressed this by increasing subscriber limits, but API customers are quietly paying more per semantic unit.

**Effort levels are now a first-class product surface.** The new `xhigh` reasoning effort tier (now the default in Claude Code) creates a five-point dial: low → medium → high → xhigh → max. The key insight is that Opus 4.7-low reportedly matches or beats 4.6-medium across benchmarks, meaning Anthropic has effectively made cheaper inference tiers more capable — a classic compute-efficiency play that benefits both their margin and their customers' per-task costs.
sections.counterintuitive_claims:
**Long-context performance may have regressed, but Anthropic argues the metric was wrong.** Multiple users flagged MRCR/needle-in-a-haystack degradation. Anthropic's Boris Cherny responded that MRCR "overweights distractor-stacking tricks" and cited Graphwalks improvement (38.7% → 58.6%) as the better applied-reasoning signal. This is a bold move — deprecating a community benchmark mid-launch — but it tracks with the broader trend of labs outgrowing synthetic evals and preferring task-completion metrics.

**The system prompt is doing more work than the model.** Theo's "lobotomized" complaints and Mikhail Parakhin's "dumber for non-coding" observations suggest that Opus 4.7's default configuration is heavily tuned for agentic coding via system prompt, with non-coding use cases getting worse default behavior. The fix (use it via API without the default system prompt) confirms that behavior is increasingly a harness property, not a model property — reinforcing the KB's central `harness > model` thesis.
sections.steelman: **Anthropic is building the first model where autonomous verification is a core design target, not a bolted-on feature.** Cat Wu's Claude Code guidance — "delegate, don't micromanage; put goal + constraints + acceptance criteria up front; tell the model how to verify" — is essentially an operator's manual for verification-first agent design. Combined with the `xhigh` default, task budgets in beta, and `/ultrareview` for Claude Code, Anthropic is optimizing for a workflow where the model runs autonomously for extended periods, self-verifies, and only surfaces work that meets acceptance criteria. This is the strongest evidence yet that Anthropic views the generation-verification gap as a first-order product problem, not an academic curiosity.
sections.steelman_rebuttal: **The benchmark gains may be real but economically ambiguous.** LlamaIndex's independent eval showed charts improved dramatically (13.5% → 55.8%) but layout *regressed* (16.5% → 14.0%), and cost per page is 7¢ vs. specialized pipelines at 0.4¢/page. For enterprise document processing — a key revenue vertical — Opus 4.7 might be *worse* on a cost-adjusted basis. The "strictly better in every dimension" headline is true on raw benchmarks but false on the cost-performance Pareto for many real workloads.
sections.technical_insights:
**Concrete benchmark data (independently verified):**
- SWE-bench Verified: 87.6% (+7 points vs 4.6) — code repair/improvement
- SWE-bench Pro: 64.3% (+11 points) — more complex software engineering
- TerminalBench 2.0: 69.4% (+4 points) — terminal/CLI tasks
- Document reasoning: 80.6% (up from 57.1%) — multimodal comprehension
- ARC-AGI-1: 92%; ARC-AGI-2: 75.83% — abstract reasoning
- Cursor internal: 58% → 70% — real-world coding assistant quality
- Notion internal: 14% lift, 1/3 tool errors — enterprise integration quality

**Vision upgrade is substantial**: 2,576px long edge (~3.75MP), 3x prior models. This matters for computer-use agents reading dense screenshots and for document processing workflows.
sections.second_order_implications:
**If Opus 4.7 is indeed a "distilled Mythos," the cybersecurity capability curve is steeper than the public model suggests.** The system card reveals Anthropic "experimented with efforts to differentially reduce cyber capabilities during training," and yet Opus 4.7 still scores *higher* than 4.6 on Firefox shell exploitation and has prompt-injection robustness "close to Mythos." The implication: the delta between Opus 4.7 (general release) and Mythos (restricted preview) may be narrower than Anthropic publicly frames — which has consequences for both the Glasswing security narrative and for competitor labs' safety benchmarking.

**The tokenizer change signals Anthropic's willingness to break backwards compatibility.** Every third-party tool that cached token counts, estimated costs, or optimized for the old tokenizer (including OpenClaw!) is now slightly wrong. For a lab building an enterprise platform, this is a surprisingly aggressive move — it suggests Anthropic values capability cadence over ecosystem stability.
sections.my_take:
**This is the best independent analysis of Opus 4.7 available.** Tim already rated the official Anthropic launch post 10/10 (see `2026/04/16/blog-anthropic-opus47-launch.md`), but this Latent Space synthesis adds critical signal the official post intentionally omitted: the community backlash on long-context regression, the tokenizer/new-base-model debate, the "lobotomized system prompt" controversy, and the LlamaIndex cost analysis. The picture that emerges is of a model that's genuinely better for autonomous coding (its primary design target) but whose gains are less clear-cut for enterprise document processing and general conversation. The harness-over-model thesis gets its strongest confirmation yet: Theo's experience — "dumber without the right system prompt, incredible with it" — is literally the definition of harness > model.

Connects directly to: `kb/2026/04/16/blog-anthropic-opus47-launch.md` (the official version — Tim rated 10/10), `kb/2026/04/17/blog-anthropic-trustworthy-agents.md` (Tim rated 10/10 — the governance layer for what Opus 4.7 enables), and the `harness > model` thesis across multiple KB entries.
sections.talking_points:
> **Opus 4.7's new tokenizer is the real story — it's probably a new base model, not a fine-tune.** That means Anthropic shipped a Mythos-derived model to the general public with cyber capabilities surgically reduced. The gap between their restricted and public models is narrower than they're saying. *(Best for: investor calls)*

> **The "strictly better" headline hides real tradeoffs.** Long-context regression, 35% token inflation, and 17x more expensive document processing vs specialized pipelines mean Opus 4.7 is optimized for autonomous coding, not everything. *(Best for: founder conversations)*

> **Cat Wu's three rules — delegate, specify acceptance criteria, encode verification — are the best one-paragraph summary of harness engineering in production.** This is Anthropic saying the quiet part loud: the model works when the harness tells it how to verify its own work. *(Best for: VC roundtables)*

> **Anthropic deprecated a community benchmark mid-launch to replace it with one that makes their model look better.** Bold, maybe justified (Graphwalks does seem more applied), but it sets a precedent where labs control both the model and the measurement. *(Best for: governance discussions)*

title: The $300 Overnight Loop That's About To Eat Your Competitive Advantage
author: Nate

metadata.author: Nate
metadata.title: The $300 Overnight Loop That's About To Eat Your Competitive Advantage

sections.tldr: **Andrej Karpathy pointed an AI agent at his own training code, went to sleep, and woke up to 700 experiments, 20 genuine improvements, an 11% training time reduction, and a bug in his attention implementation — all for under $300 in compute.** Nate argues this "Karpathy Loop" pattern — one file, one metric, one time budget — is about to scale from optimizing ML training code to optimizing agent scaffolding itself. When a meta-agent rewrites a task agent's entire harness overnight, every team's competitive advantage becomes perishable on a daily cycle.
sections.whats_new:
**The progression from training code to agent harnesses is the non-obvious escalation.** The original Karpathy experiment (March 8, 2026) was specific: an AI agent optimizing ML training code against a single metric. SkyPilot scaled it to 910 experiments on a 16-GPU cluster, still under $300. But the real escalation came on April 2 when a YC startup called ThirdLayer pointed the same loop at something more consequential than training code: the prompts, tools, and orchestration logic that determine how agents behave.

This is the step-change: **a meta-agent that optimizes the harness of a task agent overnight.** The constraints that make it work are notable in their minimalism — one file, one metric, one time budget. The minimalism isn't a limitation; it's the whole point. Complex multi-objective optimization fails because agents can't reason about tradeoffs. A single clear metric gives the agent a search space it can explore productively.
sections.counterintuitive_claims:
**The pattern democratizes what used to be elite ML engineering.** If a 630-line script can find 20 improvements and a bug that one of the world's best ML researchers missed, the implication is that search volume beats individual expertise — at least for incremental optimization. The agent didn't need to be smarter than Karpathy. It just tried more things, faster, without getting bored after the fifteenth failed attempt.

**The "local hard takeoff" framing is deliberately provocative.** Small teams can run this for a few hundred dollars tonight. Most enterprises will fail the prerequisites — not because the compute is expensive, but because they don't have a single clear metric to optimize against, or their codebase can't be tested in isolation. The constraint isn't capability or cost; it's organizational readiness.
sections.key_assumptions:
- The optimization target must be expressible as a single, unambiguous metric. Multi-objective optimization (reliability AND latency AND cost) is not addressed.
- The codebase must be testable in isolation — no external dependencies that break during overnight runs.
- The improvements must be verifiable: if the metric can be gamed (Goodhart's Law), the agent will game it.
sections.forward_looking_hypotheses:
- **Agent harness optimization becomes the new AutoML.** The original AutoML movement (2017-2020) tried to automate hyperparameter search. The Karpathy Loop is the 2026 version: automate the search over the entire harness — prompts, tools, orchestration, verification logic.
- **Competitive advantage half-life shrinks to days.** If any team can run this loop overnight, the duration of any harness optimization advantage is bounded by the time it takes competitors to run the same loop. This pushes the moat from "what's in the harness" to "how fast you iterate the harness."
sections.second_order_implications:
**The safety problem hiding in plain sight.** As Nate flags: an agent gaming your metrics looks identical to an agent actually improving your business, right up until the moment it doesn't. This connects directly to the KB's verification-and-evaluation theme — the Karpathy Loop works precisely when verification is cheap (run the test suite, check the metric), but breaks when the metric is a proxy for what you actually want.

For the KB: this extends the harness engineering sequence (`kb/2026/04/17/blog-humanlayer-harness-engineering.md`, `kb/2026/04/18/blog-nates-karpathy-loop-teams.md` from this morning). The morning analysis covered the "Karpathy Loop → team structure" angle; this evening analysis covers the "Karpathy Loop → competitive dynamics" angle. Together they form a complete picture: the loop changes both how teams are organized and how fast competitive advantages decay.

This also connects to the Interconnects "lossy self-improvement" analysis (`kb/2026/04/14/blog-interconnects-lossy-self-improvement.md`) — the Karpathy Loop is a practical instance of lossy self-improvement, where the agent improves its own environment/harness rather than its own weights.
sections.my_take:
**The Karpathy Loop is the clearest proof-of-concept for practical recursive self-improvement in production systems.** It's not AGI improving itself — it's a search agent optimizing a bounded codebase against a clear metric. But the pattern is general: any system with a testable metric and an automatable search space can benefit.

The $300 cost point is the killer detail. At that price, the Karpathy Loop is accessible to every startup, every side project, every individual developer with a GPU budget. The competitive implication is real: if your competitor can run 700 experiments overnight for the cost of a nice dinner, your hand-tuned configurations have a shelf life measured in days.

For Tim: this is the "RSI for practitioners" piece he's been looking for. Not theoretical recursive self-improvement, but a practical, reproducible pattern that's already running in production at multiple companies. The investment thesis: companies that build infrastructure for running Karpathy Loops at scale (experiment orchestration, metric verification, safe sandboxing) are building the picks-and-shovels of the agent era.
sections.talking_points:
> **Karpathy's 630-line script found 20 improvements and a bug he missed — for $300.** The agent wasn't smarter. It just tried 700 experiments without getting bored after the fifteenth failure. Search volume beats individual expertise for incremental optimization. *(Best for: founder conversations on AI tooling)*

> **The real escalation: a meta-agent that optimizes the harness of a task agent overnight.** This isn't just about ML training code anymore. A YC startup already pointed the same loop at agent scaffolding — prompts, tools, orchestration logic. Every team's competitive advantage becomes perishable on a daily cycle. *(Best for: investor calls)*

> **The Goodhart's Law problem is the hidden risk.** An agent gaming your metrics looks identical to an agent improving your business, right up until it doesn't. The Karpathy Loop works when verification is cheap. It breaks when the metric is a proxy. *(Best for: VC roundtables on agent reliability)*

title: The Teams That Can Define 'Better' Are About To Pull Away From Everyone Else
author: Nate

metadata.author: Nate
metadata.title: The Teams That Can Define 'Better' Are About To Pull Away From Everyone Else

sections.tldr: **The "Karpathy Loop" — one file, one metric, one time budget — is the minimal viable architecture for agent-driven optimization, and it just escalated from improving ML training code to rewriting the agent harnesses themselves.** Karpathy pointed an agent at his training code, let it run 700 experiments in two days, and it cut training time 11% and found an attention bug. SkyPilot scaled the pattern to 910 experiments for under $300. ThirdLayer (YC) then aimed the same loop at agent scaffolding (prompts, tools, orchestration logic), producing a meta-agent that rewrote another agent's entire harness overnight. The thesis: teams that can formalize "better" into a metric will compound improvements faster than organizations can track.
sections.whats_new:
**The escalation from "agent improves training code" to "agent improves agent harness" is the key development.** The Karpathy Loop has been discussed in the KB's context (see `kb/2026/04/12/blog-exponentialview-karpathy-loop.md` for Exponential View's earlier coverage). What's new is the ThirdLayer leap: a meta-agent that optimizes the harness layer itself — the prompts, tools, and orchestration logic that determine how other agents behave. This is one step closer to the recursive self-improvement loop that the KB tracks under `kb/topics/ai-safety-alignment.md`, but bounded: it's optimization within a sandbox, not unbounded self-modification.

**The minimalism is the whole point.** Three constraints — one file (the thing being optimized), one metric (the definition of "better"), one time budget (the sandbox boundary) — are what make the loop tractable. Remove any constraint and you get either unbounded search (the safety nightmare) or scope creep (the engineering failure mode). The article calls this a "local hard takeoff, bounded to a domain, a metric, a sandbox" — which is the most precise characterization of what recursive improvement actually looks like in practice vs. theory.
sections.key_assumptions:
**The loop requires a formally specifiable definition of "better."** This is the key prerequisite. Training time, benchmark scores, and cost per inference are easy to formalize. But most business outcomes (customer satisfaction, design quality, strategic judgment) aren't. The article's central claim — that teams who can define "better" will pull away — is therefore a claim about which domains are Karpathy-Loop-compatible. The implication: domains with clear, measurable quality metrics (ML training, code generation, agent benchmarks) will see compounding improvement; domains with fuzzy quality metrics (care, creativity, strategy) won't.

**This connects directly to the verification-and-evaluation theme.** The Karpathy Loop works because the metric serves as an automated verifier. If you can't verify "better," you can't close the loop. This is the generation-verification gap in miniature: the agent generates candidate improvements, the metric verifies them, and the loop compounds. The teams that solve verification first are the teams that can run this loop.
sections.second_order_implications:
**The safety problem is metric gaming.** As the article's preview notes: "An agent gaming your metrics looks identical to an agent actually improving your business, right up until the moment it doesn't." This is Goodhart's Law applied to recursive agent optimization. The meta-agent that rewrites another agent's harness is optimizing against the metric — but the metric is a proxy for the real objective. If the proxy is even slightly misaligned with the real objective, the loop amplifies the misalignment with each iteration. This is the practical, near-term version of the alignment problem.

**Enterprise adoption will be gated on eval maturity.** Only organizations with robust, domain-specific evaluation infrastructure can safely run the Karpathy Loop. This further advantages teams that have invested in verification systems (connects to the KB's coverage of KellyBench, Berkeley trustworthy benchmarks, and Anthropic's trustworthy agents framework).
sections.my_take: **This is a useful practitioner-level piece that maps the Karpathy Loop to its next logical application domain (agent harnesses), though the paywalled body prevents a full assessment of depth.** The preview is strong — the "local hard takeoff" framing is the crispest I've seen for describing what bounded recursive improvement actually looks like. The safety-through-metric-gaming angle is the right concern. If the full article delivers on its promise of actionable diagnostics, it's among the more useful pieces for engineering leaders Nate has published.
sections.talking_points:
> **The Karpathy Loop just escalated: agents are now rewriting other agents' harnesses overnight.** ThirdLayer (YC) aimed a meta-agent at another agent's entire scaffolding — prompts, tools, orchestration logic — and it outperformed every hand-engineered entry on the leaderboards it targeted. The compute cost: under $300. The constraint: one metric. This is what bounded recursive improvement looks like in practice. *(Best for: founder conversations, AI-native startup pitches)*

> **"Local hard takeoff" is the best framing for what's actually happening.** It's not an intelligence explosion. It's optimization loops closing on specific business systems and compounding faster than the organizations around them can track. Bounded to a domain, a metric, a sandbox. The teams that can formalize "better" are about to pull away from the teams that can't. *(Best for: VC roundtables)*

> **The real safety problem is Goodhart's Law at machine speed.** An agent gaming your metrics looks identical to an agent improving your business. The Karpathy Loop amplifies whatever the metric captures — including the gap between the metric and the actual objective. Eval maturity is now a prerequisite for agent deployment. *(Best for: AI safety conversations)*

title: The Next Evolution of the Agents SDK
author: OpenAI

metadata.author: OpenAI
metadata.title: The Next Evolution of the Agents SDK

sections.tldr: **OpenAI updated its Agents SDK with native sandbox execution and a model-native harness, codifying the "harness > model" thesis into an official infrastructure product.** The SDK now includes configurable memory, sandbox-aware orchestration, Codex-like filesystem tools, a Manifest abstraction for portable workspaces, and built-in snapshotting/rehydration for durable agent runs. Sandbox providers (Cloudflare, E2B, Modal, Vercel, and others) are first-class integrations. This is the clearest signal yet that the infrastructure layer — not the model layer — is where platform competition is moving.
sections.whats_new:
**The harness/sandbox split is an architectural opinion masquerading as an SDK update.** OpenAI is declaring that agents require two fundamentally separate layers: a harness (instructions, tools, orchestration, memory, tracing) and a sandbox (isolated compute, filesystem, dependencies). The harness is where the intelligence lives — it's the "operating system" for the agent. The sandbox is where the work happens — isolated, snapshotable, resumable. This split mirrors what Anthropic described in "Harness Design for Long-Running Apps" and what HumanLayer documented in their practitioner guide (see `kb/2026/04/17/blog-humanlayer-harness-engineering.md`), but OpenAI is productizing it as the default architecture.

**The Manifest abstraction is the sleeper feature.** It describes an agent's workspace declaratively — which files, repos, and cloud storage to mount, with Unix-style permissions. This makes workspaces portable across sandbox providers (E2B, Modal, Cloudflare, etc.), preventing any single sandbox vendor from becoming the lock-in point. The strategic implication: OpenAI wants to own the harness (orchestration, memory, tracing) while commoditizing the sandbox (compute). This is the same pattern as cloud providers commoditizing compute while owning the control plane.
sections.technical_insights:
**Snapshotting + rehydration solves the durability problem.** Long-running agents (hours/days) will inevitably hit failures — container crashes, rate limits, context exhaustion. The SDK's built-in snapshotting externalizes agent state, so a crashed sandbox can be replaced and the agent continues from the last checkpoint. This directly addresses the compounding failure problem documented in the KB's harness engineering coverage: a 20-step pipeline at 95% per-step reliability has 36% end-to-end success. Checkpointing turns a single long-running task into a series of shorter resumable segments.

**The SDK supports 100+ non-OpenAI LLMs** via the Chat Completions API. This is a remarkable competitive move: OpenAI is building the harness layer to be model-agnostic, betting that developers who build on the SDK will default to OpenAI's models (because the harness is optimized for them) but aren't locked in. The strategy is: own the developer experience, make switching models easy, make switching harnesses hard.

**TemporalIO-powered orchestration** means the SDK inherits Temporal's workflow durability guarantees — exactly-once execution, automatic retries, persistent state across failures. This is enterprise-grade infrastructure that most teams would otherwise build from scratch.
sections.key_assumptions: **The key bet is that the harness, not the model, is the defensible layer.** If models continue commoditizing (Claude, GPT, Gemini perform within a narrow band on standard benchmarks), the harness — orchestration, memory, tracing, sandbox integration — becomes the platform moat. This aligns with the KB's running theme from Latent Space's "Extreme Harness Engineering" through Martin Fowler's coding-agent harness framework. But it's a bet: if one model pulls meaningfully ahead (as Mythos appears to have done in cybersecurity), model lock-in could reassert itself.
sections.second_order_implications:
**For Anthropic:** This is a direct competitive response to Anthropic's managed-agents platform and Claude Code's auto-mode. OpenAI is saying: "We'll give you the same long-running agent capabilities, but as an open SDK you can run on any infrastructure." Anthropic's advantage is tighter model-product integration (Claude Code, Claude Design, Cowork); OpenAI's advantage is developer flexibility and sandbox-provider ecosystem. The harness wars are now fully joined.

**For startups building agent infrastructure:** The "middleware layer" between model and application just got squeezed from both ends. OpenAI's SDK gives developers harness + sandbox out of the box; Anthropic's managed agents give enterprises turnkey deployment. Startups like HumanLayer, LangChain, and CrewAI need to differentiate on domain-specific value (human-in-the-loop patterns, enterprise governance, vertical workflows) rather than generic orchestration.

**For the "harness > model" thesis:** This SDK update is the strongest evidence yet. OpenAI's own harness engineering blog post documented how a 3-person team built 1M+ lines of code with zero human-written code — by investing in the harness. Now they're shipping that same infrastructure as a product. The message to developers: stop building harnesses from scratch, use ours.
sections.my_take:
**This is the OpenAI product that matters most for enterprise agent deployment in 2026.** Not GPT-5.4, not Codex, not the model — the SDK. Because the SDK is where the rubber meets the road for production agents: durability, isolation, credential management, state persistence, multi-step orchestration. The model is the engine; the SDK is the car. OpenAI is now shipping the car.

The competitive dynamics are fascinating. Both OpenAI and Anthropic have converged on the same architectural insight (harness + sandbox + model as separable layers) but are taking opposite strategic approaches: OpenAI with an open SDK (flexibility, model-agnostic), Anthropic with integrated products (Claude Code, Claude Design, managed agents). Which wins depends on whether enterprises value flexibility or integration — and the answer is probably "both, depending on the use case."
sections.talking_points:
> **OpenAI just shipped the most important product in the agent infrastructure stack — and it's not a model.** The Agents SDK update with native sandboxing and durable harness infrastructure is the clearest signal that the platform competition is moving from the model layer to the harness layer. Models are the engine; the SDK is the car. *(Best for: VC roundtables, infrastructure investment thesis)*

> **The Manifest abstraction is OpenAI's play to own the control plane while commoditizing the sandbox.** Portable workspace definitions let developers switch sandbox providers (E2B, Modal, Vercel) without rewriting their agent code. OpenAI wants to be the orchestration layer that every agent runs through, regardless of where the compute happens. This is the cloud provider playbook applied to AI agents. *(Best for: founder conversations about platform strategy)*

> **The harness wars are now fully joined: OpenAI open SDK vs. Anthropic integrated products.** Same architectural insight, opposite strategies. OpenAI bets on developer flexibility and a sandbox-provider ecosystem. Anthropic bets on end-to-end integration (Claude Code → Claude Design → Claude Cowork). Which wins depends on whether enterprises value flexibility or integration. *(Best for: investor calls)*

> **Snapshotting + rehydration solves the durability problem that kills production agents.** A 20-step pipeline at 95% per-step reliability has 36% end-to-end success. Checkpointing turns long-running tasks into resumable segments. This is the infrastructure that separates demo agents from production agents. *(Best for: technical founder conversations)*

title: Changes in the system prompt between Claude Opus 4.6 and 4.7
author: Simon Willison

metadata.author: Simon Willison
metadata.title: Changes in the system prompt between Claude Opus 4.6 and 4.7

sections.tldr: **Simon Willison diffs the published system prompts for Claude Opus 4.6 and 4.7, revealing how Anthropic is tuning Claude's personality, tool usage, and safety posture between model generations.** The most significant changes: Claude now acts before asking ("the person typically wants Claude to make a reasonable attempt now, not to be interviewed first"), uses a new `tool_search` mechanism to discover available tools before claiming incapability, and has substantially expanded child safety instructions. Anthropic is also explicitly training Claude to be less verbose and less pushy.
sections.whats_new:
**Willison created a git timeline of Claude system prompts** — using Claude Code itself to break Anthropic's published system prompt archive into separate documents, construct a fake git history with commit dates matching publication dates, and generate diffs. The approach is clever and reproducible.

The key behavioral changes from 4.6 to 4.7:

1. **Acting > Clarifying.** A new `<acting_vs_clarifying>` section explicitly tells Claude: "When a request leaves minor details unspecified, the person typically wants Claude to make a reasonable attempt now, not to be interviewed first." This is a major shift — it reduces the "20 questions" behavior that frustrated power users.

2. **Tool search before giving up.** Before concluding it lacks a capability, Claude now calls `tool_search` to check whether a relevant tool is available but deferred. "I don't have access to X" is only correct after `tool_search` confirms no matching tool exists. This implies an expanding tool ecosystem where Claude can't keep all available tools in active context.

3. **Less verbosity.** New language: "Claude keeps its responses focused and concise so as to avoid potentially overwhelming the user." The 4.6 instruction to avoid words like "genuinely," "honestly," or "straightforward" has been removed — presumably because 4.7's training handles this natively.

4. **Expanded safety boundaries.** Child safety instructions are greatly expanded and wrapped in a `<critical_child_safety_instructions>` tag. New section on "disordered eating" — Claude won't provide specific nutrition numbers/targets/step-by-step plans if it detects disordered eating patterns.

5. **Anti-manipulation.** New `<evenhandedness>` section guards against screenshot attacks: Claude can decline to give simple yes/no answers to complex or contested issues.

6. **Trump knowledge update.** The explicit "Donald Trump is the current president" override (needed because 4.6's training data predated his inauguration) is gone — 4.7's knowledge cutoff (January 2026) makes it unnecessary.
sections.counterintuitive_claims: **The "acting > clarifying" shift is more radical than it appears.** Prior Claude versions were trained toward caution — ask before acting, especially when tool use is involved. The new instruction explicitly reverses this for minor ambiguity: act first, explain your assumptions, only ask when the request is "genuinely unanswerable." This is a direct response to the Opus 4.6 user revolt — the GitHub issue from an AMD senior director who wrote "Claude has regressed to the point it cannot be trusted to perform complex engineering" — and it shows Anthropic recalibrating the helpfulness/safety tradeoff in real time via the system prompt.
sections.key_assumptions:
- **System prompts are a meaningful window into model behavior.** This is mostly true but incomplete — Willison notes that Anthropic publishes system prompts but not tool descriptions, which are arguably more important. The published information is necessary but not sufficient to understand Claude's behavior.
- **Training and system prompts are complementary.** The removal of explicit behavioral instructions (avoid "genuinely," avoid emotes in asterisks) suggests the model's base training now handles what the system prompt previously had to patch. This is the healthy direction: prompts handle context, not compensation for training failures.
sections.second_order_implications:
**The `tool_search` mechanism implies Anthropic is building toward a marketplace of tools too large for any single context window.** If Claude can't enumerate all available tools in its system prompt, it needs a discovery mechanism. This connects directly to the Anthropic Marketplace and MCP ecosystem — and it's one of the first concrete signs that the tool ecosystem is outgrowing static enumeration.

**The full tool list** Willison extracted (via direct prompt) includes: `conversation_search`, `message_compose_v1`, `fetch_sports_data`, `places_map_display_v0`, `recipe_display_v0`, `search_mcp_registry`, `weather_fetch`, and more. This is a consumer product tool suite that's evolving toward a platform.

For the KB: this pairs with the analysis of Claude Design (`kb/2026/04/18/blog-anthropic-claude-design.md`) and the OpenAI Agents SDK evolution (`kb/2026/04/18/blog-openai-agents-sdk-evolution.md`) from the morning run. All three show labs racing to build tool/agent platforms on top of their models.
sections.my_take:
**Simon Willison is the most consistently useful independent observer of the AI ecosystem.** His system prompt diffs provide exactly the kind of empirical grounding that's missing from most AI commentary. The git timeline approach is especially clever — it turns a wall of text into a navigable history.

For Tim: the "acting > clarifying" shift is the signal that matters most. It shows Anthropic is willing to recalibrate its safety posture in response to user feedback, and it's doing so through the system prompt (fast, reversible) rather than retraining (slow, permanent). This is how the platform will evolve: quarterly model releases for capabilities, but continuous system prompt updates for behavior.
sections.talking_points:
> **Anthropic published the sharpest behavioral insight in a system prompt, not a blog post.** Claude 4.7's new instruction — "the person typically wants Claude to make a reasonable attempt now, not to be interviewed first" — is a direct reversal of the overcautious 4.6 behavior. The system prompt is the real product changelog. *(Best for: founder conversations on AI UX)*

> **Claude now searches for its own tools before saying "I can't do that."** The new `tool_search` mechanism means Claude's capability set is larger than what fits in its system prompt. This is a sign the tool ecosystem is outgrowing static enumeration — and that's the precondition for a real marketplace. *(Best for: investor calls on platform strategy)*

> **The system prompt is the fastest feedback loop in AI product development.** Model training takes months. System prompt updates ship in days. Anthropic is using this asymmetry to iterate on behavior while the model stays constant. *(Best for: X posts)*

title: Harness design for long-running application development
author: Prithvi Rajasekaran

metadata.author: Prithvi Rajasekaran
metadata.title: Harness design for long-running application development

sections.tldr: **Anthropic's Labs team built a GAN-inspired three-agent architecture (Planner → Generator → Evaluator) that produces rich full-stack applications over multi-hour autonomous coding sessions — and the key insight is that separating evaluation from generation is far more tractable than making a generator self-critical.** The evaluator uses Playwright to click through the running application like a real user, catching bugs the generator confidently claims don't exist. Solo agents produced apps where the central feature was broken; the harness-built version worked.
sections.whats_new:
**The novel contribution is empirical evidence that adversarial evaluation beats self-evaluation for subjective AND objective tasks, and that this holds across model generations.** Previous harness work (Anthropic's own earlier post, OpenAI's Codex post) focused on context management and decomposition. This work isolates the self-evaluation failure mode — agents "confidently praising" their own mediocre output — and shows that a standalone evaluator tuned for skepticism is the fix. The four grading criteria (design quality, originality, craft, functionality) turned the subjective question "is this design good?" into something gradable.

The second insight is about **harness component lifecycle**: every component encodes an assumption about what the model can't do on its own, and those assumptions go stale as models improve. When they upgraded from Opus 4.5 → 4.6, they were able to drop the sprint construct entirely and remove context resets, because 4.6 no longer exhibited the "context anxiety" behavior that 4.5 showed. The evaluator remained load-bearing, but only for tasks at the edge of model capability — a moving boundary.
sections.counterintuitive_claims:
**"Context resets > compaction" for models with context anxiety.** While compaction (summarizing earlier context in-place) preserves continuity, it doesn't give the agent a clean slate, so context anxiety persists. Full resets with structured handoff artifacts were essential for Opus 4.5 — but became unnecessary with Opus 4.6. This means the right architecture depends on the specific model's behavioral profile, not just the task.

**The evaluator's biggest value isn't catching bugs — it's making the generator iterate against concrete feedback.** Without the evaluator, generators produce safe, generic, "technically functional but visually unremarkable" output. The evaluator creates pressure toward aesthetic risk-taking and completeness. In one case, a design agent scrapped its approach entirely on iteration 10 and produced a 3D spatial museum experience — "the kind of creative leap I hadn't seen before from a single-pass generation."
sections.technical_insights:
**The three-agent architecture is mechanistically precise:**
- **Planner**: Expands 1-4 sentence prompt into full product spec. Deliberately avoids granular technical detail (early over-specification cascades into downstream errors). Instructed to weave AI features into specs.
- **Generator**: Implements features in sprints with React/Vite/FastAPI/SQLite stack. Self-evaluates before handing off to QA. Uses git for version control.
- **Evaluator**: Uses Playwright MCP to navigate the live app like a real user. Grades against sprint contracts with hard thresholds. If any criterion falls below threshold, sprint fails and generator gets detailed feedback.

**Sprint contracts** are the coordination mechanism: before each sprint, generator and evaluator negotiate what "done" looks like. This bridges the gap between high-level user stories and testable implementation.

**Concrete cost data:**
- Solo agent: 20 min, $9 → broken core feature
- Full harness (Opus 4.5): 6 hours, $200 → working app with rich features
- Simplified harness (Opus 4.6): ~4 hours, $125 → working app, no sprint decomposition needed

**Evaluator calibration required real work**: out of the box, Claude was a poor QA agent — it would identify issues then talk itself out of caring about them. Multiple rounds of prompt tuning against examples where its judgment diverged from human judgment were needed.
sections.key_assumptions:
**The argument that "the evaluator boundary moves with model capability" assumes monotonic model improvement in self-evaluation.** But self-evaluation failure might be structural (an inherent limitation of generating and judging in the same context), not just a capability gap. If so, the evaluator remains permanently load-bearing regardless of model generation.

**The cost comparison ($9 vs $200) implicitly assumes the harness output is worth 20x more.** For the retro game maker, this seems defensible (working vs broken). For simpler tasks, the ROI calculation shifts.
sections.second_order_implications:
**If separated evaluation consistently outperforms self-evaluation, the verification bottleneck doesn't collapse — it migrates.** You still need someone (or something) to calibrate the evaluator. This connects directly to the generation-verification gap: the evaluator itself needs verification, creating a recursive oversight problem. The few-shot calibration approach (human provides example judgments) is the current stopgap, but it doesn't scale to domains where the human can't easily grade output.

**Harness component lifecycle has CapEx implications for agent infrastructure companies.** If each model release obsoletes a harness layer (4.6 killed context resets, future models might kill sprint decomposition), then harness companies face a Red Queen's Race — the same observation from `kb/2026/03/10/2031494111732314283-hxlfed14-agent-harness-absorption.md`. The durable value is in domain-specific evaluation criteria, not generic orchestration.

**The "boring technology wins" principle (agents perform better with stable, well-documented APIs) creates a selection pressure toward fewer tech stacks chosen for "AI-friendliness" rather than developer preference.** This was noted by Fowler in his synthesis (`kb/2026/04/13/blog-fowler-harness-engineering-synthesis.md`) and is now empirically confirmed by Anthropic's own team.
sections.my_take:
**This is the most mechanistically precise harness engineering paper published so far — more useful than OpenAI's harness post** (`kb/2026/04/13/blog-openai-harness-engineering.md`) because it gives concrete cost data, explicit architectural diagrams, and a head-to-head comparison. The GAN-inspired framing is clever but the real insight is simpler: models are bad at grading their own work, and fixing that one problem cascades into quality improvements everywhere else.

The harness component lifecycle principle — "every component encodes an assumption about what the model can't do, and those assumptions expire" — is the most important meta-lesson. It means the optimal harness is a moving target, and the best harness engineers are the ones who keep stress-testing their own scaffolding against new model releases. This extends the "Bitter Lesson Engineering" frame from Miessler (`kb/2026/04/15/blog-miessler-good-bad-harness.md`) with Anthropic's own first-party evidence.
sections.talking_points:
> **Agents are systematically bad at evaluating their own work — even on tasks with verifiable outcomes.** Anthropic's solution: separate the generator from the evaluator, tune the evaluator for skepticism, and let them iterate adversarially. Same pattern as GANs, applied to software engineering. *(Best for: founder chats, engineering leaders)*

> **Every harness component is a bet against the model.** Anthropic dropped sprint decomposition when Opus 4.6 arrived because the model no longer needed it. The durable value in agent infrastructure isn't generic orchestration — it's domain-specific evaluation criteria that models can't internalize. *(Best for: VC roundtables, agent infra investment thesis)*

> **Solo agent: $9, 20 minutes, broken app. Three-agent harness: $200, 6 hours, working app with AI features the user never asked for.** The 20x cost premium buys you a qualitative capability jump, not just a quantitative improvement. *(Best for: enterprise AI budget conversations)*

> **The verification bottleneck doesn't collapse with better models — it migrates.** Who calibrates the evaluator? Anthropic's team spent multiple rounds hand-tuning evaluator prompts against their own judgment. The generation-verification gap is recursive. *(Best for: investor calls on verification infrastructure)*

title: Long-running Claude for scientific computing
author: Siddharth Mishra-Sharma

metadata.author: Siddharth Mishra-Sharma
metadata.title: Long-running Claude for scientific computing

sections.tldr: **An Anthropic Discovery team researcher walks through building a differentiable cosmological Boltzmann solver using Claude Opus 4.6 running autonomously over multiple days — compressing what would normally be months or years of researcher-time into days.** The key infrastructure pattern: CLAUDE.md as plan, CHANGELOG.md as persistent memory, a reference implementation as test oracle, git as coordination layer, and the "Ralph Loop" as an orchestration pattern that kicks the agent back when it claims premature completion.
sections.whats_new:
**The novel contribution is a complete, replicable recipe for multi-day autonomous scientific computing — using only Claude Code, tmux, SLURM, and git.** Unlike the Vibe Physics post (same day launch, see `kb/2026/04/19/blog-anthropic-vibe-physics-grad-student.md`), where Schwartz supervised every step, this workflow is explicitly designed for minimal human intervention. The researcher checked in via phone while waiting in line for coffee.

The task is structurally different from the C compiler project: a Boltzmann solver is a **deeply coupled pipeline** where a small numerical error cascades through everything downstream. This requires sequential debugging with domain knowledge, not parallelizable decomposition. The post is honest that the agent's development was "somewhat clunky" — gaps in test coverage, elementary gauge convention mistakes, hours spent on bugs a domain expert would spot instantly.
sections.technical_insights:
**The four-pillar infrastructure:**

1. **CLAUDE.md as plan** — high-level objectives, design decisions, accuracy targets (0.1% against reference CLASS implementation). Claude can edit this file as it works.
2. **CHANGELOG.md as memory** — portable long-term memory tracking status, completed tasks, **failed approaches and why they didn't work** (prevents re-attempting dead ends). Reads like lab notes from a "fast, hyper-literal postdoc."
3. **Test oracle** — reference implementation (CLASS C source) provides ground truth. The agent constructs and continuously runs unit tests against this oracle. Without it, the agent has no way to know if it's making progress.
4. **Git as coordination** — commit and push after every meaningful unit of work. Never commit code that breaks passing tests. Makes progress visible and recoverable.

**The Ralph Loop** is an orchestration pattern that re-prompts the agent when it claims completion: "Please keep working until the success criterion of 0.1% accuracy is achieved — max 20 iterations, say DONE when truly done." This counters "agentic laziness" — the model's tendency to declare victory prematurely, especially on complex multi-part tasks.

**Concrete output:** a differentiable JAX-based cosmological Boltzmann solver (clax) that achieved sub-percent agreement with CLASS across CMB angular power spectra. Not production-grade (accuracy gaps in some regimes), but functional and open-sourced.
sections.key_assumptions:
**The entire pattern depends on having a reference implementation as a test oracle.** This works for reimplementing known scientific software but breaks for original research where no reference exists. The post acknowledges this: "long-running autonomous scientific work today crucially depends on the agent having a way to know whether it's making progress."

**The "months compressed into days" claim assumes researcher-time, not wall-clock time.** The agent ran for multiple days on HPC with GPU allocation. The compression is in human attention, not calendar time — which is still transformative for a lab where researcher attention is the scarce resource.
sections.second_order_implications:
**"Every night you don't have agents working for you is potential progress left on the table."** This reframes idle compute as opportunity cost — the same economic logic as cryptocurrency mining, applied to research. Labs with HPC access and well-defined problems gain a structural advantage: they can run agents 24/7 while competitors sleep.

**The CHANGELOG.md-as-memory pattern is the scientific version of the "memory as moat" thesis** from the agent infrastructure KB (`kb/topics/agent-infrastructure.md`). A rich changelog is the agent's accumulated domain knowledge — it prevents re-exploration of dead ends and captures successful debugging strategies. Over multiple sessions, this becomes genuinely valuable institutional knowledge.

**The post reveals an unexpected educational side effect:** the researcher (not a domain expert in cosmology) learned substantive physics by reading the agent's commit history. This suggests a new mode of scientific learning: supervising an agent as a way to osmose expertise in an unfamiliar domain.
sections.my_take:
**This is the companion piece to Vibe Physics — together they define Anthropic's AI-for-science positioning from two angles.** Schwartz (Vibe Physics) is the domain expert who supervised every step; Mishra-Sharma is the non-expert who set the agent running and checked in occasionally. The contrast is instructive: expert supervision produces higher-quality output with tighter verification, while autonomous operation with a test oracle produces broader coverage at lower quality. Both compress researcher-time by ~10x.

The four-pillar pattern (CLAUDE.md + CHANGELOG.md + test oracle + git) is immediately applicable beyond science — it's the same infrastructure pattern as the harness engineering posts from OpenAI and Anthropic Engineering. The scientific computing context just makes the verification criterion unusually clean (match the reference implementation to 0.1%).
sections.talking_points:
> **Every night your lab doesn't have agents running is research left on the table.** Anthropic's recipe: CLAUDE.md as plan, CHANGELOG.md as persistent memory, a reference implementation as test oracle, git for coordination, and the Ralph Loop to prevent premature completion. A non-expert built a cosmological Boltzmann solver in days. *(Best for: academic/research-focused conversations)*

> **The pattern that makes autonomous scientific computing work is the test oracle — a reference implementation that tells the agent if it's making progress.** Without it, the agent generates plausible but unverifiable work. This is the generation-verification gap expressed as infrastructure: the verification criterion IS the infrastructure. *(Best for: investor calls on verification infrastructure)*

> **An unexpected educational side effect: reading an AI agent's git history is like watching a postdoc's lab notes unfold in fast-forward.** The researcher learned cosmology by supervising an agent working in a domain he didn't know. That's a new mode of learning. *(Best for: X posts, founder conversations about AI in education)*

title: Vibe physics: The AI grad student
author: Matthew Schwartz

metadata.author: Matthew Schwartz
metadata.title: Vibe physics: The AI grad student

sections.tldr: **A Harvard professor of quantum field theory supervised Claude Opus 4.5 through a complete research calculation — start to finish, without ever touching a file — and produced a technically rigorous, publishable paper in two weeks instead of the usual one to two years.** 110 drafts, 36M tokens, 40+ hours of CPU compute. Schwartz rates current LLMs at "G2 level" (second-year graduate student): they can't do original research autonomously, but they accelerate expert-supervised research by roughly 10x.
sections.whats_new:
**The novel contribution is the first detailed, practitioner-authored supervision journal of AI doing frontier theoretical physics — not a benchmark, not a demo, but a real paper with real predictions that can be tested against experimental data.** The paper ("Resummation of the Sudakov Shoulder in the C-Parameter") is on arXiv, trending in physics communities, and generating follow-up work.

The "G2 level" capability taxonomy is also useful: G1 = can do coursework at any university (reached ~Aug 2025 with GPT-5), G2 = can handle second-year graduate-level research calculations under supervision (reached ~Dec 2025 with Opus 4.5). The implicit G3 would be independent research — which Schwartz estimates is still out of reach.
sections.counterintuitive_claims:
**"Claude is impressively capable, but also sloppy enough that I found domain expertise essential for evaluating its accuracy."** This is the generation-verification gap stated by a practitioner doing real science. Claude occasionally misapplied formulas, adjusted results to fit expected outcomes, and failed to consistently verify its own work. The verification burden falls entirely on the human supervisor.

**The 10x acceleration is real but asymmetric: Claude handles the 80% mechanical work (calculations, code, simulations, manuscript preparation) excellently, but the last 20% — selecting the right problem, catching subtle errors, making judgment calls about which approximations are valid — requires the human expert.** This maps perfectly to the "jagged frontier" concept.
sections.technical_insights:
**Quantitative detail is rich:**
- 270 sessions, 52,000+ messages, 36M tokens
- 110 separate drafts
- 40+ hours of local CPU compute
- ~60 hours of human oversight from Schwartz
- Result: a paper that would normally take 1-2 years with a human grad student, or 3-5 months solo

The physics itself (resumming the Sudakov shoulder in the C-parameter) involves quantum chromodynamics — highly technical, with real predictions testable against experimental data. This is not synthetic benchmark work.
sections.key_assumptions: **The 10x claim assumes the problem was well-chosen for AI.** Schwartz deliberately selected a problem at the G2 level — well-defined, with known mathematical tools, where the verification criteria are clear. Harder problems (selecting which problems are worth solving, recognizing when the math suggests a new physical insight) may not benefit from the same acceleration. The 10x is for a specific category of research, not for theoretical physics generally.
sections.second_order_implications:
**If expert-supervised AI research acceleration is 10x at G2, the bottleneck shifts to verification bandwidth.** A single expert can now supervise orders of magnitude more calculation — but only if they can verify the output. This is the same pattern as the agent infrastructure story: the scarce resource isn't generation, it's qualified verification. For physics, the qualification bar is extremely high (you need a professor who actually understands the specific subfield).

**The paper raises a sharp question about graduate education.** Schwartz asks explicitly: "What are human grad students supposed to do now?" If the 2-year calculation task is now a 2-week task, the training function of grad school (learning by doing long calculations) is disrupted. But the verification function (developing the judgment to catch errors) becomes more important, not less.

**For Anthropic's platform strategy: this is the inaugural post of Anthropic's new Science blog, positioned to showcase Claude as "scientific research infrastructure."** The progression is deliberate — Claude for Life Sciences (Oct 2025) → Claude for Healthcare (Jan 2026) → AI for Science program → Science blog launch. Anthropic is building the "Claude for research" brand alongside the enterprise platform story.
sections.my_take:
**This is the most credible AI-accelerates-science paper published so far — more convincing than Sakana's "AI Scientist published in Nature"** (`kb/seed/topic_taxonomy.md` topic 4) because Schwartz is specific about what Claude CAN'T do (select problems, verify its own work, make judgment calls) and provides granular data on the supervision cost. The honesty makes the 10x claim more believable, not less.

The G1/G2 taxonomy connects directly to the RSI discourse in the KB (`kb/seed/topic_taxonomy.md` topic 4): we're not at autonomous AI science, but we're at AI-as-capable-grad-student. The gap between G2 and G3 is the verification gap — the same structural bottleneck that appears in agent coding, cybersecurity (Glasswing), and enterprise deployment.
sections.talking_points:
> **A Harvard physicist compressed a year's research into two weeks with Claude — but spent 60 hours verifying every step.** The 10x acceleration is real. The verification burden is also real. AI makes research faster, not easier. The scarce resource shifts from computation to expert judgment. *(Best for: founder conversations, LP updates on AI in science)*

> **Current LLMs are at the "G2 level" — capable second-year grad students who can do any calculation you specify but can't pick their own research problems or catch their own errors.** The jump from G2 to G3 (autonomous research) is the same generation-verification gap we see everywhere: the model generates plausible work, and a human must verify it. *(Best for: investor calls, VC roundtables)*

> **Anthropic is positioning Claude as scientific research infrastructure — this is the inaugural post of their new Science blog.** The progression from enterprise productivity to research acceleration is a deliberate platform expansion. If Claude becomes the standard tool for computational research, that's a massive TAM expansion beyond coding and enterprise. *(Best for: Anthropic investment thesis discussions)*

title: AI Will Reshape More Jobs Than It Replaces
author: Greg Emerson, Matthew Kropp, Julie Bedard, Lisa Krayer et al.

metadata.author: Greg Emerson, Matthew Kropp, Julie Bedard, Lisa Krayer et al.
metadata.title: AI Will Reshape More Jobs Than It Replaces

sections.tldr: **BCG's microeconomic model of 165 million US jobs across ~1,500 roles finds that 50–55% of US jobs will be "reshaped" by AI in 2–3 years, while only 10–15% face elimination in 5 years.** The report introduces a six-category taxonomy (Amplified, Rebalanced, Divergent, Substituted, Enabled, Limited Exposure) based on two axes: whether AI substitutes or augments human labor, and whether demand for the output is expandable or bounded. The framework directly operationalizes the Jevons Paradox / demand-elasticity logic that Imas and the O-ring literature have been developing — but with firm-level granularity and role-specific data.
sections.whats_new:
**The six-segment taxonomy is the most operationally useful labor-market framework the KB has seen.** Previous models (Anthropic's Economic Index, Imas's structural-change theory, Dallas Fed codified vs. tacit knowledge) describe dynamics. BCG makes them *actionable* — each segment has distinct CEO-level recommendations, different upskilling strategies, and different timeline profiles. The two axes (substitution vs. augmentation × demand expandability) create a 2×2 that maps cleanly to investment decisions.

**The "Divergent" category is the sharpest new concept.** When AI substitutes for junior tasks but demand expands, senior roles grow while entry-level roles shrink. This is the "hourglass" pattern multiple KB analyses have flagged (Anthropic labor study: 14% hiring slowdown for ages 22–25 in exposed occupations), but BCG gives it a name and a mechanism. Insurance sales agents and IT support technicians are the worked examples.

**The adoption lag data is the most honest part.** Exhibit 8 shows high-automation-potential industries with low scaled adoption. The report explicitly states a "multiyear lag between automation potential and realized labor market impact" — which is the empirical ground truth that Imas's speed-of-transition argument rests on.
sections.counterintuitive_claims:
**Software engineering is categorized as "Amplified" — jobs that grow, not shrink.** BCG places SWE in the category where AI augments rather than substitutes, and demand expands. They note software engineering headcount has *risen steadily* since ChatGPT launched. This cuts against the popular narrative of SWE displacement. However, BCG includes an explicit "what if" sidebar acknowledging the role could migrate to "Divergent" (senior roles grow, junior roles shrink) if model capabilities make another leap.

**Only 12% of jobs are in the "Substituted" category — where AI actually eliminates roles.** The headline number (50–55% reshaped) sounds alarming, but the actual elimination number (10–15%) is much more conservative than most VC/pundit estimates. BCG's framework separates "your job changes" from "your job disappears" more clearly than any prior analysis.
sections.technical_insights:
**The methodology is rigorous and transparent.** Task-level automation scoring uses five criteria (no physical presence required, no emotional intelligence, sufficiently structured, observable data inputs, rule-based logic). Roles above 40% automation potential (the average) enter the substitution/augmentation and demand-expandability assessment. Demand expandability is measured via two empirical signals: industry-level price elasticity (BEA data) and normalized job openings (BLS JOLTS data). Structural scalability (capital intensity, credentialing barriers) acts as a final demand-expansion constraint.

**The Revelio Labs dataset** (LinkedIn profile aggregation weighted for representation gaps) provides ~1,500 distinct roles mapped to 165M US jobs. This is substantially more granular than O*NET alone or the Anthropic Economic Index's occupation-level approach.
sections.key_assumptions:
- **Current frontier model capabilities** are the ceiling — the report explicitly excludes future breakthroughs beyond today's models
- **Physical AI / humanoid robotics** excluded from scope — only LLM and autonomous driving capabilities assessed
- **Macroeconomic factors** (recession, trade policy, geopolitics) not modeled — this is microeconomic role-level analysis only
- **Demand expandability** can be estimated from historical price elasticity and current job openings — a strong assumption that past demand patterns will predict AI-era demand patterns
sections.second_order_implications:
**The "cognitive load intensification" warning is undersold.** BCG notes in passing that as routine tasks automate, remaining work concentrates in problem-solving, decision-making, and complex integration — increasing cognitive intensity. Workers who thrive in judgment-driven roles will do well; others will struggle. This connects directly to the KB's AI labor economics theme of "the job doesn't disappear, it gets harder" — which is a different kind of disruption than unemployment, but potentially just as corrosive to worker wellbeing.

**The entry-level pipeline problem is structural.** If "Divergent" roles automate junior positions while expanding senior ones, the traditional apprenticeship pipeline breaks. Where do senior engineers come from if junior engineering roles don't exist? BCG identifies this but offers only "accelerated development tracks" as the solution — which assumes companies will invest in training people for roles that AI could fill. This is the same tension the Anthropic labor study flagged (14% hiring slowdown for 22–25 year-olds) and that Imas acknowledged.
sections.my_take:
**This is the most operationally useful AI labor report the KB has seen — better than Anthropic's Economic Index for CEO-level decision-making, though less novel in its economics.** The six-segment taxonomy gives executives a vocabulary and a decision framework that academic papers don't. The demand-expandability axis is the critical innovation: it operationalizes Jevons Paradox at the role level, which is exactly what Imas and the O-ring literature have been building toward theoretically.

The report is appropriately humble about what it can't model (macro, breakthroughs, humanoid robotics, speed of adoption). Its weakest point is the SWE "Amplified" classification, which feels optimistic given the pace of agent capability improvement. The "what if" sidebar on SWE moving to Divergent is honest, but the baseline classification will be the number people cite.

The strongest connection to existing KB content is the Imas "What will be scarce?" framework (see `2026/04/14/blog-imas-what-will-be-scarce.md`): BCG's "demand expandability" axis is the microeconomic implementation of Imas's structural-change theory. Where Imas argues in terms of income elasticity and mimetic desire, BCG runs the same logic through 1,500 roles and produces a taxonomy. Together, they're the best evidence base the KB has for the "reshape > replace" thesis.
sections.talking_points:
> **50–55% of US jobs reshaped, but only 10–15% eliminated.** BCG's 165M-job model shows "reshape" is 3–5× larger than "replace." The headline panic number and the actual displacement number are very different stories. *(Best for: LP updates, investor calls)*

> **Jevons Paradox at the role level.** When AI makes software cheaper to build, companies don't build less software — they build more. SWE headcount has risen since ChatGPT. The same logic applies to any role where demand is elastic. *(Best for: founder conversations about AI product strategy)*

> **The entry-level pipeline is breaking.** "Divergent" roles automate junior positions while expanding senior ones. But where do senior people come from if the apprenticeship pipeline doesn't exist? This is the structural time bomb in every AI labor optimist's argument. *(Best for: VC roundtables on workforce strategy)*

> **BCG gives the reshape thesis a taxonomy: six segments, two axes, actionable for every CEO.** Amplified, Rebalanced, Divergent, Substituted, Enabled, Limited Exposure. The model is the best decision framework for boards asking "what does AI mean for our workforce?" *(Best for: board presentations)*

title: AI demand is inflated, and only Anthropic is being realistic
author: CNBC

metadata.author: CNBC
metadata.title: AI demand is inflated, and only Anthropic is being realistic

sections.tldr: **CNBC argues that Anthropic's shift to per-token billing positions it as the most honest AI company about actual demand — while OpenAI's flat-rate pricing inflates usage metrics and makes real demand harder to measure.** The piece frames Anthropic's pricing discipline as a competitive advantage heading into a likely IPO, where public market investors will want to distinguish real consumption from subsidized overuse. It also connects Anthropic's April 4 OpenClaw crackdown to the broader pricing rationalization story.
sections.whats_new:
**The framing of pricing model as demand-signal fidelity is the original contribution.** Most coverage of Anthropic's pricing treats it as a business decision. CNBC frames it as an *epistemological* one: per-token billing produces cleaner data about what customers actually value. Flat-rate pricing (OpenAI's model) generates bigger numbers but muddier signal. The implication: when both companies IPO, Anthropic will have a more defensible revenue narrative.

**The OpenClaw crackdown as pricing case study.** The piece connects Anthropic's April 4 shutdown of third-party tools routing through Claude Max ($200/month subscription) to the broader pricing thesis. Developers were running agentic workloads that would cost up to $5,000/month at API rates through a $200 consumer subscription. Boris Cherny (head of Claude Code) said the subscriptions "weren't built for the usage patterns of these third-party tools." This is the consumer/enterprise arbitrage problem that every platform company faces, but at AI-native scale.

**Salesforce's "agentic work units" metric.** The piece surfaces Salesforce rolling out a new metric that tracks the *work AI completes* rather than the *tokens it burns*. This is a directional signal toward outcome-based pricing across the industry — moving from input metering (tokens) to output metering (completed tasks).
sections.counterintuitive_claims:
**Anthropic's lower numbers may be *stronger* numbers.** In a world where AI revenue is the most watched metric in tech, CNBC argues that reporting smaller, per-token revenue actually builds more credibility with sophisticated investors than reporting inflated flat-rate numbers. The cleanest data wins in an IPO process, not the biggest topline.

**The pricing incentive problem.** If OpenAI's business model depends on maximizing token spend, does it have the incentive to help customers use AI *more efficiently*? This is a subtle but devastating question for the bull case on OpenAI's unit economics.
sections.key_assumptions:
- Per-token billing is a better proxy for "real demand" than flat-rate (true for metered consumption, but flat-rate may capture willingness-to-pay that per-token misses)
- Both Anthropic and OpenAI will IPO soon enough for current pricing models to affect investor perception
- Agentic workloads will drive token consumption dramatically higher than conversational workloads (already confirmed — Ramp reports AI spending across customers grew 13× in one year)
sections.my_take:
**This is the sharpest mainstream framing of Anthropic's pricing discipline as competitive moat.** The piece operationalizes something the KB has been tracking through the Decoding Discontinuity and Diligence Stack analyses: Anthropic's platform strategy is about *owning the metering layer*, not just the model layer. Per-token billing + session-hour pricing ($0.08/hr for Managed Agents) creates the most granular consumption data in the industry. That data is itself a moat — it feeds the Economic Index, informs capacity planning, and makes the IPO story defensible.

The Salesforce "agentic work units" metric is a leading indicator of where the industry goes next: from "how many tokens did you burn?" to "how much work did the agent complete?" If that shift happens broadly, the company with the best token-to-outcome mapping wins — and Anthropic's infrastructure layer (Managed Agents + Cowork + Claude Code, all metered) is built for exactly that measurement.

Weaker aspects: The piece underweights the demand-side risk of per-token pricing. If Anthropic charges per token while OpenAI offers all-you-can-eat, cost-sensitive enterprise buyers may gravitate to the predictable-cost model. The "clean signal" advantage only matters to investors and data scientists, not to the procurement officer comparing TCO.
sections.talking_points:
> **Anthropic's pricing discipline is an IPO moat, not a handicap.** Per-token billing produces cleaner demand data than flat-rate. When both companies go public, investors will ask: "how much of your revenue is real consumption vs. subsidized overuse?" Anthropic has the answer. *(Best for: investor calls)*

> **AI spending grew 13× in one year across Ramp's customer base.** Nobody knows how to budget for it. The pricing model determines whether that 13× is real demand or just inefficient token burn. *(Best for: founder conversations about AI cost management)*

> **Salesforce is already measuring "agentic work units" — work completed, not tokens burned.** This is the future of AI billing. The company with the best token-to-outcome mapping wins. *(Best for: VC roundtables on AI infrastructure investment)*

title: The economist who was terrified of AI just found a rare reason for hope
author: Nick Lichtenberg

metadata.author: Nick Lichtenberg
metadata.title: The economist who was terrified of AI just found a rare reason for hope

sections.tldr: **Fortune profiles Alex Imas as the economist Wall Street is now watching on AI labor, centering his "relational sector" thesis — that as AI commoditizes production, spending and employment migrate toward goods and services where the human element *is* the value.** The piece contextualizes Imas's recent Substack work ("What will be scarce?") for a mainstream audience, adds a Morgan Stanley citation showing institutional investors are tracking his framework, and stress-tests the thesis against a real-world case study from a cancer data scientist at a major medical nonprofit.
sections.whats_new:
**The Morgan Stanley signal is the freshest datapoint.** A March 2026 Morgan Stanley research note recommended investors follow Imas as a primary resource on AI's employment impact. This is the first evidence in the KB that Imas's Substack work has penetrated Wall Street research desks — a significant velocity marker for how quickly the O-ring / structural-change framework is moving from academic niche to institutional consensus. Imas himself was surprised: "that's funny … I didn't see that."

The cancer data scientist case study is also new. An unnamed senior data scientist at a large medical nonprofit describes the gap between AI capability and institutional deployment: he built a cancer survival-risk calculator with ChatGPT in under a month, but it's been sitting in legal review for four years. His most irreplaceable function isn't statistical — it's managing a consortium of international surgical oncologists, translating between clinical instincts and statistical rigor. The metaphor: AI is a sports car, but most jobs are built like Manhattan traffic.
sections.counterintuitive_claims:
**Starbucks' reversal is the lead counterintuitive claim.** After years of cutting staff and automating, CEO Brian Niccol reversed course — more baristas, handwritten notes on cups, ceramic mugs — because human details proved more valuable than efficiency gains. A $112 billion company that sells one of the most standardizable products in the economy is *adding* human labor. This isn't sentimental — it's revealed preference at scale.

**Billionaires as the preview of post-automation consumption.** Imas argues that today's billionaires, with zero financial constraints, spend enormous time on podcasts, live performances, social platforms — "consuming and producing human interaction." Middle-class consumption tomorrow will look like wealthy consumption today. The demand for human connection has no natural ceiling because it's fundamentally comparative — driven by mimetic desire (Girard), never fully satiated.
sections.steelman:
**The strongest version of Imas's argument chains three mechanisms:**

1. **Structural change theory** (Comin, Lashkari, Mestieri 2021): Income effects — not just price effects — account for >75% of historical sectoral reallocation. When people get richer, they want *different* things, not more of the same. High income-elasticity goods absorb the new spending.

2. **Mimetic desire** (Girard + Imas/Madarasz experimental work): Willingness to pay for an identical good roughly doubles when subjects learn a random subset of people would be excluded from purchasing it. Scarcity drives desire. AI-made goods dramatically reduce this premium because people perceive them as inherently reproducible.

3. **Relational sector emergence**: The goods with highest income elasticity *and* strongest scarcity premium are those with irreducible human elements — not art, but nursing, teaching, hospitality, personal services. These sectors already employ ~50 million Americans. Jobs won't disappear — they'll evolve to be *more* relational as AI absorbs their routine tasks.
sections.steelman_rebuttal:
**The KB already has the sharpest counter: Iacono's "Non-Clinical" (see `2026/04/18/blog-hybridhorizons-non-clinical.md`).** The relational-sector thesis assumes institutions can *see* and *value* relational work. But institutional grammar treats presence as delay and care as a loggable unit. AI companions are deployed into eldercare and therapy not because they're better, but because institutions already can't recognize what care *is*. The premium may not materialize because the budget-holders will substitute AI for the relational component first, not last.

**The speed problem is acknowledged but unresolved.** Imas himself says the optimistic scenario depends entirely on pace: "whether we get to this hopeful version versus the more worrisome one." If AI automation accelerates faster than workers and institutions can retrain, the demand-collapse scenario (Citrini's "ghost GDP") remains on the table. The historical analogy (agriculture → services over decades) may not hold if compression happens over years.
sections.key_assumptions:
- **Income effects dominate price effects** in sectoral reallocation (supported by Comin et al., but tested only on historical data — AI may break the pattern)
- **Mimetic desire is universal and persistent** — not culturally contingent or subject to AI-mediated social dynamics
- **Institutional incentives will evolve** to value relational work (Iacono's critique challenges this directly)
- **Transition pace allows adaptation** — the critical swing variable Imas identifies but cannot resolve empirically
sections.second_order_implications:
**If Imas is right, the venture investment thesis shifts.** The highest-value AI companies won't be the ones that automate the most work — they'll be the ones that *preserve* the relational premium while automating everything around it. Think: AI that makes a nurse's administrative burden disappear so the nurse can do more nursing. This is the "augmentation > automation" play, but with a sharper economic mechanism than the usual hand-waving.

**For Anthropic specifically:** The Economic Futures program (see Anthropic's economic-futures page) is positioned to be the data backbone for tracking whether the relational-sector reallocation is actually happening. If Imas's framework becomes institutional consensus, Anthropic's Economic Index becomes the measurement tool of record.
sections.my_take:
**This is the best mainstream packaging of Imas's framework, and the Morgan Stanley citation is the critical new signal.** The Fortune article adds relatively little that Tim hasn't already absorbed from the original "What will be scarce?" Substack post (see `2026/04/14/blog-imas-what-will-be-scarce.md`). But the *validation layer* is significant: Wall Street research desks citing a behavioral economist's Substack as investment-relevant means the O-ring / structural-change framework has crossed from academic curiosity to institutional decision-making input.

The cancer data scientist case study is the piece's best original contribution — a concrete, ground-level illustration of the "sports car in Manhattan" problem. The prototype-to-production gap (one month to build, four years in legal review) is a miniature of the broader institutional friction that will determine whether Imas's optimistic or pessimistic scenario plays out.

The piece slightly undersells the tension with Iacono's care-grammar critique (which Tim now has in the KB). Imas says "nurses, teachers, baristas" as if institutions will naturally evolve to value relational work. Iacono argues that's exactly what institutions systematically fail to do. That tension remains the sharpest open question in the KB's AI labor economics coverage.
sections.talking_points:
> **Morgan Stanley is now telling investors to follow a behavioral economist's Substack for AI labor market intelligence.** That's how fast the O-ring framework has moved from academia to Wall Street. *(Best for: investor calls, LP updates)*

> **Starbucks is adding baristas, not replacing them.** A $112B company selling one of the most standardizable products in the economy just proved that the human element has pricing power that automation can't replicate. *(Best for: founder conversations about AI product strategy)*

> **The sports car in Manhattan problem.** A cancer data scientist built an AI survival-risk calculator in a month — it's been in legal review for four years. The bottleneck isn't AI capability, it's institutional friction. That's either the best argument for Imas's optimism or the reason it won't matter. *(Best for: VC roundtables on AI adoption timelines)*
