> **Wharton found humans accept wrong AI answers 80% of the time — and their confidence goes UP.** "Cognitive surrender" isn't a metaphor. It's measured in a lab. The humans in the loop are becoming less competent at the exact rate the systems need more oversight. *(Best for: VC roundtables)*

> **Anthropic's own research shows AI degrades learning by 17%, roughly two letter grades.** The productivity gain? Two minutes faster per task — not statistically significant. The tool that makes you faster today is degrading the skill you'll need to catch its mistakes tomorrow. *(Best for: founder conversations)*

> **The deskilling spiral: AI handles entry-level work → fewer humans build skills → remaining humans over-trust AI → errors go undetected → the humans who would have caught those errors were never trained → repeat.** This is the strongest bear case against naive AI-driven GDP projections. *(Best for: LP updates)*

> **Cory Doctorow's "reverse centaur" — a machine head on a human body.** The remaining radiologist's real function isn't oversight. It's liability absorption. That's where AI labor economics actually ends up. *(Best for: X)*

title: Anthropic Shipped Outcomes and Real Story Is Verification Becoming a SKU
author: Han Heloir Yan, Ph.D.

metadata.author: Han Heloir Yan, Ph.D.
metadata.title: Anthropic Shipped Outcomes and Real Story Is Verification Becoming a SKU

sections.tldr: **Anthropic's Outcomes API, announced at Code w/ Claude on May 6, is the first harness layer Anthropic has decided to sell — productizing the rubric→grader→retry verification loop that every production AI team has been building by hand.** Dreams (memory), Multi-Agent (orchestration), and Webhooks (lifecycle) are the same pattern: the harness is moving from custom code to a stack of composable products you buy from the model provider.
sections.whats_new:
**The novel framing isn't that Outcomes exists — it's that Anthropic is positioning verification as a purchasable SKU, not just a capability.** Every team deploying Claude agents has written this loop: define a rubric, run a grader, build retry logic, patch when things break, rewrite when the rubric drifts. Outcomes takes that exact loop and ships it as an API endpoint. The article argues this is the first time a frontier lab has explicitly sold the harness layer rather than just the model layer.

The strategic implication is that Anthropic is systematically eating the build-your-own harness ecosystem. Dreams productizes memory. Multi-Agent productizes orchestration. Webhooks productize lifecycle management. Each was previously custom code or third-party tooling. Now each is a first-party product from the model provider.
sections.counterintuitive_claims:
**Verification was always the hard part, but nobody was pricing it that way.** The entire harness engineering discourse (see [Martin Fowler's taxonomy](../../2026/04/28/blog-martinfowler-harness-engineering.md), [Latent Space's "Extreme Harness Engineering"](../../analyses/2026/04/11/blog-latentspace-extreme-harness-engineering.md)) treats the harness as something YOU build around the model. This article argues Anthropic is flipping that — the model provider absorbs the harness, and verification becomes a line item on your Anthropic invoice rather than an engineering investment on your side.

This creates a lock-in dynamic the "Agent = Model + Harness" community didn't anticipate: if your harness IS the model provider's product, switching models means rebuilding your entire verification/orchestration stack, not just swapping an API key.
sections.steelman: **The strongest version of this argument is that Anthropic is following the classic platform playbook — absorb the complementary layer to increase the value of your core product.** Just as AWS absorbed load balancing, DNS, and monitoring into its platform, Anthropic is absorbing rubric evaluation, memory management, multi-agent orchestration, and lifecycle hooks. The verification loop is the highest-value complementary layer for an LLM because it's what makes the model's output trustworthy in production. By owning it, Anthropic captures the full stack of value creation, not just the token generation.
sections.steelman_rebuttal:
**The counterargument is that first-party verification creates a fox-guarding-the-henhouse problem.** If the model provider also runs the verification layer, who verifies the verifier? Anthropic's simultaneous donation of Petri to Meridian Labs (see [Anthropic's Petri donation](https://www.anthropic.com/research/donating-open-source-petri)) suggests they're aware of this tension — outsourcing alignment evaluation while internalizing production verification. But the asymmetry is real: Petri evaluates model behavior in lab conditions; Outcomes verifies model output in YOUR production environment. The latter is where the money is.

The harness-as-product also risks the "golden handcuffs" problem Martin Fowler's team warned about: over-constraining agent behavior with provider-side controls reduces adaptability. If Anthropic's Outcomes rubric framework doesn't fit your domain's verification needs, you're stuck between their abstraction and your requirements.
sections.second_order_implications:
**If verification becomes a product category, it changes the economics of AI agent deployment in three ways:**

1. **The build-vs-buy decision shifts.** Teams currently investing in custom eval harnesses (the Bajwa/Barber "build your own eval" school — see `kb/2026/04/28/blog-bajwa-evals-openai-barber.md`) face a classic platform absorption moment. Their custom work may become obsolete, or may become the integration layer between Outcomes and domain-specific rubrics.

2. **The harness engineering job description changes.** If the model provider owns rubric execution, memory, and orchestration, "harness engineering" becomes less about building those systems and more about configuring and composing them. This shifts the skill profile from systems engineering to domain-specific rubric design — the "rubrics as rewards" thesis from the KB's verification topic.

3. **Competitive dynamics accelerate.** OpenAI is making the same move (Codex's harness is explicitly a product, not a DIY exercise). Google will follow. The window for independent harness tooling vendors (LangChain, CrewAI, HumanLayer) narrows as first-party solutions absorb their value.
sections.my_take:
**This is the single most important Anthropic platform strategy move since Managed Agents, and the KB has been building toward this thesis for weeks.** The verification-and-evaluation topic file tracks 218+ analyses all converging on the same insight: verification is the binding constraint. Now Anthropic is pricing it. The "rubrics as rewards" thesis — that domain expert rubrics are the scarce input for RL training — maps directly to Outcomes. Your production rubrics become Anthropic's training signal.

The article is paywalled on Medium so I couldn't verify all claims, but the core thesis aligns with everything we've tracked: Anthropic's Metalayer pricing ($0.08/session-hour from `blog-decodingdisc-digital-labor-tax.md`), the agent eval guide's emphasis on outcome-based grading, and the harness engineering discourse all point to verification-as-product as the natural convergence point.

**What I'd push Tim on:** the lock-in implications are real but under-discussed. If your verification stack IS Anthropic's product, you're not just buying tokens — you're buying the entire quality assurance layer. That's deeper platform dependency than API access alone.
sections.talking_points:
> **Verification just became a SKU.** Anthropic's Outcomes API ships your rubric→grader→retry loop as a product. The harness is no longer code you write — it's infrastructure you buy. *(Best for: founder chats)*

> **Anthropic is running the AWS playbook on AI.** Absorb the complementary layer (verification, memory, orchestration) to make the core product (the model) stickier. Dreams + Outcomes + Multi-Agent = the full harness stack as first-party products. *(Best for: investor calls)*

> **The harness engineering job is being redefined in real time.** Building eval harnesses becomes configuring provider products. The scarce skill shifts from systems engineering to domain-specific rubric design. *(Best for: VC roundtables on AI talent)*

> **Who verifies the verifier?** Anthropic donates Petri (alignment evaluation) to an independent nonprofit while simultaneously selling Outcomes (production verification) as a product. The asymmetry is strategically deliberate. *(Best for: governance discussions)*

title: A New Moore's Law for AI Agents
author: AI Digest / Sage Future

metadata.author: AI Digest / Sage Future
metadata.title: A New Moore's Law for AI Agents

sections.tldr: **METR's research reveals that the length of coding tasks AI agents can autonomously complete is doubling every 7 months — an exponential trend analogous to Moore's Law.** In 2022, ChatGPT could handle 30-second tasks. Today, agents manage tasks that take humans over 14 hours. Extrapolating: 1 work-day tasks by 2027, 1 work-week by 2028, 1 work-month by 2029. The trend has recently **accelerated** to doubling every 4 months. No plateau in sight. If agents improve fast enough to accelerate their own development, the trajectory becomes superexponential.
sections.whats_new:
**The R² = 0.83 correlation between task length and agent success rate is the empirical foundation that the AI agent hype has lacked.** This isn't a benchmark leaderboard or a cherry-picked demo — it's a systematic study across ~230 tasks, most coding-focused plus some general reasoning, tested against every frontier agent from 2019 to 2026. The high R² means task duration is a reliable predictor of what agents can and can't do today, and the exponential trend line makes the prediction of *when* they'll handle longer tasks uncomfortably precise.

**The acceleration in 2024-2025 is the real story.** The 7-month doubling time is the average across the full 2019-2026 period. In 2024-2025 specifically, the doubling time compressed to 4 months. If the acceleration sustains, the month-long task frontier arrives in 2027, not 2029. The piece is careful to note the single-year estimate is less robust — but the directionality of the acceleration is the signal.
sections.counterintuitive_claims:
**The superexponential possibility is not speculative — it follows from the data's own logic.** AI Digest frames this carefully: if agents improve enough to meaningfully accelerate AI R&D itself, then the time-horizon curve doesn't just grow exponentially — it accelerates. This is the recursive self-improvement thesis, but grounded in a measurable metric rather than theoretical possibility. The current trend already shows acceleration (7 months → 4 months). The superexponential case requires only that this acceleration continues rather than reverting to the historical mean.

**The gap between short and long tasks may shrink faster than expected.** AI Digest offers an intriguing framing: the skill gap between 1-week and 2-week tasks may be smaller than between 1-hour and 2-hour tasks. Early agent capabilities hit the steepest part of the learning curve first. If true, the extrapolation is conservative — agents may cross human-week thresholds faster than the exponential trend predicts.
sections.steelman:
**This is the single most important empirical finding in frontier AI capability research.** Moore's Law worked as a planning assumption for the semiconductor industry for 50 years because it was measurable, extrapolatable, and sustained. METR's agent time-horizon metric has the same properties: it's measurable (task duration × success rate), it extrapolates cleanly (R² = 0.83), and it's been sustained across 7 years and multiple architectural generations. If this trend holds for even 3 more years, every knowledge-work industry must plan for agents that autonomously handle week-long projects by 2028.

The link to Forethought's research on AI R&D automation adds the theoretical scaffolding: once agents can autonomously do 1-week coding tasks, they can meaningfully contribute to their own capability development. That's the flywheel that turns exponential into superexponential — and the data says we're 12-18 months from that threshold.
sections.steelman_rebuttal:
**Coding tasks are not representative of all knowledge work.** METR's dataset is ~230 tasks, mostly coding. Coding has unusually clean feedback signals (does the code run? do the tests pass?) that make it the ideal domain for autonomous agents. Tasks requiring judgment, negotiation, ambiguity resolution, or stakeholder management may have fundamentally different scaling properties. Extrapolating from coding time-horizons to "month-long autonomous work" conflates a domain-specific finding with a general capability claim.

**The 7-year trend line conceals multiple architectural transitions.** The agents tested from 2019 are not the same technology as the agents tested in 2026. Each architectural generation (GPT-2 era → GPT-4 → Claude 3 → o1 → Claude Opus 4.7) contributed differently to the trend. The smooth exponential is an artifact of multiple S-curves overlapping — and each individual S-curve may plateau. The fact that we're currently in the steep part of the latest S-curve (explaining the 4-month doubling) doesn't mean the underlying trend is truly exponential.
sections.forward_looking_hypotheses:
**Embedded bet: agent time-horizons become the primary AI capability metric for enterprise planning.** If METR's finding becomes widely adopted, it replaces benchmarks like MMLU and HumanEval as the planning tool for when AI agents can handle specific business processes. "Our accounts-payable workflow takes 4 hours — agents can do it in 2027" becomes the standard enterprise planning heuristic.

**Implicit prediction: the flywheel kicks in by 2027.** The piece explicitly links the Forethought research on AI R&D automation to the time-horizon data. The logical implication: once agents cross the 1-work-day threshold (predicted 2027), they become productive contributors to AI R&D, which accelerates the time-horizon curve, which makes them more productive at AI R&D. This is the mechanism behind the superexponential case.
sections.technical_insights:
**The R² = 0.83 is surprisingly high for a single-variable predictor.** Task duration alone explains 83% of the variance in agent success rates across 230 tasks and 7 years of models. This means the primary determinant of whether an agent can do a task is how long it takes a human, not what domain it's in, how much specialized knowledge it requires, or how creative the solution needs to be. Duration is a proxy for complexity, and the correlation suggests that agent capabilities scale smoothly along the complexity axis.

**The extrapolation timeline:**
- 2027: 8 hours (1 work day)
- 2028: 40 hours (1 work week)
- 2029: 167 hours (1 work month)
- Accelerated timeline (4-month doubling): month-long tasks by 2027
sections.key_assumptions:
1. **The exponential trend must survive the transition from narrow coding tasks to broader knowledge work.** If coding is uniquely amenable to agent automation (clean feedback, well-defined success criteria), the trend may flatten when agents attempt messier domains.

2. **No architectural plateau.** Each frontier model generation must continue to extend the time-horizon frontier. If scaling laws saturate or model architectures stagnate, the trend breaks.

3. **The R² must hold for tasks beyond the current 8-hour ceiling.** METR's dataset tops out at tasks that take humans "over 8 hours." Whether the correlation extends to day-long and week-long tasks is extrapolation, not measurement.
sections.second_order_implications:
**If the trend holds, the venture capital thesis for human-in-the-loop AI startups inverts by 2028.** Today, the standard pitch is "AI + human hybrid." If agents can autonomously handle week-long tasks by 2028, the viable pitch becomes "fully autonomous agent, with human oversight for edge cases." The hybrid model becomes an interim stage, not a steady state. This directly challenges the GTM strategy of every "copilot" startup in the current portfolio.

**The labor economics implications compound with today's GitLab analysis** (see `blog-tnw-gitlab-agentic-layoffs.md`). METR's trend provides the empirical backing for GitLab's organizational bet: if agent time-horizons are doubling every 4-7 months, then restructuring for agentic workflows today — even before the agents are ready — is rational because the capability gap closes faster than an enterprise can restructure. The companies that wait for agents to be "good enough" will restructure under duress rather than by choice.
sections.my_take:
**This is the most important chart in AI right now.** Not because it tells us something we didn't suspect, but because it quantifies it with enough rigor (R² = 0.83, 230 tasks, 7 years of data) to make it actionable for investment and planning. The 7-month doubling time is the base case; the 4-month acceleration is the upside case. Both are scary for any business whose competitive advantage depends on the complexity of tasks only humans can do.

For Tim: the superexponential scenario (agents improving agents, flywheel kicks in 2027) is the single most important upside risk for the frontier AI investment thesis. If the flywheel triggers, the capability curve goes vertical, and the investment window for "AI infrastructure" closes much faster than current models assume. The downside risk is that the coding domain doesn't generalize — but the R² says otherwise.
sections.talking_points:
> **Agent capabilities are doubling every 7 months — and recently accelerated to every 4 months.** This is METR's data across 230 tasks and 7 years, with R² = 0.83. Not a demo, not a benchmark — an empirical law. *(Best for: investor calls, LP updates)*

> **By 2028, agents handle week-long coding tasks autonomously. By 2029, month-long.** These are baseline extrapolations from the data — the acceleration case puts month-long tasks at 2027. Plan accordingly. *(Best for: founder conversations, portfolio planning)*

> **The flywheel threshold is 2027.** When agents can do 1-day tasks autonomously, they can meaningfully contribute to AI R&D itself. That turns exponential into superexponential. We're 12-18 months from that threshold. *(Best for: VC roundtables, macro positioning)*

> **Every "copilot" startup has an 18-month clock.** If the trend holds, the hybrid human+AI model becomes an interim stage by 2028. Fully autonomous is the steady state. Invest in the orchestration layer, not the copilot layer. *(Best for: deal evaluation, portfolio strategy)*

title: Focus areas for The Anthropic Institute
author: The Anthropic Institute

metadata.author: The Anthropic Institute
metadata.title: Focus areas for The Anthropic Institute

sections.tldr: **Anthropic's new research institute publishes a four-pillar agenda — economic diffusion, threats & resilience, AI systems in the wild, and AI-driven R&D — that reads as much as a governance confession as a research plan.** The most striking move: openly asking how to run a "fire drill" for an intelligence explosion, and admitting the company sees "early signs of AI contributing to speeding up the research and development of AI itself." This is a frontier lab publicly naming the RSI dynamic as a research priority, not a hypothetical.
sections.whats_new:
**The novelty isn't any single question — it's the institutional frame.** Anthropic is creating a research body (TAI) whose explicit job is to study the externalities of the company's own products, then publish those findings to help "external organizations, governments, and the public make better decisions about AI development." Three specifics stand out:

1. **The "fire drill" question on intelligence explosion** — "How do we run a 'fire drill' for an intelligence explosion? What would a tabletop exercise look like that actually tests the decision-making of lab leadership, boards, and governments?" This is the first time a major lab has framed RSI preparedness as analogous to nuclear crisis simulation.

2. **The Cold War hotline analogy** — "During the Cold War, the American president had a hotline directly to the Kremlin, for use in the event of a nuclear crisis. What geopolitical infrastructure would be needed in the event of a crisis scenario involving AI systems?" The analogy frames AI risk at state-to-state scale — deliberately.

3. **The professional pipeline problem** — "If AI absorbs the tasks that historically built expertise, how do people become experts in the first place?" This is the deskilling spiral identified in the KB's labor economics coverage, but now framed as a research priority by the company building the tools that cause it.
sections.counterintuitive_claims:
**A frontier AI lab is funding research into whether its own products should be deployed more slowly.** The agenda explicitly asks: "Can AI diffusion be modulated? Are there analogous dials that AI companies might turn to control the rate of AI diffusion on a sector-by-sector basis?" This is the equivalent of a pharmaceutical company funding research into whether its drugs should have smaller dosages. It could be strategic positioning — or genuine epistemic humility.

**They also ask whether AI makes firms bigger or smaller** — and hint they don't know. "If a 3-person team or company can now do what required 300 before, what happens to industrial organization?" is directly relevant to the SaaS disruption thesis the KB has been tracking.
sections.steelman: **This is the strongest possible version of "responsible scaling" as a governance strategy.** Rather than waiting for external regulators (who can't keep up), Anthropic is building the informational infrastructure that would make external governance *possible*: monthly economic data, telemetry for AI R&D speed, dual-use threat assessments, and a research fellowship pipeline to train people who can ask these questions independently. The LTBT connection means these findings can actually constrain Anthropic's decisions, not just inform press releases.
sections.steelman_rebuttal: **The structural conflict of interest is inescapable.** A company that profits from AI deployment is funding research into whether AI deployment should slow down. Even with the LTBT's structural independence, TAI's agenda is set by Anthropic staff. The most dangerous omission: the agenda says nothing about what happens if TAI's research recommends an action that would hurt Anthropic's competitive position. Would they actually slow down unilaterally? The Roon/Askell debate (see [kb/2026/05/06/blog-zvi-what-is-anthropic.md](../2026/05/06/blog-zvi-what-is-anthropic.md)) frames this precisely — Claude's constitutional right to refuse instructions is meaningless if the institution writing the constitution is also the one deciding when to override it.
sections.forward_looking_hypotheses:
**The fire-drill framing implies Anthropic believes RSI is close enough to warrant crisis simulation.** You don't run fire drills for fires you think are decades away. Combined with Jack Clark's public statements about "2028 as the most likely date for autonomous RSI," this places Anthropic's internal timeline at 2-3 years — not "someday."

**The "modulating diffusion" question implies sector-by-sector deployment throttling is on the table.** If AI companies coordinate with government on deployment rate dials, this would be the first technology in history with industry-level adoption speed controls. The historical analogy is pharmaceutical regulation — but drugs have a single-domain impact. AI is general-purpose.

**The agent governance questions signal that Anthropic expects autonomous agents in the wild within the LTBT's governance horizon.** Questions about "unique identity that agents reliably output," naval law for abandoned ships applied to abandoned agents, and AI governance of AI all assume a world where agents operate without human oversight. This is not hypothetical for Anthropic — it's a product roadmap question.
sections.key_assumptions:
**The agenda assumes transparency is a competitive advantage, not a handicap.** Publishing economic data, threat assessments, and R&D telemetry gives competitors (and regulators) information Anthropic currently monopolizes. This only works if the reputational benefit exceeds the competitive cost — or if Anthropic believes regulation is coming anyway and wants to be the one writing the rubric.

**It assumes the LTBT has real power.** The agenda says TAI's work will "increasingly serve as important inputs" to the LTBT. "Inputs" is a carefully chosen word — it doesn't say "constraints" or "binding recommendations." The governance architecture matters enormously here, and the agenda is silent on specifics.
sections.second_order_implications:
**If TAI publishes high-cadence economic data on AI labor displacement, it becomes the de facto scorecard for the entire industry.** No one else has this data (usage patterns, task-level automation rates, sector-by-sector penetration). This could make Anthropic the Bureau of Labor Statistics for AI — a position of enormous soft power.

**The fire-drill framing could catalyze a new industry norm.** If Anthropic publicly runs tabletop exercises for intelligence explosion scenarios, other labs face pressure to do the same. This is the "norm entrepreneurship" strategy the KB's governance coverage has been tracking (see [kb/2026/05/04/blog-hyperdimensional-aviate-navigate-communicate.md](../2026/05/04/blog-hyperdimensional-aviate-navigate-communicate.md)).

**The professional pipeline question has investment implications.** If the junior → senior expertise pipeline breaks (paralegals, junior analysts, associate developers), the value of existing senior expertise increases dramatically in the short term, even as the long-term supply of it collapses. This is a window of arbitrage that every knowledge-worker company should be pricing.
sections.my_take:
**This is the most important strategic document Anthropic has published since Core Views on AI Safety.** It's less a research agenda than a governance manifesto — Anthropic is staking out the position that frontier labs should be the primary producers of AI-impact research, not just the primary producers of AI. The fire-drill question on RSI is the headline: this is a company that believes it might be building something that could recursively self-improve within 2-3 years, and is asking — publicly — how to prepare for that.

The structural weakness is real: you can't be both the subject and the investigator of your own externalities. But the alternative — waiting for governments to build this capacity from scratch — is worse. TAI is a bet that transparency is a faster path to governance than regulation. For Tim's investment thesis, the key signal is that Anthropic is now publicly treating RSI, deployment-rate throttling, and agent autonomy as *current* research priorities, not future ones.
sections.talking_points:
> **Anthropic just published a fire-drill playbook for intelligence explosion.** They're asking how to run tabletop exercises for RSI — the same way the Pentagon does nuclear crisis sims. You don't build fire-drill infrastructure for a fire you think is far away. *(Best for: investor calls, VC roundtables)*

> **The Anthropic Institute is positioning itself as the Bureau of Labor Statistics for AI.** Monthly economic data, sector-level displacement signals, high-frequency telemetry. No one else has this data — whoever publishes it first becomes the scorecard. *(Best for: LP updates, macro conversations)*

> **Anthropic is openly asking whether AI diffusion should be throttled sector-by-sector.** Imagine pharma-style deployment controls for a general-purpose technology. They call them "dials." The fact that they're asking the question means they think the answer might be yes. *(Best for: founder conversations, policy discussions)*

> **The junior-expertise pipeline is about to break.** If AI absorbs the tasks that train paralegals, junior analysts, and associate developers, who becomes the senior expert in 10 years? Anthropic named this as a research priority. It's also an investment signal: senior talent gets more valuable short-term as the supply pipeline collapses. *(Best for: founder chats, portfolio reviews)*

> **Anthropic's governance strategy is: be the one writing the test.** If you can't stop regulation, shape the rubric. TAI publishes the data, sets the metrics, and feeds them to the LTBT. It's norm entrepreneurship dressed as research. *(Best for: VC roundtables, governance conversations)*

title: Scaling Managed Agents: Decoupling the Brain from the Hands
author: Lance Martin, Gabe Cemaj, Michael Cohen

metadata.author: Lance Martin, Gabe Cemaj, Michael Cohen
metadata.title: Scaling Managed Agents: Decoupling the Brain from the Hands

sections.tldr: **Anthropic's Managed Agents architecture virtualizes agents the way operating systems virtualized hardware: session, harness, and sandbox become decoupled interfaces that outlast any particular implementation.** The core insight is that harnesses encode assumptions about what Claude *can't* do — and those assumptions go stale as models improve. By separating the "brain" (Claude + harness) from the "hands" (sandboxes + tools), every component becomes cattle instead of pets: stateless, replaceable, independently scalable. This delivered a 60% p50 and 90%+ p95 drop in time-to-first-token.
sections.whats_new:
**The architectural thesis isn't "build better agents" — it's "build infrastructure that accommodates future agents you can't predict."** The blog explicitly frames Managed Agents as solving the operating systems problem: designing for "programs as yet unthought of." Three design decisions stand out:

1. **Session as durable context object outside the context window.** The session log is an append-only event stream that persists independently of Claude's context window. `getEvents()` lets the brain interrogate context by selecting positional slices — rewinding, fast-forwarding, or rereading arbitrary spans. This is the structural fix for context engineering: instead of making irreversible compaction decisions (which tokens to discard), you keep everything durable and let the harness decide what to surface at inference time.

2. **Credential isolation as a structural security guarantee.** In the old coupled architecture, prompt injection could reach credentials because code execution shared a container with auth tokens. The decoupled design moves credentials to an external vault, with an MCP proxy handling authenticated calls. Claude never sees the tokens — it calls tools through a proxy that fetches credentials from the vault per-session. This is a non-negotiable design choice for enterprise deployment.

3. **The "context anxiety" observation.** Sonnet 4.5 would wrap up tasks prematurely as it sensed its context limit approaching. The harness added context resets to compensate. When Opus 4.5 arrived, the behavior was gone — the resets became dead weight. This is a concrete example of the Bitter Lesson applied to agent harnesses: harness assumptions about model limitations become liabilities as models improve.
sections.technical_insights:
**The architecture has three virtualized interfaces:**

| Component | Interface | Role |
|-----------|-----------|------|
| **Session** | `getEvents()`, `emitEvent()` | Append-only event log; durable context outside context window |
| **Harness** | `wake(sessionId)`, `getSession(id)` | Stateless loop calling Claude + routing tool calls; crashes are recoverable |
| **Sandbox** | `execute(name, input) → string`, `provision({resources})` | Execution environment; cattle, not pets; can be container, phone, or Pokémon emulator |

**The `execute(name, input) → string` interface is deliberately minimal.** The harness doesn't know whether the sandbox is a container, a phone, or a custom tool — it sends a name and input, gets a string back. This is the same level of abstraction as `read()` in Unix: agnostic to the underlying implementation. The consequence is that brains can pass hands to one another, and a single brain can orchestrate many hands in parallel.

**The pets-to-cattle migration solved three problems simultaneously:**
- **Debugging opacity** — in the coupled design, harness bugs, packet drops, and container failures all looked the same. The only diagnostic window was the WebSocket event stream, which couldn't distinguish failure modes.
- **Network coupling** — customers wanting Claude to work against resources in their VPC had to peer their network with Anthropic's, because the harness assumed everything was co-located.
- **TTFT penalty** — every session paid the full container setup cost upfront (clone repo, boot process, fetch events) even if it would never touch the sandbox. Decoupling dropped p50 TTFT ~60% and p95 over 90%.
sections.steelman:
**This is the clearest articulation of "platform as meta-harness" in the agent infrastructure space.** Anthropic isn't just building one good harness (Claude Code) — they're building the abstraction layer that accommodates *any* harness, including future ones they can't predict. The operating system analogy is apt: just as Unix outlasted every specific hardware generation by virtualizing into process/file/device abstractions, Managed Agents aims to outlast every specific model generation by virtualizing into session/harness/sandbox.

The credential isolation design is genuinely best-in-class. Most agent frameworks treat security as an afterthought — Managed Agents makes it structural: the sandbox where untrusted code runs *never* has access to the tokens that authorize actions. This isn't defense-in-depth — it's defense-by-architecture.
sections.steelman_rebuttal:
**The abstraction might be too early.** Operating systems standardized abstractions after decades of hardware diversity taught the industry what the right interfaces were. Managed Agents is standardizing after 18 months of agent development. If the session/harness/sandbox decomposition turns out to be wrong — if, say, future models need the brain and hands tightly coupled for latency-critical real-time tasks — the abstraction becomes a constraint, not an enabler.

**The meta-harness is also a lock-in mechanism.** Once you build to `execute(name, input) → string` and `getEvents()`, your agent logic is portable across Anthropic's infrastructure — but not portable away from it. The comparison to Unix is flattering, but Unix was open. Managed Agents is a proprietary platform with proprietary interfaces. The more "future-proof" it is, the deeper the lock-in.
sections.second_order_implications:
**If the session log is the durable context object, it becomes the most valuable data asset in enterprise AI.** Every agent interaction, every tool call, every decision trace lives in the session. This is richer than any CRM log. The company that owns the session data owns the audit trail — and the fine-tuning data for next-generation agents.

**The "many brains, many hands" architecture implies agent teams, not agent singletons.** Once brains can pass hands to one another, the unit of work shifts from "one agent doing a task" to "a team of agents coordinating on a project." This is the architectural foundation for Anthropic's multi-agent research system (see [kb/2026/05/07/blog-anthropic-multi-agent-research-system.md](../2026/05/07/blog-anthropic-multi-agent-research-system.md)) — the orchestrator-worker pattern that achieved 90.2% improvement over single-agent Opus 4.

**Context anxiety disappearing in Opus 4.5 is a leading indicator for harness simplification.** Every model upgrade could make another harness feature obsolete. Teams building elaborate context-management scaffolding today should budget for ripping it out. The Bitter Lesson applies to harnesses, not just models.
sections.my_take:
**This is Anthropic's most architecturally ambitious engineering post — and it's not about models at all.** It's about infrastructure abstractions. The operating system analogy isn't marketing; it's a genuine design philosophy that treats today's harness patterns as temporary and builds interfaces meant to survive model generations. For Tim's investment thesis, the platform lock-in implication is the headline: once enterprise customers build to Managed Agents' session/harness/sandbox interfaces, migration cost becomes structural, not just switching-cost. This is Anthropic's moat within the moat.

The connection to the Anthropic Institute agenda (analysis 1/8 today) is direct: if RSI accelerates model improvement, harness assumptions go stale faster, and a meta-harness that accommodates future models becomes more valuable — not less. The two posts are the infrastructure play and the governance play for the same underlying dynamic.
sections.talking_points:
> **Anthropic just built Unix for AI agents.** They virtualized the agent into session, harness, and sandbox — the same way OS designers virtualized hardware into process, file, and device. The bet is that these abstractions outlast every model generation. *(Best for: founder chats, technical investor calls)*

> **Harness features are technical debt that models are paying off.** Sonnet 4.5 had "context anxiety" and needed harness workarounds. Opus 4.5 didn't. Every model upgrade could make your scaffolding obsolete. Build for the abstraction, not the model. *(Best for: portfolio company CTOs)*

> **The session log is the most valuable data asset in enterprise AI.** Every agent interaction, every tool call, every decision trace — durably stored outside the context window. Whoever owns the session data owns the audit trail and the fine-tuning corpus. *(Best for: LP updates, data infrastructure conversations)*

> **Managed Agents dropped time-to-first-token by 90% at p95.** Not through model optimization — through architecture. Decoupling the brain from the sandbox meant inference doesn't wait for container provisioning anymore. Infrastructure wins > model wins for latency. *(Best for: technical due diligence)*

> **Lock-in as a feature, not a bug.** Once enterprise builds to `execute(name, input) → string` and `getEvents()`, they're portable across Anthropic's stack but not away from it. This is the AWS playbook: open enough to adopt, deep enough to trap. *(Best for: VC roundtables, competitive analysis)*

title: AI is simultaneously aiding and replacing workers, wage data suggest
author: Scott Davis

metadata.author: Scott Davis
metadata.title: AI is simultaneously aiding and replacing workers, wage data suggest

sections.tldr: **AI is automating entry-level workers (codified knowledge) while *raising wages* for experienced workers (tacit knowledge) — and the data show this happening simultaneously in the same occupations.** The Dallas Fed finds that employment in the top 10% of AI-exposed sectors has fallen 1% since ChatGPT's launch, while wages in those same sectors have risen 8.5% (vs. 7.5% nationally). The key variable: the experience premium. Occupations where experience commands a high wage premium see *positive* wage effects from AI exposure, while occupations with low experience premiums see negative effects. AI is splitting the labor market along the codified/tacit knowledge boundary.
sections.whats_new:
**The codified-vs-tacit knowledge distinction is the most predictive framework for AI labor impact I've seen backed by Federal Reserve data.** Three empirical findings:

1. **Employment down, wages up — in the same sectors.** Computer systems design employment has fallen 5% since fall 2022, but nominal wages in the sector have risen 16.7% (vs. 7.5% nationally). The top 10% of AI-exposed industries show 1% employment decline but 8.5% wage growth. This is incompatible with simple automation (which would depress both) and simple augmentation (which would raise both). The data demand a framework where both forces operate simultaneously.

2. **The experience premium correlates positively with AI exposure.** Occupations most exposed to AI tend to have higher experience premiums — the percentage gap between entry-level and experienced worker wages. Fast-food cooks have <10% experience premiums; lawyers, credit analysts, and marketing specialists exceed 100%. The most AI-exposed occupations are also the ones where experience matters most.

3. **AI exposure's wage effect depends entirely on the experience premium.** At the median experience premium (40%), a one-standard-deviation increase in AI exposure has essentially zero wage effect. But for occupations with 0% experience premium, the effect is -0.28 percentage points. For occupations at the 90th percentile of experience premium, the effect is +0.2 percentage points. The sign of AI's wage effect *flips* depending on how much tacit knowledge the job requires.
sections.counterintuitive_claims:
**AI-exposed occupations are seeing *faster* wage growth than the national average.** The headline "AI is replacing workers" coexists with wage data showing the opposite of what simple displacement predicts. The resolution: AI is replacing some workers (entry-level) and making others (experienced) more productive. The net wage effect is positive because the experienced workers it complements earn more per capita than the entry-level workers it displaces.

**Young workers' problem isn't layoffs — it's not getting hired.** Dallas Fed economist Tyler Atkinson shows the employment decline for under-25s in AI-exposed sectors is driven by low job finding rates, not layoffs. Companies aren't firing juniors — they're not hiring new ones. This is a quieter, harder-to-detect form of displacement: the jobs just don't appear in the first place.
sections.technical_insights:
**The methodology is clean and reproducible.** Davis uses the Felten-Raj-Seamans AI exposure index (2021) to classify 205 occupations by AI exposure, BLS modeled wage estimates for entry-level vs. experienced wages to compute experience premiums, and a simple interaction regression:

    wage_growth = β₁(AI_exposure) + β₂(AI_exposure × experience_premium)

The result: β₁ is negative (AI exposure alone depresses wages), but β₂ is positive (the interaction with experience premium reverses the effect for high-tacit-knowledge occupations). The 90% confidence interval at the median experience premium includes zero — meaning for the average occupation, AI exposure has no detectable wage effect yet.

**The Autor task-bundle framework provides the micro-foundation.** The same innovation can automate the expert component of one job's task bundle while automating the routine component of another — freeing the experienced worker to focus on higher-value tacit work. This maps directly to the NBER chaining model (analysis 3/7 today): which tasks get automated depends on their position in the sequence, and experienced workers hold the tacit-knowledge tasks that AI can't chain through.
sections.second_order_implications:
**The apprenticeship pipeline is about to break — and the Dallas Fed knows it.** The paper's conclusion is explicit: "The current model of white-collar career progression involves taking an entry level job right out of school and doing codifiable tasks while slowly learning the tacit knowledge to become an experienced worker. Firms are going to find that AI is making this method of employee development cost-ineffective." This is the same deskilling-pipeline concern the Anthropic Institute flagged as a research priority (analysis 1/7 today).

**The experience premium becomes a moat for individual workers.** If AI complements tacit knowledge and substitutes for codified knowledge, then the value of experience increases — but only for workers who already have it. New entrants face a catch-22: they need experience to be valuable, but the entry-level jobs where they'd gain experience are being automated away. This creates a "last generation" risk for certain professions.

**Investment implication: platforms that help experienced workers leverage AI will compound value; platforms that target entry-level automation may cannibalize their own market.** The former creates long-term lock-in (experienced users become more productive, stay longer); the latter creates short-term revenue but destroys the pipeline of future users.
sections.my_take:
**This is the most data-grounded AI labor analysis I've seen from the Federal Reserve system.** The codified-vs-tacit knowledge framework isn't new (it echoes Polanyi, Nonaka, and decades of knowledge management literature), but the empirical validation against BLS wage data and the Felten-Raj-Seamans AI exposure index gives it teeth. The sign-flip in Chart 5 — where AI exposure goes from wage-depressing to wage-boosting depending on the experience premium — is the single most important chart in current AI labor economics.

The convergence with today's other analyses is striking. The Anthropic Institute flags the apprenticeship pipeline break. The NBER chaining model explains *why* sequential task structure determines automation outcomes. And the Dallas Fed shows it actually happening in wage data. Three independent sources, three different methodologies, all pointing at the same dynamic: AI is splitting the labor market along the experience/tacit-knowledge boundary.
sections.talking_points:
> **AI-exposed occupations have *higher* wage growth than the national average.** Computer systems design: +16.7%. National: +7.5%. The simple "AI replaces jobs and depresses wages" story is wrong. AI depresses employment AND raises wages — because it replaces cheap junior labor while making expensive senior labor more productive. *(Best for: investor calls, macro conversations)*

> **The sign of AI's wage effect flips depending on one variable: experience.** Zero-experience-premium jobs see negative wage effects from AI exposure. High-experience-premium jobs see positive effects. The codified-vs-tacit knowledge boundary is the fault line. *(Best for: LP updates, labor economics discussions)*

> **Young workers aren't being fired — they're not being hired.** The Dallas Fed shows employment decline in AI-exposed sectors is entirely driven by depressed job finding rates for under-25s, not layoffs. The jobs just don't appear. This is displacement without pink slips. *(Best for: founder conversations, policy discussions)*

> **The apprenticeship pipeline break is now acknowledged by a Federal Reserve bank.** The Dallas Fed explicitly says the current model of white-collar career progression — codifiable tasks first, tacit knowledge later — is becoming "cost-ineffective." Same conclusion as the Anthropic Institute. *(Best for: VC roundtables, governance conversations)*

title: Anthropic Takes Shot at Consulting Industry in Joint Venture with Wall Street Giants
author: Nick Lichtenberg

metadata.author: Nick Lichtenberg
metadata.title: Anthropic Takes Shot at Consulting Industry in Joint Venture with Wall Street Giants

sections.tldr: **Anthropic has partnered with Blackstone, Hellman & Friedman, and Goldman Sachs to launch a $1.5B standalone AI services company that puts Claude in direct competition with McKinsey, BCG, and Bain.** The entity embeds Anthropic engineers and models directly into mid-size business operations via the PE portfolio pipeline — a Palantir-style forward-deployment model backed by the most concentrated pool of corporate clients in the economy. OpenAI is pursuing a near-identical structure with TPG and Bain Capital.
sections.whats_new:
**The real insight is the distribution hack, not the AI.** For every dollar companies spend on software, they spend six on services. The consulting industry's multi-trillion-dollar revenue base has been protected by implementation complexity — you need humans who can translate between the model and the business. Anthropic is bypassing the consulting talent bottleneck by embedding its own engineers directly into client operations, and gaining distribution through the PE portfolio pipeline. Blackstone, H&F, Goldman, Apollo, General Atlantic, Leonard Green, GIC, and Sequoia collectively control hundreds of portfolio companies. That's a pre-qualified client list that would take a traditional consulting firm decades to build.

**Anthropic's CFO Krishna Rao said the quiet part out loud:** "Enterprise demand for Claude is significantly outpacing any single delivery model." The JV isn't a new product — it's a confession that API access and enterprise sales aren't sufficient to capture the value Claude creates. Anthropic needs to wrap the model in services to capture the full margin.
sections.counterintuitive_claims:
**The AI lab is becoming a consulting firm — not the other way around.** The standard narrative is that AI will commoditize consulting. The Anthropic JV suggests the opposite dynamic: the value capture requires consulting-style operations wrapped around the AI, not AI sprinkled into consulting. Anthropic is building a services business because the model alone, no matter how good, doesn't generate revenue commensurate with the value it creates when deployed inside complex enterprises.

**PE is the natural beachhead, not tech.** 85% of PE-backed CFOs now factor AI-enabled finance capabilities into company valuations. Firms that fail to integrate AI risk being penalized at exit. The JV converts sponsor pressure into guaranteed demand: PE firms invest in the JV, then deploy it across their portfolios to increase the AI readiness (and therefore exit multiples) of their holdings. The incentives are perfectly circular.
sections.steelman:
**This is the most capital-efficient enterprise AI distribution strategy anyone has devised.** Traditional enterprise sales is slow, expensive, and linear — you sell to one company at a time, each with its own procurement cycle, security review, and integration timeline. The PE portfolio pipeline changes the economics fundamentally: Blackstone alone has ~$330B in private equity AUM across hundreds of companies. A single relationship with the sponsor gives Anthropic's JV access to an entire portfolio. Goldman's Marc Nachmann frames this explicitly: the venture will "democratize access to forward-deployed engineers" for companies that can't afford Big Three consulting fees.

Sequoia partner Julien Bek's thesis provides the framing: the next great company won't sell software at all — it will sell outcomes, delivered by AI and billed like consulting. The Anthropic JV is literally that thesis capitalized and staffed.
sections.steelman_rebuttal:
**The Palantir comparison cuts both ways.** Palantir's forward-deployment model is famously high-touch, expensive, and hard to scale. If each JV deployment requires significant Anthropic engineering time, the JV faces the same bottleneck it claims to be solving — just with different engineers. The question is whether Claude is good enough that the human engineering component is truly a thin wrapper (in which case the model does scale) or whether each deployment requires deep customization (in which case this is just another consulting firm with a better model).

**The circular PE incentive structure creates moral hazard.** PE sponsors invest in the JV, then deploy it across their portfolios to boost exit multiples. But who evaluates whether the AI integration actually creates value, versus creating the appearance of AI readiness? If the JV becomes a box-checking exercise for PE exits ("we implemented Claude across the portfolio"), the quality bar may be low and the long-term reputation damage significant.
sections.forward_looking_hypotheses:
**Embedded bet: services revenue will eclipse software revenue for frontier AI labs.** If the 6:1 services-to-software spending ratio holds, and if AI labs can capture the services side via forward deployment, then the API/licensing business becomes the loss leader and the services business becomes the profit center. This would fundamentally change how AI labs are valued — from SaaS multiples to services multiples with a technology moat.

**Prediction: OpenAI's parallel structure with TPG/Bain Capital and Anthropic's JV will converge on a "forward deployment as a service" category.** Within 12 months there will be a name for this model. The competitive dynamic between Anthropic's JV and OpenAI's DeployCo (see `kb/2026/05/11/blog-tnw-anthropic-pe-pipeline.md`) will define the enterprise AI battleground of 2027.
sections.key_assumptions:
**For the thesis to hold:**

1. **Claude must be good enough to justify forward deployment** — not just autocomplete, but genuine business process transformation. If enterprise deployments produce marginal improvements, the PE pipeline becomes a liability (sponsors deploy the JV for optics, not outcomes).

2. **Anthropic must maintain model leadership** during the deployment cycle. A forward-deployed engagement that starts with Claude Opus 4.7 and ships results 6 months later needs the model to still be competitive. If GPT-5 or Gemini 3 leapfrog Claude mid-engagement, the JV's value proposition evaporates.

3. **The JV entity must maintain independence from Anthropic's core business.** If the JV becomes a captive channel (only deploying Claude, never recommending competitors), enterprise buyers will treat it like any other vendor professional services arm — useful but conflicted.
sections.second_order_implications:
**The consulting industry's response will determine whether this is a disruption or an incremental challenge.** McKinsey, BCG, and Bain have model-agnostic AI practices. If they can integrate Claude (and GPT-5, and Gemini) faster than Anthropic's JV can build consulting muscle, the Big Three survive by becoming the orchestration layer above the model. If they can't, the JV model — AI lab + PE distribution — becomes the template.

**This accelerates the "lab as platform company" narrative for Anthropic's IPO.** The JV demonstrates that Anthropic isn't just a model company — it has a services moat, an enterprise distribution channel, and a recurring revenue base that doesn't depend on API pricing. For a $900B IPO valuation, this is exactly the narrative that bridges the gap between current revenue ($30B ARR) and the implied future.
sections.my_take:
**This is the most important strategic move Anthropic has made since launching Claude Code.** Not because the JV itself is revolutionary — Palantir proved the forward-deployment model works — but because it shows Anthropic has realized that model quality alone doesn't win the enterprise. Distribution wins, and the PE portfolio pipeline is the single most capital-efficient distribution channel for enterprise AI ever constructed. Every other AI lab should be watching.

The question for Tim: does the JV de-risk or increase risk for the Anthropic IPO thesis? I'd argue de-risk — it demonstrates a services revenue stream that's more defensible than API pricing, and it anchors Claude in the highest-value enterprise use cases. But it also implies that Anthropic doesn't believe API-first can capture enough value, which is a bearish signal for the pure-software valuation multiple.
sections.talking_points:
> **Anthropic just built the most capital-efficient enterprise AI distribution channel ever.** One relationship with Blackstone gives them access to hundreds of portfolio companies. The PE pipeline bypasses years of enterprise sales cycles. *(Best for: LP updates, investor calls)*

> **For every $1 companies spend on software, they spend $6 on services — and Anthropic just entered the services business.** The JV is the clearest signal that AI lab revenue will come from outcomes, not APIs. This reframes how frontier AI labs should be valued. *(Best for: founder conversations, VC roundtables)*

> **85% of PE-backed CFOs factor AI into company valuations.** The JV turns sponsor pressure into guaranteed demand: invest in the JV, deploy it across your portfolio, boost exit multiples. The incentive alignment is unprecedented. *(Best for: LP updates, PE-focused conversations)*

> **The McKinsey question: can Big Three consulting survive model-native competition?** Anthropic's JV doesn't just compete on price — it competes on model access. The consulting firm owns the model, not just the methodology. *(Best for: VC roundtables, macro positioning)*

> **Watch OpenAI's parallel move with TPG and Bain Capital.** The convergence of both leading AI labs on identical PE-backed services structures is a category signal, not a company-specific one. "Forward deployment as a service" is the new enterprise AI battleground. *(Best for: deal evaluation, sector thesis)*

title: AI Is Starting to Build Better AI
author: Matthew Hutson

metadata.author: Matthew Hutson
metadata.title: AI Is Starting to Build Better AI

sections.tldr: **Recursive self-improvement is no longer a thought experiment — pieces of the loop are closing, but the full loop remains human-gated.** IEEE Spectrum surveys the current RSI landscape: OpenAI reports GPT-5.3-Codex was "instrumental in creating itself," Anthropic claims most of its code is Claude-written, Ricursive Intelligence ($335M from Sequoia/a16z/NVIDIA) is building the AI→chips→AI cycle, and Darwin Gödel Machines can modify their own meta-improvement mechanisms. But every system still relies on humans to set goals, define success, and decide which changes to keep. The question isn't whether RSI exists — it's how much of the loop is actually closed.
sections.whats_new:
**The article's value isn't any single system — it's the composite picture of how many independent RSI efforts are converging simultaneously.** Five distinct loops are partially closing:

1. **Code writing code.** OpenAI's GPT-5.3-Codex helped debug its own training, manage deployment, and analyze evaluation results. Anthropic says "the majority of its code is now written by Claude Code." David Scott Krueger's red line — 99% of code written by AI — is something he says "we're maybe crossing about now."

2. **AI designing AI chips.** Ricursive Intelligence (Azalia Mirhoseini and Anna Goldie, ex-Google AlphaChip) has a three-phase plan: Phase 1 helps human designers, Phase 2 automates for companies without in-house designers, Phase 3 "recursively uses AI to design better chips to train better AI." They expect to reduce chip design cycles "from one or two years to days."

3. **Agents modifying their own behavior.** Darwin Gödel Machines (UBC + Sakana AI) use evolutionary algorithms to improve LLM-based coding agents. Critically, agents can alter their own code (though not the underlying LLM). A newer version "can even alter its meta-mechanisms for improving itself."

4. **AI automating the research loop.** The AI Scientist (Sakana AI, published in Nature, March 2026) "can generate research ideas, run experiments in software, write up the results in papers, and then review those papers."

5. **Algorithm discovery.** Google DeepMind's AlphaEvolve uses LLMs to guide the evolution of solutions for neural-network architectures, chip design, and data-center scheduling. Matej Balog: "Our mission is to use AI to discover new algorithms that have evaded human intuition."
sections.counterintuitive_claims:
**The full loop may never look like one AI getting smarter — it might look like ecology.** Krueger suggests "something like a Cambrian explosion of artificial life forms" with "ecosystems, cultures, and economies." Clune agrees that "collaboration between agents" and open-ended evolutionary processes "which explore without a strong objective" will be more important than single-system intelligence gains. This reframes RSI from a scalar (one system getting better) to a network (many systems co-evolving).

**The "grunt, not the genius" framing is the strongest rebuttal in the piece.** Dean Ball argues that current RSI systems automate "the grunt who grinds through the algorithmic efficiency games," not the creative leaps. This is the codified-vs-tacit knowledge distinction the Dallas Fed paper also identifies (analysis 7/7 today) — and it's the key bottleneck that determines whether RSI compounds or plateaus.
sections.steelman: **RSI is already happening on at least three fronts simultaneously (code, chips, research), and each front makes the others more potent.** Code-writing AI makes chip-design AI faster to iterate. Better chips make AI training cheaper. Cheaper training enables more experiments, which close the research loop faster. The fact that these loops are semi-independent means progress on any one accelerates all three — and humans are increasingly in the supervisory role rather than the execution role. Clune: "We are right around the corner from recursively self-improving systems."
sections.steelman_rebuttal:
**Nathan Lambert's "lossy self-improvement" framing is the strongest counter.** Instead of compounding, each iteration adds friction: systems grow more complex, the management burden increases, and "no one wants to set an AI loose with billions of dollars." Ball adds that many RSI steps require physical-world execution — "building data centers, running power plants, and mining metals, all using self-reproducing robots" — which can't be automated with code alone. TSMC's capabilities "emerge from the collective intelligence of its 90,000 interacting employees" — tacit knowledge that can't be bundled into one AI mind.

The 23/25 expert survey (where all but two entertain intelligence explosion) is alarming — but "entertain" is a low bar. The same experts might entertain asteroid impacts without changing their daily behavior. The paper finding that experts expect self-improving models to stay internal rather than be deployed publicly is more actionable.
sections.forward_looking_hypotheses:
**The human role in AI research will follow a predictable career-ladder trajectory.** Clune's prediction is specific: researchers first become "professors or team leads" (picking directions), then "program officers or CEOs" (setting agendas), then "oversight" (a role he "hopes humans never forfeit"). This maps to the Anthropic Institute's agenda (analysis 1/8 today), which frames agent governance as a near-term research priority. Both sources converge on the same timeline: human execution → human supervision → human oversight.

**Krueger's 99% code threshold is a meaningful red line.** If the majority of AI code is now AI-written (both OpenAI and Anthropic claim this), the 99% threshold may arrive within 12-18 months. At that point, the debugging, training, and evaluation loops would be overwhelmingly AI-executed, with humans reduced to strategic direction and safety oversight.
sections.my_take:
**This is the best mainstream survey of the RSI landscape I've seen — balanced between the hype and the friction, with enough expert quotes to let readers triangulate.** The convergence between this piece and the Anthropic Institute agenda (analysis 1/8 today) is striking: both published May 7, both treat RSI as a current phenomenon rather than a hypothetical, both acknowledge the human-in-the-loop constraint as the key governance variable.

For Tim's thesis, the Ricursive Intelligence play is the most investable signal: a startup explicitly building the AI→chips→AI loop, with $335M from top-tier VCs, founded by the team that built AlphaChip. Phase 3 is the recursive loop itself. The Lambert "lossy self-improvement" counter is worth tracking as a bear case: if friction dominates compounding, the RSI thesis becomes an asymptote, not an exponential.
sections.talking_points:
> **RSI isn't one loop — it's three loops feeding each other.** Code-writing AI makes chip-design AI faster. Better chips make training cheaper. Cheaper training closes the research loop. Each front accelerates the others. *(Best for: investor calls, technical conversations)*

> **The AlphaChip co-founders raised $335M to build the AI→chips→AI cycle.** Ricursive Intelligence's Phase 3 is literally recursive self-improvement through hardware. Design cycles going from years to days would collapse the capex timeline for the entire industry. *(Best for: VC roundtables, semiconductor investors)*

> **23 of 25 AI experts entertain intelligence explosion as a possibility.** The same survey found they expect self-improving models to stay internal at labs rather than be deployed publicly. Alarming combination: high-risk research behind closed doors. *(Best for: governance conversations, LP discussions)*

> **"They're automating the grunt, not the genius."** Dean Ball's framing is the best one-line rebuttal to RSI hype. Current systems handle algorithmic efficiency games, not creative leaps. The question is how long that distinction holds. *(Best for: X, founder conversations)*

title: Chaining Tasks, Redefining Work: A Theory of AI Automation
author: Demirer, Horton, Immorlica, Lucier, Shahidi

metadata.author: Demirer, Horton, Immorlica, Lucier, Shahidi
metadata.title: Chaining Tasks, Redefining Work: A Theory of AI Automation

sections.tldr: **The sequential structure of production matters as much as individual task capability — and this breaks the standard comparative advantage logic for AI automation.** Demirer, Horton (Anthropic advisor), Immorlica, Lucier, and Shahidi model production as a sequence of steps that can be manual, AI-augmented, or fully automated in contiguous "chains." The key insight: AI steps that are adjacent can be chained together, and chaining creates non-linear productivity gains that isolated task automation doesn't capture. The model admits a CES representation at the macro level, bridging the gap between micro (firm-level task allocation) and macro (economy-wide labor demand) that has plagued AI labor economics.
sections.whats_new:
**This is the first formal model where AI automation depends on the *topology* of task sequences, not just task-level capability.** Three predictions, all empirically confirmed:

1. **AI-executed steps co-occur in chains.** Automation isn't scattered — it clusters in contiguous blocks. A firm doesn't automate steps 1, 3, and 7; it automates steps 1-2-3 as a unit. This is because breaking a chain with a human-executed step forces a handoff that destroys the productivity gain.

2. **Dispersion of AI-exposed steps lowers AI execution at the job level.** If the automatable steps in a job are scattered across the sequence (rather than adjacent), the job is *less* likely to be automated, even if each individual step is easy for AI. This is deeply counterintuitive: more AI-capable steps can mean *less* automation if they're in the wrong positions.

3. **Adjacency to AI-executed steps increases the likelihood that a step is AI-executed.** Once a step's neighbors are automated, it becomes much more valuable to automate that step too — even if it's marginal on its own. This creates a cascade dynamic: automation spreads outward from initial footholds.
sections.counterintuitive_claims:
**Comparative advantage logic can fail with AI chaining.** In standard trade theory, you automate the tasks where AI has comparative advantage, and humans do the rest. But chaining breaks this: it might be optimal to automate a step where AI is *worse* than humans, if that step sits between two AI-automated steps and removing it enables a longer chain. The chain value exceeds the per-step quality loss. This is the O-ring model in reverse — instead of "the weakest link determines quality," it's "the break in the chain determines whether automation works at all."

**The model also implies that AI quality improvements produce non-linear productivity gains.** A small improvement in AI capability can suddenly make a chain viable that wasn't before — flipping a step from human to AI extends the chain, which extends it further through the adjacency effect. This is a phase-transition dynamic, not a gradual substitution.
sections.technical_insights:
**The three-mode framework (manual, augmented, automated) maps cleanly to what firms actually do:**

| Mode | Description | AI Role |
|------|-------------|---------|
| Manual | Human executes step without AI | None |
| Augmented | Human executes step with AI assistance | Copilot |
| Automated | AI executes step within a contiguous chain | Autonomous |

**The CES representation at the macro level is the bridge the field has been missing.** Micro models of task allocation (Acemoglu & Restrepo, Autor) produce predictions about individual tasks, but translating those to aggregate labor demand requires aggregation assumptions. This paper shows that the chaining model admits a CES production function at the macro level, which means macro economists can use standard tools (elasticity of substitution, factor shares) to reason about AI's aggregate impact — but with the chaining dynamics baked in.

**Firms optimally bundle steps into tasks and tasks into jobs, trading off specialization gains against coordination costs.** This means AI doesn't just change *which* tasks are automated — it changes the *shape of jobs themselves*. A job might be restructured to move automatable steps into a contiguous block, even if that restructuring reduces specialization efficiency for the human steps.
sections.key_assumptions:
**The model assumes production is a sequential chain, not a graph.** Real production processes often have parallelism, feedback loops, and branching paths. If the topology is a DAG rather than a sequence, the adjacency effects become more complex and the clean CES aggregation may not hold.

**It assumes AI quality is uniform across step types.** In practice, AI is much better at some steps (data transformation, code generation) than others (judgment under ambiguity, stakeholder negotiation). The "jagged frontier" of capabilities means chains might be limited by specific step types, not just adjacency.
sections.second_order_implications:
**Job redesign becomes a strategic priority, not just a cost optimization.** If the topology of task sequences determines whether automation works, firms should be restructuring jobs to create longer contiguous automatable blocks — even at the cost of some specialization efficiency. This is already visible: companies are creating "AI-native" roles designed around chain topology rather than traditional functional specialization.

**The adjacency cascade implies automation accelerates once it starts.** Each step that gets automated makes its neighbors more attractive to automate. This predicts a pattern of long plateaus followed by rapid automation waves — not the smooth gradual substitution that most labor models predict. For investors, this means AI labor displacement may be lumpier and faster than current employment data suggests.

**The chaining model gives a micro-foundation for the O-ring theory.** Kremer's O-ring model (1993) argued that the weakest link determines output quality in sequential production. This paper provides the AI-era complement: the weakest *chain* determines automation viability. Both models share the insight that sequential structure creates non-linearities — but the implications point in opposite directions. O-ring says "invest in the weakest human"; chaining says "automate around the strongest AI."
sections.my_take:
**This is the most important AI labor economics paper of 2026 so far.** The chaining model finally gives a rigorous micro-foundation for what practitioners have been observing informally: automation clusters, it cascades, and it depends on workflow topology, not just task-level capability. The CES bridge to macro is the technical contribution that will make this paper influential — it lets macro economists use their standard tools without hand-waving about aggregation.

For Tim's investment thesis, the headline is the adjacency cascade: once a firm automates a block of steps, the economics of automating adjacent steps improve dramatically. This predicts fast-follower dynamics in enterprise AI adoption — and it explains why AI-native companies (which design workflows around chain topology from day one) have a structural advantage over incumbents (which are constrained by legacy job structures). Horton's position as an Anthropic advisor is also notable: this is the intellectual framework that likely informs Anthropic's own thinking about how their products reshape work.
sections.talking_points:
> **AI automation cascades — it doesn't substitute step-by-step.** The NBER chaining model shows that automating one step makes its neighbors dramatically more valuable to automate. This creates wave dynamics: long plateaus, then rapid rollouts. The smooth substitution curve in most labor models is wrong. *(Best for: investor calls, macro conversations)*

> **The topology of your workflow determines whether AI works, not just the capability of the AI.** Two firms with identical AI tools will get wildly different results based on how their tasks are sequenced. Jobs with scattered automatable steps get *less* automated than jobs with clustered ones — even if total AI capability is the same. *(Best for: founder conversations, portfolio company reviews)*

> **AI-native companies win because they design around chain topology.** Incumbents are constrained by legacy job structures — automatable steps scattered across functional silos. AI-native firms cluster automatable steps into contiguous chains from day one. The structural advantage is architectural, not technological. *(Best for: VC roundtables)*

> **This paper bridges the micro-macro gap in AI labor economics.** It admits a CES representation at the macro level — which means we can finally use standard elasticity-of-substitution tools to reason about aggregate AI impact, with chaining dynamics baked in. No more hand-waving about aggregation. *(Best for: LP updates, academic-practitioner conversations)*

title: The AI Agent Stack in 2026
author: Aishwarya Naresh Reganti

metadata.author: Aishwarya Naresh Reganti
metadata.title: The AI Agent Stack in 2026

sections.tldr: **The agent "stack" is no longer a stack — it's an operating system with nine layers plus two vertical rails (observability and governance) running down the sides.** The three shifts driving the reorganization: agents escaped the chat window (now in IDEs, Slack, browsers, approval queues), coding harnesses became their own product category (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor agent mode), and protocols (MCP, A2A) standardized the wires between agents. The most consequential finding: **governance is now the layer that decides enterprise procurement, not the model choice.**
sections.whats_new:
**The "stack" → "operating system" metaphor shift is the central insight.** A stack implies one direction of dependency: build on top of what's below. The actual shape in 2026 has a surface layer (human-agent interfaces), a core (runtime + protocols + tools), a middle (knowledge + memory), a foundation (models), and two vertical rails (observability/evals, governance/security) that touch every other layer. The vertical rails are the most important addition — they didn't exist as distinct layers a year ago.

**The runtime layer commoditized faster than expected.** Picking a runtime (LangGraph, OpenAI Agents SDK, Google ADK, CrewAI, etc.) was the most consequential agent decision in 2025. In 2026, it's a fit-for-stack preference, not a strategic bet. The consequential decision has moved up to Layer 1 (which harness/surface) and down to the vertical rails (governance, observability).

**Memory and knowledge are now distinct layers.** In 2025, they were conflated. Knowledge pulls external information in (RAG, vector retrieval). Memory holds what the agent itself produces across steps, sessions, and users. The convergence direction: a single context layer that decides when to vector-retrieve vs. when to recall from agent memory, with that decision pulled out of application code.
sections.counterintuitive_claims:
**The model question is "usually settled in the first meeting" for enterprise deals — governance takes the rest of the evaluation.** Every enterprise audit Reganti runs "spends most of its time on [the governance] layer." This inverts the 2024-era assumption that model capability was the binding constraint for enterprise adoption. The binding constraint is now: can the agent act without a human reviewing each step, and if so, who overrides it, what gets recorded, and what's the audit trail?

**Coding harnesses are the new IDEs, not the new frameworks.** Claude Code, Codex, Cursor agent mode, and Replit Agent ship the entire agent loop fused into the surface. The job is "picking the right harness for your workload, the same way you would pick an IDE." This is a product-category claim, not just a technical observation — it implies these harnesses will consolidate the way IDEs consolidated (VS Code won, with 2-3 niche alternatives surviving).
sections.technical_insights:
**The nine-layer model with two vertical rails is a useful reference architecture:**

| Layer | Role | Key Tools (2026) |
|-------|------|------------------|
| 1. Interface/Harnesses | Where humans meet agents | Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Slack agents, browser agents |
| 2. Runtimes | Agent loop execution | LangGraph, OpenAI Agents SDK, Google ADK, CrewAI |
| 3. Protocols | Inter-agent wiring | MCP, A2A, AG-UI |
| 4. Tools/Sandboxes | Agent action surfaces | E2B, Modal, Browserbase, Composio |
| 5. Knowledge/Retrieval | External context | Pinecone, Weaviate, Glean, LlamaIndex |
| 6. Memory/State | Agent-produced context | Zep, Letta, Mem0, Temporal |
| 7. Models/Inference | Foundation intelligence | OpenAI, Anthropic, Groq, vLLM, LiteLLM |
| 8. (Rail) Observability | Watching every layer | LangSmith, Langfuse, Braintrust, OpenTelemetry |
| 9. (Rail) Governance | Control + audit | Auth0 FGA, Lakera, OPA, human-in-the-loop queues |

**MCP ships in every major harness now.** Publishing an MCP server "is starting to take the place of writing a custom integration for every tool." A2A is in production at some teams. This is the standardization event that enables the rest of the stack to modularize — once the wires are standard, each layer can evolve independently.
sections.steelman: **This is the clearest practitioner's map of the agent infrastructure landscape published in 2026.** The nine-layer model gives enterprise teams a vocabulary for decomposing their agent architecture decisions, and the "vertical rails" framing correctly elevates governance and observability from afterthoughts to first-class architectural concerns. The harness-consolidation prediction (6-7 down to 2-3 over the next few quarters) is directionally correct and actionable for teams making tooling bets today.
sections.steelman_rebuttal:
**The OS metaphor may be too generous.** An operating system implies stability, standardization, and interoperability across the full layer set. The agent "OS" in 2026 is more like the Unix wars of the 1980s — multiple competing standards at every layer, with integration burden still falling on the developer. The MCP/A2A standardization is real but young; most production agent deployments still involve significant custom glue.

**The piece is deliberately neutral on which tools win.** This is a survey, not an analysis with a thesis about competitive dynamics. The most interesting strategic question — which layer captures the most value, and therefore which companies will dominate? — is left unanswered. Reganti's enterprise consulting practice benefits from neutrality, but an investor wants to know: is it Layer 1 (harnesses), Layer 7 (model providers), or Layer 9 (governance) that captures the margin?
sections.second_order_implications:
